note: Kural 725 says to learn by the proper path so as to answer without fear in the assembly; Nanmanikkadigai says the learned man crosses the deep of the assembly.
teaches: The couplet gives the purpose of learning as fearless reply; the verse calls the assembly a deep like the sea and a battle line, which shows why that fear is real.
list_adds: It ranks the learned man's crossing of the assembly with the sailor's sea, the horseman's army and the ascetic's penance, so speaking before an assembly is made as perilous as war or the sea.

note: Pattinathar says not to talk of எச்சில் and of fit and unfit, since people do not know where the impurity lies; Innaa 2 counts animals entering a brahmin's house as a pain, on the reading that the pain is ritual defilement.
teaches: The Innaa locates defilement in what crosses a brahmin's threshold, while Pattinathar denies that impurity sits in outward things at all, so the pair shows the purity code and its later Siddha rejection.

note: 75 says pleasure comes easily to those who embrace hardship; 76, reversing the same two words, says pain comes easily to those who crave pleasure.
teaches: Placed side by side the two lines make one law from two sides: desire turns its object into its opposite, so the way to pleasure runs through accepted pain and the chase of pleasure ends in pain.

note: Kural 828 says a weapon hides in an enemy's folded hands; Thirikadugam calls the bowing of hardened enemies a mire.
teaches: The couplet names what the homage hides, a weapon, and the verse what it does to the one who trusts it: he sinks.
list_adds: It puts an enemy's homage beside a courtesan's sweet words, so political and sexual flattery are reckoned one kind of trap.

note: Kural 30 says those called அந்தணர் are the virtuous, kind to every creature; Nanmanikkadigai names striving always after good as the mind of the அந்தணர்.
teaches: The Kural derives the name from the conduct; the quatrain lists the அந்தணர் with women and kings as a station with its proper striving, so read together they show the word moving between a status and a virtue.
list_adds: It puts the அந்தணர் in a row of stations, each with its own work, which turns the Kural's definition into a duty of a group.

note: Thirikadugam 28 names the man who sits craving what he does not have (இல்லது காமுற்று இருப்பான்) as one who pounds husk; the line calls unattainable desire the worst desire.
teaches: Thirikadugam gives the image of the wasted labour and the line gives the verdict, so the pair says why futile wanting is worst: it spends effort with nothing to show.

note: Kural 134 says a forgotten Veda can be relearned but a brahmin's birth is ruined when conduct fails; Iniyavai 7 names brahmins' keeping of the Veda as very sweet.
teaches: The verse praises the recitation the couplet treats as recoverable, and the couplet ranks conduct above it, so a reader sees the Kural demoting the very possession the later list holds up as the brahmin's excellence.
list_adds: Its own third item puts restraint above even a father, so within the list conduct also outranks the ties of birth, which brings it closer to the couplet than its first item suggests.

note: Kural 1159 says fire burns only when touched, but love burns when one moves away; Nanmanikkadigai says entering fire is better than parting from those one is bound to.
teaches: Both weigh separation against fire and find separation the worse, the couplet in a lover's voice and the verse as a general rule of attachment.
list_adds: It carries the lover's comparison into a list of plain preferences, so parting from one's own becomes a general loss, not only love's.

note: Kural 104 says those who know the fruit of a kindness count a millet's worth as a palm; Iniyavai calls living with the fruit of a kindness weighed very sweet.
teaches: The couplet says how to weigh a kindness and the verse says living by that weighing is a pleasure, so the pair shows gratitude as a habit of measuring that becomes a way of life.
list_adds: It joins gratitude to honest speech in the assembly and keeping a deposit, so the three become one virtue of rendering to each what is owed.

note: Kural 98 says sweet speech free of pettiness brings joy here and hereafter; the verse runs sweet speech through kinship and grace to release.
teaches: The Kural promises joy in two worlds; the verse names the mechanism, speech producing grace and grace producing release, and sets harsh speech's enmity beside it.
list_adds: Its items are links in a chain rather than peers, so the list becomes a ladder from manners to release, a sequence the couplet does not draw.

note: Akananuru 60 calls the mother who will guard the girl அறன்இல் யாய்; 336 calls the mother who reared the girl's beauty அறன்இலன் and பண்புஇல் தாய்.
teaches: Both poems blame the mother with the same word, but the akam friend blames her for guarding the girl too closely and the puram poet for rearing a beauty that draws war, which shows that the girl's beauty, a private matter in akam, becomes a public danger in the kaanchi poems.

note: The Kural names desire, anger and confusion as the triad whose very names must perish; the verse counts fear, craving and anger as self-consuming.
teaches: Fear takes the place of confusion: Thirikadugam treats terror as a passion of the same kind as craving and anger, burning the one who holds it, which the Kural's triad leaves out.
list_adds: It replaces confusion with fear and gives the triad an image of self-frying in one's own ghee, so the harm is shown as self-inflicted.

note: Kural 402 likens the unlearned man's wish to speak to a breastless woman's desire; Thirikadugam sets the unlearned man's eager talk beside a blind man's wife's beauty and lute-music heard by one who cannot tell its modes.
teaches: The couplet's image locates the lack in the speaker; the verse's neighbours locate it in a missing receiver, so the pair shows unlearned speech failing both for want of substance and for want of anyone able to take it.
list_adds: It groups unlearned speech with beauty unseen and music unheard, making it one kind of waste with them rather than a lone figure of incapacity.

note: Kural 247 says that world is not for those without grace as this world is not for those without wealth; verse 2 gives enjoyment to wealth and dharma to grace, then spells out grace as three refusals.
teaches: Where the couplet only assigns grace its world, the verse says what grace does here: it refuses blame, sin and tale-bearing, so grace is chiefly a restraint of deed and tongue.
list_adds: It pairs wealth and grace as the first two items and then gives grace three more, so the list tips the balance the couplet keeps even.

note: Thirikadugam joins people of a long line without learning to poverty; Nanmanikkadigai says lineage and family standing die beneath want of learning.
teaches: Thirikadugam names the outcome, poverty, and Nanmanikkadigai the death of the family's standing itself, so together they make unlearning ruin both the purse and the name of an old house.

note: Thirikadugam 55 names a friendship that does not keep a precious secret (அருமறை) as one of three spies; Elathi 15 counts not letting a precious secret slip to sweet talkers as good.
teaches: Together they show the secret's danger from both sides: Thirikadugam names the friend who leaks it as a spy, and Elathi locates the leak in the listener's trust of pleasant speech.

note: Kural 525 says one who gives and speaks sweetly is ringed by kin; Nanmanikkadigai says the throng of kin rises in the pit of sweet speech and liberality grows in the bed of plenty.
teaches: The couplet gives two causes of a crowd of kin; the verse splits them, puts each in its own soil, and pairs them with the bad crops of harsh speech and poverty.
list_adds: It makes each disposition a crop of its condition, two good and two bad, so kin-gathering is shown with its opposite, concealment from harsh speech.

note: Kural 96 says sweet speech of good things makes dharma grow; Nanmanikkadigai traces gentle speech through a mind of grace to release.
teaches: The Kural carries sweet speech to dharma in this life; the quatrain carries it through grace to வீடு, so speech becomes the first step of release.
list_adds: It makes speech the start of a chain ending in release, with harsh speech as the branch that turns the mind to blame.

note: Kural 82 says eating alone while a guest waits outside is not to be wished even if the food is ambrosia; Thirikadugam calls a day on which one ate without a guest a sickness to the strong.
teaches: The couplet rejects the guestless meal before eating; the verse counts its cost afterwards as an illness, so the same refusal is given both a motive and a symptom.
list_adds: It sets the guestless day beside the unembraced night and the morning without giving, so hospitality becomes one of three duties that together fill the householder's whole day.

note: Verse 2 says enjoyment belongs to the man with wealth and dharma to the man with grace; verse 34 repeats the pairing as cause and effect.
teaches: The book states the wealth and grace pairing twice; in verse 34 it becomes causal and the grace is qualified as melted, so the second statement tightens the first.

note: Verse 89 names the graceless heart, buried wealth and harsh speech as unmaking a birth; verse 90 names earning for giving, studying for dharma and gracious speech as the way past the dark world.
teaches: Verse 90 answers 89 item for item on wealth and speech, so the book shows the same two goods (wealth, words) as either cancelling a life or saving it, depending on use.

note: Kural 410 says others are to the learned as beasts are to people; the verse says those who love the learned are like the learned.
teaches: The couplet draws a line between the learned and all others; the verse lets those who love the learned cross it, so the pair shows the divide is passable through devotion rather than study alone.
list_adds: It closes a list in which each group is lifted to the rank of another (poets to gods, townsfolk to kin, servers to parents), so loving the learned becomes one of several ways nearness confers rank.

note: Kural 805 tells one to read a friend's hurtful act as folly or intimacy; Nanmanikkadigai says friends, even angry, do nothing that makes one tremble.
teaches: The couplet expects friends to wound and supplies a charitable reading, while the verse sets a limit no anger crosses, so the pair marks how far a friend's hurt may go.
list_adds: It ranks the friend with the elephant and the beaten child as bonds that hold under strain, against the enemy who never stays, a contrast the couplet lacks.

note: Kural 1057 tells of the seeker's joy at givers who do not scorn; Thirikadugam gives lasting fame to the man who does not scorn those who seek him.
teaches: The same courtesy pays both parties: the seeker gets inner joy and the giver lasting renown.
list_adds: It turns the seeker's joy into the giver's renown and ranks the courtesy with vigilance and freedom from envy.

note: Both verses list works for others' use of water, land and shelter; 62 promises great enjoyment, 65 heaven.
teaches: Together they mark a scale of public works and fruits: water, shade and halls bring enjoyment, while tanks, roads and wells bring heaven itself.

note: Innaa Narpathu 39 calls liberality in a man who has nothing to give painful; verse 11 calls the generosity of a man without food laughable.
teaches: The two name the same thing from two sides: painful to the would-be giver and laughable to the onlooker, so empty generosity fails both inwardly and in public.

note: Kural 911 says the sweet words of women who want wealth, not love, bring harm; Thirikadugam names a courtesan's sweet speech a sinking mire.
teaches: Kural names the harm; the verse names the mechanism, a pleasing surface over a hook, and its effect, a slow sinking rather than a blow.
list_adds: It groups the courtesan's speech with bait on a hook and an enemy's bowing, so it becomes one of three lures whose sweetness hides the danger.

note: Kural 657 sets the utter poverty of the worthy above wealth won under blame; Muthumozhikkanchi 31 sets the wealth of the blameworthy level with poverty.
teaches: The couplet ranks clean poverty above tainted wealth, while the line only levels them, and holding both shows a scale with two steps: tainted wealth is already worth no more than want, and the worthy man's want is worth more still.
list_adds: It makes tainted wealth one of ten things measured against a plain lack (hunger, solitude, refusal), so blame is shown to empty wealth of what wealth is for, not merely to rank below virtue.

note: Kural 686 names the envoy as learned, fearless of hostile eyes, persuasive and knowing the time; Elathi 26 has the same four and adds a tested beauty of mind and fame known to the world.
teaches: The pair shows the envoy's qualities carried from the Kural into a later list that makes reputation itself a qualification, so the envoy is chosen partly for being known.
list_adds: It sets world-known fame as a sixth excellence beside the Kural's four, ranking renown with skill as something an envoy must already have.

note: Naladiyar 135 says learning has no shore and life is short, so the wise choose what to learn; Sirupanchamoolam 30 says no one has learned the whole of the treatises, and no one knows all or nothing.
teaches: The quatrain draws from the boundlessness of learning a method of choosing; the verse draws from the same limit a judgment of persons: no one is complete in knowledge or virtue, and no one wholly lacks knowledge either.
list_adds: It sets the limit of learning beside matching limits on knowing, not knowing and faultlessness, so the shoreless field becomes one case of a rule that no person is complete either way.

note: Kural 542 says the people live looking to the king's sceptre as the world looks to rain; Thirikadugam names people who live in awe of the sceptre as a support of the king.
teaches: The sceptre has two faces to the people, hope in the Kural and fear in Thirikadugam, and the verse counts that fear as an asset of rule.
list_adds: It makes the subjects' awe of the rod one of three things a king keeps, with a minister and a guard.

note: 396 praises Ezhiniyathan of Vattaru, whose land has the toddy-drinking Kosar; Akananuru 216 names Athan Ezhini, lord of Selli, among whose people the young Kosar make garlands, and compares the parathai's pain to the elephant his spear pierced.
teaches: If the two Ezhinis are one chief (both are named with the Kosar), akam remembers him by a war wound inflicted on an elephant, used as a courtesan's image of suffering, while puram remembers him as feeder of the kinless, showing how a patron's two reputations were divided between the genres.

note: Kural 915 says those of refined understanding do not plunge into the charms of common women; Thirikadugam says the learned do not eat from such a woman's hand.
teaches: The Kural's avoidance is of her body; the verse's is of her food, so the learned man's refusal reaches even to accepting maintenance from her.
list_adds: It groups her with the arrogant petty man and the robber of a charity, so the bar falls on all who live by a wrong means, not on sex alone.

note: Iniyavai 32 names not living under a king without care for his people as foremost sweet; Innaa 3 names living under fierce kings of bent sceptre as painful.
teaches: The two books say the same thing from both sides, and the Iniyavai adds that the sweet thing is a choice (not to live there), while the Innaa's float image shows the subject who has no such choice.

note: Kural 959 says a person's words show the lineage he was born in, as a sprout shows the soil; Nanmanikkadigai asks who can know the family a good woman is born in.
teaches: On the plain reading the couplet treats the person as evidence of the family, while the verse denies that inference: goodness, like agil from the spurge, does not reveal its stock.
list_adds: Its three images of precious things from unlikely sources make the point by pattern: if agil comes from the kalli, the source cannot be read from the product.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 253-255 (நெடும்பெருஞ் சிமையத்து நீலப் பைஞ்சுனை ... அறுவர் பயந்த) and Paripadal 5.48-49 (இமயத்து நீலப் பைஞ் சுனைப் பயந்தோர்) set the birth in the same blue pool and give him six mothers.
teaches: Both poems use நீலப் பைஞ்சுனை and the six who bore him, but only the Paripadal says who the six were and why their chastity stayed whole, so the guide poem's single epithet is seen to presuppose a full birth story its hearers already knew.

note: Verse 38 makes swelling anger part of an army that breaks wealth; verse 40 makes the strength that wears anger thin the work of the wise.
teaches: The book measures anger by quantity, swelling or thinning, and ties the first to lost wealth and the second to old wisdom.

note: Kural 726 asks what use treatises are to those who fear the subtle assembly; Iniyavai 12 calls sweet the learning of one who does not fear the clamorous assembly.
teaches: The couplet denies the fearful scholar the worth of his books; the verse grants the fearless one sweetness, so the pair shows courage before the assembly as the condition on which learning pays.
list_adds: It sets fearless learning between a healthy child and lasting wealth, so learning appears as one of the household's goods kept safe from its typical failure.

note: Thirikadugam 37 says the extent of friendship shows in backbiting; the line says a good friendship shows in help.
teaches: The two give friendship a positive and a negative test, help given and slander withheld, so neither alone measures it.

note: Verse 9 calls virtue one's own ornament for the world one goes to; verse 15 says that if one wants what goes along with oneself, one should do virtue.
teaches: Within the book virtue is twice the one thing that crosses death, once as an ornament worn and once as a companion that goes along.

note: Both honour the feet of one who walked on the flower: மலர்மிசை ஏகினான் in the Kural, தண்டாமரைமேல் நடந்தான் in the Neelakesi.
teaches: An avowedly Jain poet uses the flower-walking epithet for his god, so the Kural's disputed epithet was current in Jain praise and not only open to other readings.

note: Innaa Narpathu 25 opens with seeing a friend's troubles as painful; verse 13 opens with distress among friends as painful.
teaches: Both works put a friend's distress first among painful things, but Sirupanchamoolam pairs it with not giving, so the pain is also a call to help.

note: Naladiyar 2 says wealth turns like a cart wheel and urges sharing its food at once; the verse says no one has passed through prosperity without ruin.
teaches: The quatrain draws a counsel of giving from wealth's turning and the verse draws none, so set together they show the same observation used once as an argument and once as a bare fact.
list_adds: It compresses the impermanence of life, strength, youth and wealth into four negations in one verse, where the Naladiyar gives them separate chapters.

note: Kural 799 says friendship with those who desert one in ruin burns the heart even at death; the Innaa verse closes its run of poverty's pains with the friendship of those who abandon one at the time of ruin.
teaches: The Kural measures the desertion by the burn it leaves; the Innaa verse shows it as the last support lost, after the wish to give, the rich city and others' doors have already hurt.
list_adds: It places the desertion at the end of a falling householder's sequence, so betrayal is the last stage of poverty, not a separate fault.

note: In 200 Kapilar offers Pari's daughters to Vichikko as a suppliant and brahmin; in 201 he offers them to Irungovel as their father's friend, naming himself அந்தணன், புலவன்.
teaches: Read together, Kapilar's two offers show him grounding the same gift in different claims, his standing as suppliant and brahmin in 200 and his friendship with their father in 201, so the reader sees how a bard, not a kinsman, asserted the right to give a dead patron's daughters.

note: Kural 431 says the prosperity of those without arrogance, anger and smallness is dignified; Thirikadugam names arrogance, anger and the smallness of coveting as an army that breaks wealth.
teaches: The same triad is the condition of wealth's dignity when absent and the force that destroys wealth when present.
list_adds: It turns the couplet's three absent faults into one hostile army and defines the third, smallness, as coveting many things.

note: Verse 11 says one must always let go of one's anger; verse 15 says one who wants to win should give up anger.
teaches: The two verses together give the rule and its reason: anger is let go not only as a duty but because giving it up is how one wins.

note: Naladiyar 53 counts goods that fail (home, youth, beauty, repute, wealth, strength) as the reason to renounce; Elathi 21 counts the same failing goods together with what arrives, disease and old age.
teaches: Held together, the two show that the case for release can be argued from loss alone or from loss and arrival, and Elathi's version gives the body's afflictions equal weight with the goods that slip away.
list_adds: It pairs what leaves with what comes in one list of five, so the argument moves from fading goods to arriving afflictions, which the quatrain does not count.

note: Innaa Narpathu 27, item 3, calls beauty in those without means painful; the line calls ornament on an aged body poor.
teaches: One list makes beauty depend on wealth and the other makes adornment depend on youth, so together they show that beauty in these works is never good alone and fails when either support is gone.

note: Iniyavai Narpathu 23 calls giving gold with cows to brahmins foremost sweet; verse 49 names gold and herds among great gifts and sets with them food with ghee for great ascetics.
teaches: The same gifts of gold and cattle are aimed at brahmins in Iniyavai and joined to a meal for ascetics in Elathi, showing the two codes differ on who is the worthy recipient.

note: Kural 288 says deceit stands in the heart of those who know stealth; Nanmanikkadigai says the thief knows the misery of concealment.
teaches: The Kural shows deceit settled in the thief; the quatrain shows it as his torment, which only he knows, so the thief is both the home and the sufferer of his concealment.
list_adds: It sets the thief's misery among sufferings known only from inside, the drunkard's, the bird's and the many-wived man's.

note: Kural 70 says the son's help to his father is that people ask what penance his father did; the verse says a son tells of his father's goodness.
teaches: The couplet makes the praise a debt the son repays; the verse states it as a fact of inference, so read together the son repays his father by being the evidence others read.
list_adds: It places the son among natural signs (the face, the field, the sky), so the father's repute is shown to be inferred as surely as rain is from cloud.

note: Kural 247 says this world is not for those without wealth as the other is not for those without அருள்; Nanmanikkadigai says the way of virtue is born of அருள் and everything is born of wealth.
teaches: The same pair of அருள் and பொருள் appears in both, but the verse turns the couplet's two worlds into two sources: one of virtue, one of everything else.
list_adds: It sets the pair after the gem from stone and delight from the beloved's word, and closes on wealth as the source of all, which makes the couplet's balance end in wealth's favour.

note: Kural 85 asks whether the field of a man who feeds guests and eats the leftovers even needs sowing; in 333 the wife has fed guests until she must pound the seed millet itself.
teaches: The Kural's rhetorical promise that the hospitable house needs no seed is played out literally in the poem, where hospitality has eaten the seed, so the pair shows the real cost that the maxim's confidence passes over.

note: Kural 127 says to guard the tongue above all, or suffer through faulty words; verse 10 says abuse is death to the tongue as its own eggs are to the spider.
teaches: The couplet warns of the speaker's suffering; the verse's animals show why: the harm grows from the speaker's own body, as a creature is killed by its own young or horns.
list_adds: It sets abusive speech last after four creatures killed by their own parts or offspring, so the tongue's ruin is shown as self-made.

note: Thirikadugam 18 names old age and great disease as two separate things to fear more than thieves; the Innaa line joins them as one pain, sickness that comes once one is old.
teaches: Read together, the two dreads compound: the Innaa line shows disease and age not as two risks but as one in which each makes the other worse.

note: Kural 650 likens those who cannot expound what they have learned to flowers in bloom without scent; Innaa 7 counts the beauty of a scentless flower as painful.
teaches: The Innaa places the scentless flower directly beside the speech of one who cannot reply, which is the Kural's comparison spelled out as two counted pains.
list_adds: It turns the Kural's simile into two items, a scentless flower and a speaker who cannot answer, and adds weapon and daring as two more things without their ground.

note: Kural 930 asks whether the drinker, seeing another drunk, does not think of the lapse (சோர்வு) of his own drinking; the line says a drinker without lapse is false.
teaches: The couplet hopes the drinker may see his own lapse in another man, and the line states that lapse as certain, so the pair shows the Kural's appeal resting on a fact the drinker refuses: that his lapse is not occasional but sure.
list_adds: It makes the drinker's lapse one of ten impossibilities with the greedy judge and the impure ascetic, a type-judgement on a kind of man rather than the couplet's question put to one drinker.

note: Kural 60 calls a home's excellence its blessing and good children its ornament; Nanmanikkadigai makes the wife the light of the house, sons hers, learning theirs and understanding learning's.
teaches: The Kural stops at children; the quatrain continues the chain to learning and understanding, so the household's worth is finally measured by knowledge.
list_adds: It turns the couplet's pair into a chain of four lights, each lit by the next.

note: Kural 1253 has a woman say her desire breaks out like a sneeze though she would hide it; Nanmanikkadigai says desire goes where it was going though obstructed.
teaches: The Kural gives the experience in a lover's voice; the quatrain states it as a law beside a hidden killing, which shows the ethics books treating akam's confession as a fact about desire in general.
list_adds: It turns a lover's admission into one of four laws of what cannot be stopped or hidden, placed next to murder.

note: Kural 663 says the strength of a deed is that it is revealed only at its end, and that it brings trouble if it comes out midway; Innaa 5 counts a deed done without secrecy (மறை) as painful.
teaches: The couplet explains when secrecy matters (until the end), and the Innaa supplies the images for an exposed undertaking: unfenced cane and a leaking roof.
list_adds: It pairs the open deed with rule without justice and gives both two images of unguarded keeping, so secrecy is grouped with protection rather than with cunning.

note: Both lines set an aged body against a good of youth: desire in an old woman (82), ornament on an old man (86).
teaches: The ten applies the same verdict to both sexes, desire for the woman and adornment for the man, so the pairing shows how the period divided what each was faulted for in age.

note: Kural 85 asks whether the field of one who feeds guests and eats the leftovers even needs sowing; the verse says hospitality thrives when vessels are spread and guests fed.
teaches: The couplet claims the host's field prospers without seed; the verse supplies the mechanism by analogy, since fire grows by the ghee it consumes and the cow by the milk the calf takes, so the host's outflow is itself what increases.
list_adds: It sets guest-feeding beside fire fed with ghee, gods given praise and a cow let to its calf, so hospitality becomes one case of a general law that things thrive by being drawn on.

note: Kural 376 says what is one's lot will not stay though guarded nor go though thrown away; the verse says the same of life itself at birth and at death.
teaches: The couplet's law of lot, said of possessions, is extended to the life that holds them: being born and dying are the first goods one cannot keep or refuse.
list_adds: It sets life's coming and going beside Fortune's swelling and ruin's vanishing, so birth, death, gain and loss become one set of things outside command.

note: Kural 260 says all beings worship the one who neither kills nor eats flesh; verse 42 widens the refusal to consenting to killing and to the company of killers, and rewards it with kingship on a killing elephant.
teaches: The couplet's reward is the reverence of the spared creatures; the verse pays the same abstention with conquest, showing a Jain work content to reward non-killing with a war elephant.
list_adds: It splits the couplet's one refusal into three degrees of complicity (killing, consenting, keeping killers' company) and then joins them to feeding, so non-killing is graded by distance from the act.

note: Kural 816 says being a stranger to the wise is ten million times better than close friendship with a fool; the line counts a fool's support as no better than solitude.
teaches: The couplet sinks the fool's friendship far below even estrangement from the wise, while the line only equates it with having no one, and the pair shows the range of the same judgement from mild to extreme.
list_adds: It measures the fool's company against solitude, the measure the same ten uses for unshared pleasure in 40, so a bad companion and a joy kept to oneself are shown to leave a person equally alone.

note: Kural 108 says it is not good to forget a good done and good to forget at once what is not good; Nanmanikkadigai asks one not to be embittered by harsh acts and to hold the good done as good.
teaches: Both pair forgetting injury with remembering help; the verse goes on to one's own anger and ruinous deeds, so the inward work follows the outward.
list_adds: It follows the couplet's pair with two rules about oneself (letting anger go, destroying the self-ruining deed), so forgiving others is set beside disciplining oneself.

note: The Naladiyar prizes salt born in barren ground above rice from fertile fields and puts the learned of low origin in the highest place; Nanmanikkadigai says agil, orpiment and pearls come from mean sources and no one knows the family a good woman is born in.
teaches: Both books use a precious thing from a poor source to cut worth loose from birth, the Naladiyar for the learned man and Nanmanikkadigai for the good woman.
list_adds: Its three natural instances (spurge, deer's belly, sea) build to a question rather than a command, so the reader is left unable to trace goodness to a family.

note: Kural 920 names double-minded women, liquor and dice as the company of those Fortune has left; Thirikadugam names the courtesan, the gambler and the money-dealer themselves as sinking in craving.
teaches: The couplet ruins the customer of these trades; the verse drowns the traders too, so vice is shown to consume both sides of the bargain.
list_adds: It replaces liquor with the money-dealer, so all three are people who live by others' wants and are judged by their own greed rather than by the harm they do.

note: Kural 1034 says farmers see many kings' umbrellas under their own; verse 45 traces a king's rise to the rising of the field's water and paddy.
teaches: The couplet's claim that farming underwrites kingship is given its mechanism: the height of the crown is measured from the height of the field bank.
list_adds: It sets out each link from field to throne in order, where the couplet states only the end result.

note: The Kural says those who resolve to live by a spotless lineage do nothing unworthy through deceit; the verse says three positive habits are found only in those of spotless family.
teaches: The Kural shows lineage as a restraint on wrongdoing; Thirikadugam shows it as a source of positive conduct, so a pure line both forbids and produces.
list_adds: It names three habits of a good family, avoiding the base, constancy in friendship and guarding against blame, where the couplet gives one restraint.

note: Kural 401 likens holding an assembly without full learning to a board game with no board; the Innaa line names the same act, கல்லாதான் கோட்டி கொளல், as painful.
teaches: The Innaa verse adds exposure to the Kural's emptiness: paired with the unlearned man on a prancing horse, holding court becomes a display that can throw him.
list_adds: It frames the verse with the unlearned man, mounting a spirited horse at the start and holding court at the end, two displays he cannot carry.

note: Saying 39 reckons disgraced old age no better than anger; saying 50 says age that does not know rebirth is not old age.
teaches: The book judges old age twice and never by years: once by the disgrace it carries, once by what it knows of the birth to come, so elderhood is a moral and a spiritual standing.

note: Kural 90 says a guest wilts when the host's face changes; the verse says a guest dies before those without the wish to receive.
teaches: The couplet locates the guest's wilting in a visible face, the verse in the host's absent desire, so the face is shown as the sign of a want of welcome that kills even before it shows.
list_adds: It sets the guest beside gratitude, song and sulk, so hospitality is a gift that needs a fit receiver, like art.

note: Kural 969 likens those who die when honour is touched to the yak that dies once its hair is lost; Iniyavai 13 calls not living after honour is lost foremost sweet.
teaches: The couplet treats the act as a matter of nature, the verse as a pleasure chosen first, so the pair shows dying for honour justified both as instinct and as preference.
list_adds: It ranks death before dishonour ahead of restrained living and flawless wealth, so honour is set above the two things that would make a long life comfortable.

note: Kural 630 says that one who takes what hurts as pleasure gains a distinction his enemies admire; the line says pleasure comes easily to those who take on hardship.
teaches: The couplet pays the man who embraces hardship in esteem, the line pays him in pleasure itself, so together they show the old claim that welcomed toil returns both honour and the very joy that was given up.
list_adds: Paired in the ten with its mirror line 76, it turns the couplet's single reward into one half of a reversal law: what is chased flees and its opposite arrives, a symmetry the couplet does not draw.

note: Kural 834 calls the greatest fool one who studies, understands and teaches but does not restrain himself; Elathi 14 says that for one who keeps six restraints the books are beside the point.
teaches: Held together the two state the same principle from opposite ends: learning without restraint is folly, and restraint without learning already has what the books are for.
list_adds: It names the restraints (no lying, no flesh, no toddy, no evil, no base company, no reviling) that 834 leaves as a single self-restraint, and puts flesh and toddy among them.

note: Kural 223 says not uttering the misery of 'I have nothing' and giving belong only to the well-born; the verse says saying 'nothing' to beggars is hard for anyone.
teaches: The couplet makes the refusal to refuse a mark of birth, the verse makes the reluctance to refuse universal, so lineage is no longer needed to explain it.
list_adds: It sets refusing beggars among difficulties tied to kinds of person (the eminent, the kin-born, the stingy) and frees this last one from any kind.

note: Naladiyar 111 says saying 'I have none' of what one cannot give is no disgrace and is the way of the world; the verse says saying 'nothing' to beggars is hard for anyone.
teaches: The quatrain frees refusal from blame and the verse says it is still hard to say, so together they separate guilt from difficulty: refusal is no fault but costs everyone.
list_adds: It ranks refusal as the hardest of four hard things, the only one hard for anyone, whereas the quatrain only judges it.

note: Iniyavai 37 calls knowing youth as old age sweet; Innaa 27 calls entering old age within youth painful. They do not disagree: one is foresight of age, the other its untimely arrival or imitation.
teaches: Read together they keep the counsel to remember age while young from turning into premature decline, the sweet awareness and the painful condition being kept apart.

note: 394: Kuttuvan gives a killer elephant, and when the frightened bard returns it gives a bigger one, ashamed the first seemed small; Kural 221: true giving is giving to those who have nothing.
teaches: The Kural defines a gift by the receiver's want, but Kuttuvan's elephants are sized to the giver's honour and are useless to a hungry bard, so the poem shows a royal giving that the Kural's definition would hardly count as ஈகை at all.

note: Kural 1012 says food and clothing are common to all living beings and shame is the mark of humans; the line says a life without shame is no better than hunger.
teaches: The couplet sets shame above food as what makes a person human; the line turns the same order into a verdict on the shameless man, whose full table counts for no more than an empty one.
list_adds: It measures the lack of shame in the coin of food, the very thing the couplet put aside as common to all, so the ranking is applied as a judgement on a life rather than stated as a definition.

note: Kural 304 says anger kills smile and joy and is the worst enemy; Nanmanikkadigai says before the angry everything fails to show and is ruined.
teaches: The couplet names what anger kills in the angry man; the verse widens it to everything before him, so anger blinds as well as destroys.
list_adds: It sets anger's ruin after three things that do not show before the learned, the resolved and the wrongdoer, so anger closes a list of what each kind of person cannot see.

note: Verse 85 names five subjects that make a first-rank learned man; verse 86 names five arts that make a middle-rank one.
teaches: Together they grade learning in tiers: doctrine, logic and release make the first rank, while arithmetic, music and crafts make only the middle.

note: Akananuru 54 calls Pannan of Sirukudi one who does not live for himself but belongs to others, and sets the hero's homecoming by the gooseberries of his garden; 388 tells how Pannan fed a drummer in famine.
teaches: The akam poet can use Pannan's name as a byword for living for others without explaining it, which shows that the puram reputation 388 records was common knowledge by the time an akam homecoming could borrow it as a landmark.

note: Kural 57 asks what use guarding women by confinement is and makes their own steadfastness the chief guard; Thirikadugam counts the man who neglects guarding his woman among those without right conduct.
teaches: The couplet moves a woman's guard inside her; the verse keeps an outer guarding as the husband's duty and faults him for neglecting it, so the group holds both views of where the guard lies.
list_adds: It ranks neglect of guarding a woman with courting the unfriendly and faulty speech, so it becomes a lapse of the man's own conduct, not a question of the woman's virtue.

note: Kural 395 has the learner yearn like the poor before the rich; Iniyavai goes further and calls learning sweet even if it must be had by begging.
teaches: The couplet makes the poverty a simile for the learner's humility, while the verse makes it literal, so together they show the tradition moving from 'learn as if a beggar' to 'learn even as a beggar'.
list_adds: It puts learning got by begging first among four sweet things, ahead of the assembly and the company of the great, so the list ranks learning above the dignity it costs.

note: Kural 228 asks whether hard-eyed hoarders who keep and lose do not know the joy of giving; the verse ranks those without wealth above those who have it and only guard it.
teaches: The couplet says the hoarder misses a joy; the verse goes further and ranks him below the man who has nothing, so wealth kept unused is shown to be worse than poverty, not merely less than giving.
list_adds: It frames the point as a ranking and repeats it with the poor over the hoarder, then sets forbearance over reviling in the same form, so hoarding is placed among vices of the same weight as abuse.

note: Kural 139 says those with conduct cannot speak evil even by a slip; Nanmanikkadigai says deceitful words do not appear in the mouths of the learned even if they die.
teaches: The Kural rules out the accident, a slip; the quatrain rules out the extremity, death, so between them neither chance nor pressure draws evil speech from the good.
list_adds: It mirrors each good mouth with a bad one, the learned and worthy against the graceless and base, so the same kinds of word are shown present and absent.

note: Kural 227 says the evil disease of hunger hardly touches one accustomed to பாத்தூண், sharing before eating; the line says பாத்தூண் comes easily to those who willingly bear a burden.
teaches: The couplet gives what the habit of shared eating protects against, the line gives what makes the habit easy, so together they show shared food as both the fruit of shouldering a charge and the guard against the hunger the miser fears.
list_adds: It traces the Kural's habit to a prior disposition to bear a load and sets it among good desires with good yields (fame, kindness, hardship), a cause the couplet does not give.

note: Kural 454 says understanding seems to be in the mind but lies in one's company; the verse says blame and fame come from company but understanding from the mind.
teaches: On the plain reading the two divide the same pair the opposite way: the Kural puts understanding in company, while Sirupanchamoolam keeps it in the mind and gives company only reputation.
list_adds: It splits the effect of company by kind, reputation (பழியும் புகழும்) against understanding (மதி), a division the couplet does not make.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 70 promises kingship to those who give to prisoners and to people keeping fasts; Elathi 35 promises rule of the earth to one who gives food to renouncers, the needy and the young.
teaches: The two Jain lists share the reward of kingship for feeding, but Sirupanchamoolam's recipients are mostly ascetics fasting by rule while Elathi's are mostly the needy, which shows the same promise attached to two different kinds of worthy receiver.

note: Kural 942 regulates the meal by digestion, eating only after the last meal is spent; Acharakkovai 20 regulates it by direction, posture, silence and worship.
teaches: The two books divide the same act between body and rite: the Kural cares when and how much one eats, the Acharakkovai how one sits and where one looks, and neither addresses the other's concern.

note: Kural 720 likens speaking before those not of one's circle to nectar spilled in a dirty yard; Innaa 10 counts reciting a song where no one grasps its meaning as painful.
teaches: The couplet locates the waste in the hearers' unfitness, and the Innaa, by setting the song beside the poor man's generosity, shows it as a gift wasted on both sides: the giver of words has no receiver, the would-be giver of goods has nothing.
list_adds: It sets the wasted recital beside a lonely dark path and the penniless man's liberality, so the song without listeners is counted among gifts that cannot arrive.

note: 37 treats Death as the overpowering thing no plea escapes; 39 calls dying easy beside the hard work of character.
teaches: Within one chapter the work views death from two sides, as the terror that drives penance and as the easy thing beside lasting virtue, and the pair shows death's weight depends on what it is measured against.

note: Verse 14 says begging rises quickly in the pit of poverty; verse 15 says one who wants pain should rise to beg.
teaches: Read together, the book gives begging both a cause and a fruit: it grows from poverty and it yields pain.

note: Kural 1014 says shame is the ornament of the worthy and without it a proud walk is a disease; verse 11 says the worth of a shameless man is laughable.
teaches: Both deny worth without shame, but the verse makes the failure social ridicule where the couplet makes it a sickness of the man himself.
list_adds: It sets shameless worth among four other claimed virtues without ground (vow, generosity, soldiering, poetry), so shame is shown as the ground the others also need.

note: Kural 300 says nothing seen as true is better than truthfulness; saying 4 sets truthfulness specifically above liberality.
teaches: The Kural's absolute claim for truth is tested against the one virtue its rival tradition prizes most, open-handed giving, and truth still wins.
list_adds: It names the rival virtue that truth outranks, liberality, where the couplet compares truth with everything at once.

note: Naladiyar 17 says youth falls like fruit, so do not desire a woman for her eyes; Kalittokai 15 says wealth can be made any day but youth cannot be brought back, so do not leave her.
teaches: From the same fact that youth passes, the moralist counsels turning from desire and the love poet counsels holding fast to it, so the two books read the brevity of youth as a reason for opposite lives.

note: Kural 664 says speaking is easy for all and doing as one said is hard; the line counts an undertaking left undone as no better than folly.
teaches: The couplet names the gap between word and deed as a difficulty, and the line names its cost to the man who leaves it open: he is counted a fool, so failure to perform becomes a matter of judgement, not only of strength.
list_adds: By measuring the broken undertaking against சிதடி, it moves the couplet's point from firmness in action to the standing of the one who fails, among other things judged as their opposites.

note: Verse 1 offers the book as rain that ends a great famine; the payiram calls the author's hand rain that ends the famine of not learning.
teaches: Together they show the famine pun is the book's own gloss on its title: the five roots cure, and the rain they bring is learning.

note: Both invocations of the group open on Vishnu's stride across the earth: Thirikadugam counts it among three deeds of the feet, Nanmanikkadigai among four deeds of the 'son'.
teaches: Set side by side, the two invocations show the counted form fitted to the god before it is fitted to conduct: each book praises him in its own number, three deeds or four.

note: Kural 575 calls kindly regard the eye's only jewel and an eye without it a wound; Nanmanikkadigai says where the gentle eye of the worthy grows dharma grows.
teaches: The Kural judges the eye by its kindness; the quatrain gives each kind of eye its harvest, and makes the hard eye a source of strength in one line and of sin in another.
list_adds: It sets the gentle eye among four eyes, two of them hard, so kindly regard is ranked against daring and cruelty rather than praised alone.

note: Kural 507 says trusting the ignorant out of fondness brings every folly; Sirupanchamoolam 39 says giving treasury, accounts and stores to men without understanding is setting a crow to guard rice.
teaches: The couplet locates the fault in the master's fondness; the verse measures the appointee (understanding that does not match his size) and shows the result as the guard eating what he guards.
list_adds: It names the particular offices of trust and closes with the crow image, where the couplet speaks only of trust in general.

note: Kural 796 calls ruin a rod that measures one's people; Nanmanikkadigai says the use of kin is known by being ruined, after the washing of gems, riding of horses and burning of gold.
teaches: Together they show ruin as an assay: the couplet names its single benefit, and the verse sets it in the craftsman's sequence of tests, where the tester pays the cost.
list_adds: It makes testing kin by ruin the last of four assays with gem, horse and gold, so the kin test is the one that burns the tester, not the thing tested.

note: Kural 302 calls anger bad where it cannot avail and worse where it can; Nanmanikkadigai bids anger be curbed where it cannot avail.
teaches: The quatrain stops where the Kural's first half stops and, after bidding pride against enemies, leaves anger where one is strong unmentioned; the Kural's second half closes that gap.
list_adds: It sets curbing anger beside a call to be proud against enemies at the right time, so the anger left out is partly licensed by the list.

note: The Kural commands making wealth as the sharpest weapon; the hero leaving for wealth that is hard to earn counts what the going costs the girl he leaves.
teaches: The Kural's bare imperative to make wealth is weighed here against a girl's quoted plea not to stay long, showing that the duty the maxim states without condition was, in akam, always paid for by someone left behind.

note: Innaa Narpathu 29 counts begetting children without understanding (அறிவறியா மக்கட் பெறல்) among painful things; the line calls the getting of children, unqualified, the greatest gain.
teaches: Read plainly, the two works give the same act opposite values, and only the qualifier about the child's understanding, which the Kural supplies, reconciles a supreme gain with a pain.

note: Thirikadugam 96 names the knowing wife, the ascetic who keeps his vow and the good king as three at whose word rain falls; the verse makes rain rest on ascetics, ascetics on the king, the king on householders.
teaches: Both books make human virtue the cause of rain, but Thirikadugam sets three causes side by side while the verse lines them up, so one gives co-equal powers and the other a chain of dependence ending in the household.

note: Kural 1097 says small words without real anger and hostile looks are the signs of those who are close while seeming distant; 100 says the one who wants love does not give up hinted speech.
teaches: The line says the lover speaks by hint and the couplet shows how hints are read, even harsh ones turned inside out, so the pair gives both the speaker's practice and the hearer's skill.
list_adds: It closes a ten of public goals and their practices with love and its indirection, so hinting stands beside justice and toil as a discipline, where the couplet treats it as a sign within the lovers' scene.

note: Kural 49 says that what is called virtue is household life; the verse ends that in the Kali age household life alone is true.
teaches: Both favour the household, but the Kural grounds it in what virtue is and the Jain verse in the corruption of the age, so one preference has a timeless and an historical ground.
list_adds: It reaches the household's primacy by eliminating a list of ascetic forms, a route the couplet does not take.

note: Kural 348 says those who wholly renounce reach the head and the rest are caught in the net; the verse says those who delight in dharma are born again and those who renounce are of heaven.
teaches: The couplet's net becomes in the verse rebirth earned by dharma itself, so even the righteous householder is among those still caught, while renunciation alone leaves.
list_adds: It sets renunciation after the rule that deeds follow their doers, so release is the end of a sequence on karma rather than a standalone praise.

note: Kural 717 says learning shines among those who can examine words; the line says learning is known by the learner's own discernment.
teaches: The Kural needs a qualified audience for learning to appear, while the line finds the proof inside the learner, in how he sees.
list_adds: By setting learning between friendship and eminence in a run of signs, it treats learning as one more inner fact read from outward evidence rather than as display before an assembly.

note: Kural 929 says giving reasons to a drunk is like searching with a torch for a man under water; the Innaa line says the business a drunkard himself speaks of is painful.
teaches: Together they close talk with the drunk in both directions: reasons cannot reach him, and his own account of affairs cannot be relied on.
list_adds: It sets the drunk's counsel beside walking on thorns and the deceitful's company, as pains that come through trusting the wrong ground.

note: Kural 1001 says one who hoards great wealth and does not eat it is as good as dead; Innaa 16 counts storing great wealth without enjoying it as painful.
teaches: The couplet judges the hoarder as already dead, and the Innaa, by setting him beside the handsome blind man, makes him one who owns a good he cannot use.
list_adds: It pairs unused wealth with unseeing beauty, so the hoard is grouped with gifts that their owner cannot enjoy rather than with failures of giving.

note: Kural 1041 says nothing is more painful than poverty except poverty itself; Nanmanikkadigai names poverty the most painful of all things.
teaches: The couplet leaves poverty incomparable, while the verse places the hand that never refuses right after it, so the extreme of want is paired with the extreme of giving.
list_adds: It makes the pain of poverty one of four superlatives and follows it with the generous hand, so the list supplies the remedy the couplet leaves out.

note: Kural 61 knows no gain like children who come to know (அறிவறிந்த); the line names the getting of children the greatest gain with no condition.
teaches: The couplet's praise hangs on a single qualifier the line drops, so the pair shows the Kural deliberately narrowing a common saying that children are the greatest gain.
list_adds: Set first in a ten of superlatives that ranks fame as the greatest legacy (58) and giving as the greatest distinction (60), the line makes offspring one of several 'nothing greater' goods, so its supremacy is one claim among rival ones rather than the couplet's single ranking.

note: 70 promises kingship to those who feed fasting ascetics; 76 makes feeding the hungry a duty even to the low who are not ascetics.
teaches: The book first rewards gifts to ascetics who fast, then widens the duty past them, so the receiver's worth governs the reward but not the obligation to feed.

note: Kural 225 ranks the strength of enduring hunger behind the strength of removing it; the verse names kinds of fasters and promises kingship to those who feed them.
teaches: The couplet ranks feeder over faster, while the verse honours both, making the faster the fit receiver and the feeder the one rewarded, so the ranking becomes a partnership.
list_adds: It names kinds of fasting (alternate days, crescent to full moon) and sets the prisoner among them, and attaches kingship as the reward, which the couplet does not.

note: Kural 484 says even the world comes to hand (கைகூடும்) if one weighs the time and acts by the place; the line says gain coming to hand (கையுறல்) for one who does not know the time is false.
teaches: The couplet makes knowing the time enough for even the greatest gain, and the line makes it necessary for any gain, so together they give timing both halves of a condition: without it nothing comes to hand, with it even the world can.
list_adds: It states as an impossibility, beside nine others, the negative half that the couplet's promise leaves unsaid, and drops the couplet's second condition of place.

note: Verse 20 lists not stealing, not gambling and not befriending the black-hearted among five abstentions; verse 27 says the friend of outsiders picks up toddy, theft and gambling.
teaches: Verse 20 puts bad company beside theft and gambling as one more abstention; verse 27 shows it as their cause, so the book's ban on bad friends is a ban on the way the other vices are learned.

note: Kural 1060 says the one who asks must not be angry; Iniyavai calls it foremost sweet that one who lives by alms does not clamour.
teaches: Both place restraint on the receiver rather than the giver, and the pair shows the ethics group laying a duty on the needy as well as on the rich.
list_adds: It moves the rule from askers in general to the one who lives by alms and joins it to calm in a borrowed lodging, so it becomes part of a renouncer's poverty.

note: Kural 541 defines justice as inquiry, no favour to anyone, holding to the ruler's part and acting after thought; the line says justice done by one who craves wealth is false.
teaches: The couplet's definition is a procedure and says nothing of the judge's appetites; the line adds a condition on the judge himself, so the pair shows that the four steps can be kept in form and still be false if greed sits behind them.
list_adds: It sets greed for wealth among ten lacks that falsify an act, so justice is judged by the character of the one who does it, not by the steps the couplet lists.

note: Naladiyar 60 says fools long for pleasure while suffering mounts, and the higher ones see the pain in each pleasure and do not cling; 98 names the unchecked pleasure-seeker as one who in effect wants pain.
teaches: The quatrain describes the wise seeing pain inside pleasure, and the line describes what follows when that is not seen, so the pair joins the renouncer's insight to the verdict it passes on the one who lacks it.
list_adds: The line compresses the quatrain's contrast of fool and sage into a single reversed formula, and its mirroring with 97 makes the point by form alone, without the quatrain's turn to renunciation.

note: Kural 83 says the life of one who tends guests daily does not fall into ruin; the verse says a family gains glory by the food it gives.
teaches: The couplet answers the fear that giving food ruins a house; the verse claims more, that it is the source of the family's distinction, so feeding is shown as both safe and the very thing that ranks a house.
list_adds: It ranks the family's food-giving with a bull's herd and a town's people, so a house's glory is made to come from those it sustains.

note: Naladiyar 20 urges keeping Death's stealth in mind and taking provisions in time; Thirikadugam names not reflecting on Death's certain coming as one of three things that lead to hell.
teaches: The quatrain makes remembering death prudent; the verse makes forgetting it a sin with a penalty, so heedlessness is turned from folly into guilt.
list_adds: It places forgetting death beside two acts against others, so an inward lapse is judged on the same scale as cruelty and concealment.

note: Purananuru 109 is Kapilar's boast during the siege of Paari's Parambu that the three kings cannot take it by force; Akananuru 78 recalls Paari with Kapilar beside him, holding out for years and driving away the kings with elephants.
teaches: The akam poem treats as settled fame what the puram poem speaks in the middle of the siege, so Paari's resistance with Kapilar had become a reference point another poet could use to praise a girl's fragrance.

note: Kural 1014 calls shame the ornament of the worthy; Nanmanikkadigai calls modesty the ornament of a woman's beauty.
teaches: The Kural gives shame to the worthy of either sex as their ornament, while the verse assigns it to women's beauty, so the pair shows the virtue narrowed into a gendered adornment.
list_adds: It puts women's modesty in a row of ornaments with paddy for land and lotus for pond, which makes the virtue something that decorates a seen beauty, where the Kural makes it a guard of conduct.

note: Kural 959 reads lineage from a person's speech; the line reads great birth from kindness.
teaches: Both read birth from a sign, but the sign moves from what is said to what is felt, so the Muthumozhikkanchi's test is harder to counterfeit.
list_adds: Set in a ten of signs, the line makes kindness the test of birth and the next line makes giving the test of kindness, a chain the couplet does not build.

items: தடமென் பணைத்தோள் தளிரிய லாரை விடமென் றுணர்தல்
நில்லாத காட்சி நிறையில் மனிதரைப் புல்லா விடுதல்

note: Kural 226 says removing the hunger of the destitute is where a man with wealth should store it; verse 53 names six kinds of destitute to be fed in the house and pays the store back as command of armies.
teaches: The couplet's metaphor of storage is made literal: the verse says what the stored wealth returns as, an army in a later life.
list_adds: It breaks the couplet's one class of the destitute into six (the indebted, unprotected, empty-handed, lame, old and young), so need is named by its causes.

note: Purananuru 195 tells grey-haired elders in useless age that Death will bind them and urges them at least to refrain from harm; saying 50 says age without knowledge of the next birth is not old age.
teaches: The puram poet shames old men by the coming of Death, while the saying denies them the name of age unless they know what follows death, so the heroic warning about the end becomes a doctrine of rebirth.

note: Kural 978 says greatness always bows and smallness adorns itself in self-admiration; the line says one who cannot bear lowliness cannot rightly seek greatness.
teaches: The couplet describes greatness as bowing once it is had, and the line makes the bearing of low estate the road to it, so together they show humility as both the way to greatness and its mark once reached.
list_adds: Paired in its ten with its own mirror (68), it turns the couplet's contrast of two characters into a test of endurance applied to both high and low estate.

note: Verse 90 names giving, study for dharma and gracious speech as the way past the dark world; verse 99 names forsaking the learned, self-will and unchecked wrongdoing as barring the good world.
teaches: Study is on one list and the abandonment of the learned on the other, so the book makes learning the hinge between the dark world and the good one.

note: 71 counts delivering a child, caring for the pregnant and taking up an infant as great virtue; 73 sets out the care of pregnancy, birth and infancy step by step.
teaches: Together the two verses make care of mother and newborn a sequence of virtues, from sheltering the pregnant to medicine for the child, which the Kural does not treat.

note: Kural 1263: she lives on, longing for the return of the man who went desiring victory with his resolve as his only companion. Kar Narpathu 7: the friend says he went to give to seekers and crush foes, and the rain will bring him back.
teaches: The couplet's woman treats his heroic aim as the rival that left her behind, while the friend names the same aim, giving and conquest, as a reason to trust he will return in the rains: one motive is a grievance in the Kural and a guarantee in the venba.

note: Innaa Narpathu 22 calls eating flesh to swell one's flesh painful before all else; verse 12 calls enjoying meat a cruel poison.
teaches: Both counted works single out meat-eating with a stronger word than their other items (முன்னின்னா, கொடுநஞ்சு), so the ranking is shared across the group.

note: Kural 86 says the host who tends the guest and watches for the next becomes a guest of the gods; Elathi 7 says the gods hasten to receive as guest one who gives sweet speech, mingling, a seat and good food without harsh words.
teaches: The couplet promises the reward and Elathi spells out the hospitality that earns it, so the pair shows the heavenly reciprocity resting on manner of speech as much as on food.
list_adds: It itemises hospitality into speech, mingling, a seat and food, with harsh words removed, a grading from word to meal that 86 does not make.

note: Kural 55 says the wife who worships her husband makes it rain at her word; Thirikadugam says the wife who crosses the bounds of the house cuts the rain off.
teaches: Together the two books give the period's belief in both directions, a chaste wife commands rain and a transgressing one stops it, so the wife's conduct is treated as a lever on the weather.
list_adds: It sets the wife's transgression beside the king's plunder and men's deceit, so her fault is ranked with misrule as a cause of drought.

note: The Kural says wealth does not stay, so do at once what stays; the verse lists giving to the needy and the path of one who considers impermanence side by side.
teaches: The Kural derives giving from impermanence as a single argument; Thirikadugam presents them as two coordinate marks of the wise, so awareness of transience is a conduct in its own right.
list_adds: It lists giving and awareness of impermanence as separate items with harmlessness, rather than deriving one from the other.

note: Naladiyar 195 says good and bad lineage are only words and that lineage is made by austerity, learning and effort; the line treats a small house of birth as a fact that pride reveals.
teaches: Read together they show two answers in one group: the Naladiyar dissolves birth rank into achievement, while the Muthumozhikkanchi keeps rank and reads it from conduct.
list_adds: Its pairing with line 11 sets great and small houses as fixed ranks with opposite marks, which is exactly the distinction the quatrain calls empty words.

note: Acharakkovai 1 names learning as one of eight seeds of ஆசாரம்; Nanmanikkadigai says ஆசாரம் is learning.
teaches: The book of ஆசாரம் makes learning one root among eight and goes on to ritual rule, while the quatrain makes learning the whole of it, so the word is defined far more narrowly and less ritually here.

note: Kural 546 says victory comes from the unbending sceptre, not the spear; verse 6 makes the unbending its beauty and gives the army elephants and the soldier courage.
teaches: The couplet sets the sceptre against force; the verse keeps both, giving force its own beauties and joining the sceptre's straightness to truthful speech by one word, கோடா.
list_adds: It gives the sceptre the same quality as unbending speech and sets it among the army's and soldiers' beauties, so justice is ranked with force instead of against it.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 28 says the fit pupil serves his teacher with love; saying 8 ranks serving the learned above learning.
teaches: One counted work names service of the teacher as the mark of a fit pupil and the other ranks it above learning itself, so the group treats reverence for the learned as prior to knowledge.

note: Kural 240 says those who live without blame are the ones who live; the verse names the means of a life the worthy bless, beginning with remembering one's birth-house.
teaches: The couplet gives the verdict of blame and fame on a life and the verse the means of earning the good verdict, so memory of lineage becomes a guard on reputation.
list_adds: It sets lineage, self-hold and awareness of others' regard as causes of the good name the couplet only judges, ending on two opposed speeches of others.

note: Purananuru 204 says giving at 'take' is high and refusing a gift is higher still (கொள்ளேன் என்றல் அதனினும் உயர்ந்தன்று); the line says no distinction exceeds giving to those who ask. The tension holds on the plain reading of the line's 'nothing greater'.
teaches: The bard's poem ranks the proud refusal of a gift above the gift, where the ethics line puts the giver at the summit, showing the puram ethic of honour placing the poet's self-respect above the patron's generosity.

note: Verse 87 calls five men dogs for lacking shame, friendship and reverence or for serving another; verse 88 names shame, friendship, the soldier and reverence as what comes easily.
teaches: The second verse answers the first word for word, so the pair shows the same qualities as failures in one man and as natural ease in their proper holders.

note: Kural 585 asks a spy to have an appearance that raises no suspicion and to let nothing spill; Thirikadugam asks him to be of a despised kind, to forget nothing he hears and to report the hidden matter fully.
teaches: The verse makes the couplet's unsuspected look specific: contempt is the cover, because people do not guard their words before the despised, and it adds the report that the couplet's silence serves.
list_adds: It pairs the disguise with memory and accurate report, so the spy's work is a sequence (hear unseen, keep, deliver) where the couplet gives only concealment.

note: Naladiyar 280 says earning, guarding, losing and ruin of wealth are all suffering; Nanmanikkadigai says those who plan to make wealth and those who guard it get no sleep.
teaches: The quatrain says wealth is suffering at every stage; the verse names the suffering as sleeplessness and gives it to the thief and the lover as well.
list_adds: It ranks the earner and guardian of wealth with the thief and the lovesick as sleepless men, so lawful wealth shares its unrest with theft and longing.

note: Kural 560 says the six-duty brahmins forget their texts when the king fails to guard; Thirikadugam sets the brahmin who has paid his debts beside the just king and orderly people as the world.
teaches: The Kural makes the brahmin's ritual learning depend on good rule; the verse makes it a coordinate pillar beside the king.
list_adds: It lists priest, king and people as three parts of one order rather than as cause and effect.

note: Purananuru 18 urges the Pandya Nedunchezhiyan to build up tanks where the land dips, for those who bind water win wealth hereafter, sole rule and fame; the verse makes tank-digging one of five works that take any doer to heaven.
teaches: The duty the Sangam poet urged on one king becomes in the ethics work a merit open to any man of means, and the promised reward narrows from rule and fame to heaven.

note: The Naladiyar says true living is never to ask even of the dearest; Nanmanikkadigai forbids only taking so that the hand of those one should not receive from is above one's own.
teaches: Against the quatrain's ban on all asking, the verse draws the line at the giver: receiving is shameful when the hand above is one that should not be.
list_adds: It sets the rule on receiving beside rules against contempt for the lowly and rage at the humble-born, so the shame of the raised hand is one of four checks on rank-pride.

note: 67 denies greatness to one who cannot bear lowliness; 68 swaps the two words and denies lowliness to one who cannot bear greatness.
teaches: Read as a pair, the two lines make the capacity to bear one's station, high or low, the single condition of moving between them, so neither ambition nor humility is genuine in one who cannot endure the other state.

note: Kural 421 calls understanding the tool that guards against ruin; Nanmanikkadigai says understanding is found standing where trouble befalls oneself.
teaches: The couplet gives understanding its use as a guard, and the verse gives the place where it is proved, one's own adversity.
list_adds: It sets understanding among things known by where they settle (water in a hollow, sin under blame, desire in a crowding), so understanding is defined by its location in trouble.

note: Both lists put killing and eating flesh beside a fault of speech: Nanmanikkadigai saying what should not be said, Sirupanchamoolam speaking evil of a girl without inquiry.
teaches: Two counted works independently join a speech fault to the code of non-killing, so harmful words are filed with harm to bodies across the group.

note: Both poems are on the death after Venni: 65 mourns the king who sat north ashamed of a back wound, and 66, addressed to the victor Karikal, says that king is better than him; both use the phrase புறப்புண் நாணி.
teaches: Read together they show the honour code reversing a battle's result: the loser's chosen death, mourned in 65 as the stopping of a whole country's life, is used in 66 to rank him above the victor, said to the victor's face.

note: Kural 969 compares men who die when honour is lost to the yak that dies when its hair is gone; Nanmanikkadigai has the asunam die at the drum and nobility die at an unworthy word.
teaches: Read together, the couplet says honour's loss kills its owner, and the verse adds that a single unfit word is enough to kill nobility, so the threat is speech, not only deed.
list_adds: It sets nobility's death beside three natural deaths (the asunam, the strong, the seeding bamboo), so the word that kills it is ranked with the drum and the bamboo's own fruit as a fatal cause.

note: 27 counts beauty in those without means as painful; 35 counts a handsome man who is a fool as painful.
teaches: The poet twice makes beauty a pain when what should go with it is missing, wealth in one verse and sense in the other, so beauty is judged by its company.

note: Kural 54 asks what is greater than a woman with the firmness of chastity; saying 7 names lineage as one of the things chastity outranks.
teaches: Where the Kural leaves chastity's superiority open-ended, the saying sets it against birth itself, so a woman's fidelity is made to count for more than the family she comes from.
list_adds: It pits chastity against lineage, one specific good of birth, a contrast the couplet does not draw.

note: Kural 395 praises those who learned yearning before the learned like the poor before the rich; saying 46 says learning without நேர்தல் is not learning.
teaches: The Kural ranks the humble learner highest; the saying goes further and denies that learning without that assent or submission is learning at all, on the reading of நேராமல் as not submitting.
list_adds: It turns the couplet's ranking into a definition and puts learning beside friendship and penance as things that exist only when entered into by consent or undertaking.

note: Kural 221 says giving to those who have nothing is true giving; the verse makes feeding the hungry a duty even when they are low and not ascetics.
teaches: The couplet defines giving by the receiver's need; the verse tests that against rank and lets need prevail over lowness and lack of austerity.
list_adds: It sets feeding the hungry among duties of impartiality and restraint of anger, and names the low receiver the couplet does not.

note: Kural 1323 asks whether any heaven equals sulking with one joined to you as water to earth; in Akananuru 26 the wife cannot sulk because her husband melted like ploughed red earth taking the rain.
teaches: The couplet makes the earth-and-water bond the reason sulking is sweet, while the poem uses the same image to end the sulk, which shows the likeness can either sustain lovers' quarrel or dissolve it, depending on who is melting.

note: Purananuru 195 tells aged worthies that the axe-bearing one will bind them, so if they cannot do good they should at least avoid harm; Sirupanchamoolam 25 sets four commands under the certainty of Death's coming.
teaches: Both rest counsel on the certainty of death, but the Sangam poem bargains down to a minimum (at least do no harm) while the ethics verse turns the same ground into four positive and negative rules and adds a reckoning after death.

note: Thirikadugam 7 names the hard learning of one who fears assemblies as a mute's dream; Nanmanikkadigai says the learned man crosses the deep of the assembly.
teaches: The same claim is put from two sides: learning that fails in the assembly is useless, and learning is what carries a man across it.

note: Kural 890 likens living with those not in accord to sharing a hut with a snake; the line calls joining with a hostile intimate poor.
teaches: The couplet stresses the danger of living beside the hostile, the line the futility of allying with them, so together they show the enemy within is both a threat and a bad bargain.
list_adds: It moves the couplet's fear into a reckoning of worth, counting such a union among things that are simply poor, which the snake image does not do.

note: Kural 510 says doubting one already trusted brings endless trouble; Nanmanikkadigai says not to pry into a task left with friends.
teaches: The couplet states the general error of doubting the trusted, and the verse turns it into a working rule about checking up on a delegated task.
list_adds: It puts non-interference with friends' work beside refusing a crore against one's conscience, so trust in friends is counted as part of one's own integrity.

note: Kural 523 says one who does not mingle with kin lives like a tank filling with no bank; Nanmanikkadigai says casting off kin is the gain of ruin.
teaches: The couplet shows the loss in an image of wealth spilling away; the verse names it ironically as ruin's prosperity, closing a list of what builds.
list_adds: It sets casting off kin after three true sources of prosperity (a good wife, uprightness, a king's good name), so the last item undoes the predicate by calling ruin a gain.

note: Kural 642 says gain and ruin both come from speech, so lapses must be guarded; Elathi 79 says death, ruin, enmity, sorrow, joy and exile all come by the tongue.
teaches: The couplet's two outcomes are spread into six, from joy to death and exile, so the pair shows speech held responsible for the whole range of a life's fortunes, not only for profit and loss.
list_adds: It splits the Kural's gain and ruin into six named fates, adding death and banishment, so the stakes of speech rise to life and country.

note: Kural 1268: let the king fight and win; let us join the house and keep the evening feast. Kar Narpathu 20: the king's work is finished, so the roads home are sweet.
teaches: The couplet is the wish spoken while the war goes on and the venba is the same man once it is granted, so read together they give the before and after of one situation, the hero held by the king's war until it ends.

note: Both verses list what Death disregards and close with a book as the remedy; 22 names the defences Death does not fear, 23 the occasions and qualities he does not look at.
teaches: Together they show the chapter's argument that no strength, wealth, virtue or auspicious time stops Death, and that the Jain answer in both is scripture, not effort or rite.

note: Kural 428 calls not fearing what should be feared folly; Nanmanikkadigai says that if one fears anything, it should be fearlessness itself.
teaches: The couplet sorts objects of fear, while the verse turns fear on the fearless disposition, so the danger moves from the thing feared to the temper of the man.
list_adds: It makes the fear of fearlessness the first of four checks on oneself, with not falling short, not swerving for wealth and trusting friends, so fear opens a short code of integrity.

note: Kural 322 calls sharing one's food and sustaining many lives the chief of all virtues; verse 44's giver, who gives white rice before eating, is reborn a king whose lot is to share and eat.
teaches: The couplet ranks sharing first among virtues; the verse makes it also the shape of the reward, so the king of the next birth is the sharer of this one on a larger scale.
list_adds: It sets sharing after truthfulness, refusing flesh, not reviling and clearing the road, so the couplet's chief virtue closes a list that joins speech, diet and public work.

note: Naladiyar 99 says never call a gift too little, for like the ascetic's bowl it fills slowly; the verse lists the pittances (a handful, begged salt, a rag) given without calling them small.
teaches: The quatrain argues from the receiver's slowly filled bowl and the verse from the poor giver's actual pittances, so the same rule on small gifts is seen from both ends of the gift.
list_adds: It names five concrete pittances, salt the giver himself begged and a torn rag among them, so the rule is tested on gifts a beggar could make.
