note: Kural 542 says the world looks to the sky and the people to the sceptre; Nanmanikkadigai keeps both and adds the infant at the breast and Death looking to the world's end.
teaches: The verse borrows the couplet's two dependencies and closes them with Death's grim watch, so the image of living by looking to a giver ends in the one watcher who takes.
list_adds: It adds the infant's dependence on milk and inverts the series with Death, so the king's sceptre is one giver among nurturers set against a taker.

note: Kural 110 says there is no escape for one who kills a good done to him; the line counts withdrawing regard after receiving as no better than cruelty.
teaches: The couplet ranks ingratitude as the sin without remedy, and the line names what it is in act: the ungrateful man, who strikes no one, is reckoned as cruel as one who does harm.
list_adds: It classes ingratitude with கொடுமை, an act of harm, where the couplet ranks it among sins by its consequence, so the list says what kind of wrong it is rather than how grave.

note: Kural 786 says friendship that smiles in the face is not friendship and friendship that smiles in the heart is; saying 45 says one whose heart does not agree is no friend.
teaches: Both deny the name of friendship by the same 'is not' form, and the saying narrows the Kural's heart-smile to consent, so the friend is one whose heart has come into agreement, not only one who feels warmth.
list_adds: It sets the false friend beside the false spouse, kinsman, learning, giving and penance, so the Kural's one test for friendship becomes a general method: each bond or practice is named by an inner condition.

note: Kural 322 crowns sharing food and sustaining life as the head of all the authors gathered; Thirikadugam crowns three things as the head of all that is heard: selective learning, unbroken sharing household life, and making wealth by effort.
teaches: Sharing food is the head in both, but Thirikadugam shares the crown with the learning that guides the giving and the earning that supplies it.
list_adds: It divides the couplet's single crown among three, adding learning and self-made wealth to the act of sharing.

note: Saying 11 says birth into a great house is known by ஈரம; saying 43 says kin-friendship without ஈரம் is no kin-friendship.
teaches: The book uses the same moistness of heart twice, as the sign of good birth and as the condition of kin's bond, so blood and lineage are both made to depend on a tenderness that birth alone does not give.

note: Both use the felling of the old punnai at Kurukkai in the war of Anni and Thithiyan: in 45 the gossip is louder than the bards' cheers that day; in 145 the foster mother curses her own hand to be cut down like that tree.
teaches: One puram event served the akam poets as a measure of two different things, public noise in one poem and deserved ruin in the other, so the war's fame had become a store of ready comparisons.

note: Kural 33 bids one do dharma as far as one can and without ceasing; Iniyavai 6 calls dharma done to the measure of one's strength foremost sweet.
teaches: The couplet sets the measure as a demand, the verse as a pleasure, so the pair shows the capacity clause working two ways: it limits what is owed and it is what makes the act sweet rather than a burden.
list_adds: It joins measured dharma to hearing good counsel and choosing worthy guards, so doing good is ranked first among the supports of a life rather than stated alone.

note: Line 11 reads great birth from kindness; line 12 reads kindness from giving.
teaches: Taken in order the two lines make a chain of evidence, so in this ten noble birth is finally proved by the act of giving.

note: Kural 1039 says land left by an owner who does not go to it sulks like a wife; verse 49 counts negligence first among five ruins of the ploughman.
teaches: The couplet's single fault of absence is set at the head of a list that adds pride, unfinished work, quarrels and a broken tie with the craftsman, so a farm fails socially as well as by neglect.
list_adds: It sets negligence among social and moral causes of ruin, where the couplet names absence alone.

note: In Mullaippattu the old women seeking an omen hear a herd girl tell the calves 'இன்னே வருகுவர் தாயர்' and take it as a sign; in Kar Narpathu 2 the lightning speaks his message, 'இன்னே வருவர் நமர்'.
teaches: The same formula of reassurance, 'they will come at once', is an overheard chance word in the idyll's omen rite and the sky's own message in the venba, so the later poem turns the ritual of listening for a sign into the season speaking for the absent man.

note: Kural 392 says numbers and letters are the two eyes of living beings; Innaa 16 sets the good looks of a man without eyes beside accounts kept by one who does not know numbers.
teaches: The Innaa places the literal blind man next to the innumerate one, which makes the Kural's metaphor into two counted pains of one kind: both are blind.
list_adds: By putting eyelessness and innumeracy side by side as items 3 and 4, the list enacts the couplet's equation of number with sight without stating it.

note: Kural 225 says the strength of the strong is enduring hunger, though it ranks below relieving others' hunger; Thirikadugam counts hunger that eats away wisdom as one of three forces that drive out good deeds.
teaches: The verse shows why enduring hunger is a strength in the couplet: hunger is an army against merit, so bearing it is holding a line, and relieving it removes the enemy itself.
list_adds: It sets hunger in one army with desire and anger, so a bodily need is ranked as a moral enemy beside two passions.

note: Kural 707 asks whether anything is as knowing as the face, which reaches first in joy or anger; the verse says nothing tells the intention beforehand as the face does.
teaches: Both make the face faster than speech, and the verse sets this speed against slower signs, scent, weighed words and the mind, so priority in time is what makes the face the best witness.
list_adds: It ranks the face above three other signs (scent, words, mind), making the couplet's claim a contest won rather than a lone assertion.

note: The Kural likens wealth in a just man's hands to a fruit tree ripening in town; the verse likens wealth in a generous man's hands to a tree hardened without hollow.
teaches: Both use a tree for the good man's wealth, but the Kural praises its fruit given to all and Thirikadugam the soundness of its wood, so the same image teaches use and durability.
list_adds: It sets wealth beside learning and a fit leader as three sound trees, ranking generosity with understanding.

note: Both verses open with laughter among friends: in 24 its good grows there, in 37 it is sweet there.
teaches: The book twice makes friendship the condition of laughter, once as growth and once as pleasure, so laughter is never praised in itself but only in company.

note: Naladiyar 279 makes a cow milked by force the image of the base giver; the verse names milking by a stuffed calf-skin as a cruelty the good refuse.
teaches: The quatrain uses forced milking only as a figure for grudging gifts; the verse shows the literal act was itself judged wrong, so the image carried moral weight before it became a figure.
list_adds: It sets the milking trick in a list that ends with killing creatures, so a small deceit on an animal is ranked with taking life, which the quatrain's figure never claims.

note: Innaa Narpathu 40 calls fierceness in a man of self-restraint painful; verse 16 says anger is good before people without worth.
teaches: The pair marks a limit: fierceness is unfitting in the restrained man in general, but Sirupanchamoolam carves out the base as the one place it serves.

note: Kural 460 says nothing brings more affliction than bad company; the verse says the bad delighting in the bad is ruin.
teaches: The couplet warns the good against bad company, the verse looks at the bad among themselves, so ruin comes not only from joining them but from the pleasure they take in each other.
list_adds: It closes a list of fitting delights (kings in elephants and horses, good men in modest women) with a delight that is ruin, so the last item undoes the pattern.

note: Kural 1060 says the asker must not be angry; 196, after naming the king's fault, blesses his sons and leaves.
teaches: The poet shows how the Kural's demand for an asker without anger can be met without silence: he names the fault plainly and still blesses, so rebuke and the absence of anger are shown to go together.

note: Kural 745 praises a fort that is hard to take, holds stored food and is easy for those inside to hold; 44 tells a besieged king that sitting secure behind shut gates and a long wall is shameful while his elephants starve and his people cry for milk and water. On the reading that both judge the king who holds out in a fort, they disagree.
teaches: The Kural values the fort as a means of holding out, while Kovur Kizhar sees the same holding out from inside, through starving beasts and infants, and calls it neither aram nor maram, so the pair shows the fort's strength and its moral cost as two views of one siege.

note: 41 denies the name of spouse to one who does not act knowing the other's nature; 42 denies the name of household life to a house whose wife is not excellent.
teaches: Read as written, the ten opens with a condition on the husband before it measures the house by the wife, so the household is made to fail from either side and not from the wife alone.

note: Kural 410 says others stand to those learned in the shining books as beasts stand to people; Thirikadugam says one who knows not a single letter is born yet unborn.
teaches: The couplet lowers the unlearned to beasts; the verse goes further and denies them birth, and sets the bar at one letter rather than at the great books.
list_adds: It sets the illiterate beside the low-born and the boaster, pairing a lack of letters with a lack of lineage as one kind of void life.

note: The Kural grants effort its wage even when the end fails; the line adds that the unfinished work itself is not censured.
teaches: The couplet secures the striver's inner reward and the line secures his standing among others, so an honest shortfall costs neither the wage nor the name.
list_adds: Set among excuses for nature, poverty and foreign custom, the shortfall becomes one of the things beyond a person's power that the ten exempts from blame, which the couplet on effort does not frame.

note: Kural 256 says no one would sell flesh if the world did not kill to eat; Thirikadugam names the man who says the killing happens without his consent as self-deceived.
teaches: The verse names the buyer's excuse in his own words, and the couplet supplies the answer: the purchase is the cause.
list_adds: It puts the eater who disclaims the killing beside the flesh-eater who claims compassion and the sacrificer, so three justifications are one kind.

note: Kural 328 says gain that comes by killing is the lowest for the worthy however great; verse 47 ends that those who know will not kill whatever they gain.
teaches: The verse takes the couplet's refusal of gain by killing and widens killing to the hope of the needy, the kin's meal, one's generosity and fame, so neglect becomes a kind of slaying.
list_adds: Its pun on கொல் puts killing a life beside killing a hope or a reputation, making non-killing a rule for social conduct as well as for life.

note: Kural 409 says the unlearned born high are worth less than the learned born low; Innaa 19 counts lack of learning in one born to a good family as painful.
teaches: Both make learning the test of birth, but the Kural overturns the ranking while the Innaa keeps it, counting the unlearned noble as a failed seed and union outside family rank as another pain.
list_adds: It sets the unlearned noble beside a seed that fails to sprout and a union without family standing, so birth is kept as the frame that learning fulfils, not one it overturns.

note: Kural 50 says one who lives on earth as life should be lived is placed among the gods; Elathi 32 says one who keeps six silences about himself and others and gives before eating is god of gods.
teaches: The pair fills the Kural's undefined 'as life should be lived' with particular restraints of speech and the act of giving, and raises the reward from a place among the gods to their head.
list_adds: It spells out the good life as six named silences, mostly about one's own birth, wealth and years, joined to giving before eating.

note: Kural 256 says that if none killed to eat, none would sell flesh; the verse divides the sin among killer, consenter, taker, cook and eater.
teaches: The couplet ties the eater to the seller by demand; the verse spreads the sin along the whole chain, so even one who only consented or only cooked is guilty.
list_adds: It names five links of the chain and makes them one guilt, where the couplet names only the eater and the seller.

note: Kural 167 says the fair goddess, grudging the envious man, shows him to her elder sister; the verse says that if the bright lady is grieved the fortune perishes.
teaches: The verse states only that her displeasure ruins, and the couplet names one thing that displeases her, envy, so the pair turns a bare warning into a cause and its effect.
list_adds: It sets the loss of fortune as the reversal of its own previous item, so the list moves from gaining to losing with one goddess at both ends.

note: Kural 265 says penance is pursued here because it gains whatever one wishes, as one wishes; 94 names one such wish, to stand firm, and says its seeker never leaves off penance.
teaches: The couplet makes penance a means to any wish at all, while the line ties it to one wish and requires it without a break, so the pair moves from penance's open promise to its continuing cost.
list_adds: It sets penance among nine other practices each tied to its own goal, so penance becomes one specialised means among learning, toil and justice rather than the universal means the couplet makes it.

note: Kural 742 names water, open ground, hill and shady forest as a fort; verse 48 names deep water, forest, saline waste, a lofty hill and the people, and makes having them the rule for crowning a king.
teaches: The fort of the couplet gains a fifth wall made of people, and its possession becomes the test for who may be made king rather than a feature of a stronghold.
list_adds: It adds the people as a fifth defence and turns the list into a qualification for kingship, which the couplet's list of terrain does not do.

note: Naladiyar 341 says the base man, though books of weighty meaning are opened for him, goes his own way like a hen scratching rubbish; the Innaa line says even an excellent book is a pain to one who does not want it.
teaches: The pair moves the loss from the learner to the teaching: the Naladiyar shows the base mind wasting the book, the Innaa line the book itself suffering a reader who does not want it.
list_adds: It sets the unwanted book beside counsel spoken to the unruly and friendship with the despised, all goods given where they do not fit.

note: Kural 148 calls not looking at another's wife great manhood and full conduct; Iniyavai 15 calls not looking after her a dignity that is very sweet.
teaches: The couplet names the restraint a heroism, the verse a pleasure, and the verse narrows the act to the backward glance, so the pair shows the restraint tested at the smallest motion of the eye.
list_adds: It sets the restraint beside rain on parched crops and elephants roaring at a king's gate, so a private abstention is ranked among the large public pleasures of the land.

note: Kural 298 divides outer purity, made by water, from inner purity, seen in truth; Thirikadugam lists bathing before meals with impartial speech and unfailing nobility as the work of the pure.
teaches: The couplet separates the two purities; the verse joins them in one list and implies that a claim to purity needs both at once.
list_adds: It counts the water-purity and two inner purities as one work without ranking them, where the couplet ranks them by kind.

note: Purananuru 219 addresses a warrior wasting his body as he sits to die, with many sitting with him; the verse counts those who sit facing north among the needy to be fed.
teaches: The act the Puram honours as heroic resolve the Jain ethics verse counts as a state of need beside age and disease, so the dying hero becomes a receiver of care.

note: Kural 251 asks how one who eats flesh to swell his own can hold to grace; the verse redefines the sweet eater as one who eats without killing.
teaches: The couplet argues against flesh-eating from grace, the verse from the word 'sweet' itself, so the claim moves from the eater's heart to the meaning of a good meal.
list_adds: It sets the non-killing eater among redefinitions of the shunned, the lonely and the pleasant, so diet is judged by the same test of conduct as social standing.

note: Kural 812 dismisses the friendship of misfits who come with gain and leave without it; the verse says friends' friendship perishes when the good changes.
teaches: The couplet blames a bad kind of friend, while the verse makes the fading of friendship with advantage a natural law, like a crop without water, so the fault may lie in friendship itself.
list_adds: It sets friendship's decay beside a crop dying without water, so the end of interested friendship reads as nature, not as a vice of some.

note: Naladiyar 13 says aged men who cling to desire in the house have no path to safety; the line calls a very old woman's desire poor.
teaches: The quatrain condemns aged desire because it bars release, and the line condemns it with no thought of release and names a woman, so the pair shows one judgement on old age held on ascetic grounds and on plain worldly fitness.
list_adds: It places the old woman's desire among ten misfits of condition (a sick man's pleasure, an old man's ornament), judging it as unfitting rather than as a danger to the soul.

note: Kural 260 says all creatures worship the one who neither kills nor eats flesh; Elathi 2 says the one who has the right to kill and does not, and is not deluded by flesh, rises above gods as well as men.
teaches: The pair shows the Jain ethics raising the stake: the Kural's worship by the spared creatures becomes rank above the gods, and the abstention counts most in the one who has the power to kill.
list_adds: It puts non-killing and refusing flesh first in a list with not tormenting, not deceiving and not swerving, so the two abstentions of 260 become the head of a five-part code rather than its whole.

note: Reading என்செயினும் with line 1, Nanmanikkadigai holds the brahmin's birth best whatever he does; Kural 134 says a brahmin's birth is ruined when his conduct fails.
teaches: On that reading the two make incompatible claims about whether conduct can forfeit a high birth, which shows the group divided on birth against conduct.
list_adds: It ranks brahmin birth alongside the mother, prosperity and youth as unequalled goods, so birth is treated as a fixed endowment like youth, not a standing to be kept.

note: Kural 856 says the life of one who finds it sweet to excel in hostility is close to failure and ruin; the line says that a hard battle comes easily to one who loves contention.
teaches: Read together they give two links of one chain: the relish for rivalry brings battle near, and the man who relishes it has ruin near, so both texts measure the quarrelsome man by what lies close at hand rather than by what he chooses.
list_adds: In a ten where each desire draws its own easy consequence, battle is set beside disease for the glutton and blame for the lecher as the natural yield of an appetite, which the couplet, inside a chapter on hostility alone, does not do.

note: Kural 262 says penance comes to those who have penance and is futile for those without it; the line says penance done by one who is not pure is false.
teaches: The couplet's condition for penance is circular, penance belongs to those who already have it, and the line names what that prior possession is, purity, so the pair turns the Kural's riddle into a stated precondition.
list_adds: In a ten that names the one lack that falsifies each act, it gives the precondition of penance a name, வாலியன், where the couplet leaves it as penance itself.

note: Kural 1308 asks what use suffering is where no lover knows of it; the line calls sulking poor where one is not cherished. Both turn on an absent beloved's care (இல்லா வழி, போற்றாவழி).
teaches: The couplet speaks of grief with no one to notice and the line of sulking with no one to appease it, so together they show that every display of hurt in love has worth only before someone who cares.
list_adds: It takes a lover's sulk out of the Kural's love book and sets it among public ills like misrule and empty anger, treating it as one more act that fails without its ground.

note: Kural 367 says that if one cuts desire fully, the deeds that do not fail come; Elathi 11 echoes it (அவாஅறுப்பின் ஆற்ற) and adds the fate of one who does not cut it.
teaches: The near-verbatim echo shows Elathi reading the couplet and supplying its other half: what 367 leaves unsaid, the failure to cut desire, is rebirth under the five senses.
list_adds: It sets the one who cuts desire beside the one who does not, so the couplet's promise becomes one branch of a choice with a stated penalty.

note: Verse 17 names lying with women and keeping house as the fruits of the unrenounced body; verse 18 says not turning to women who want him is a way out of rebirth.
teaches: The book grants the householder's body its fruits but sets the higher reward, not being born again, on giving up exactly those fruits.

note: Kural 381 names six limbs of a king (army, people, resources, ministers, allies, fort); Thirikadugam names three: a loyal army, a fort fearless of numbers, and uncountable treasure.
teaches: The Thirikadugam's king needs only the three material limbs and drops people, ministers and allies, a narrower and more martial account of what makes a king than the Kural's.
list_adds: It selects three of the six and qualifies each (loyal, fearless, uncountable), so the list sharpens the quality of each limb where the couplet only counts kinds.

note: Naladiyar 273 says the fool who neither enjoys nor gives his wealth is mocked by that wealth and by the world's compassion; Thirikadugam counts the graceless heart and the buried wealth as two separate items.
teaches: The quatrain fuses the failure of compassion and the failure to use wealth into one mockery; the verse separates them, showing the Naladiyar's single fault as two distinct ways of being unborn.
list_adds: It counts the graceless heart and the buried treasure as two items with harsh speech as a third, where the quatrain treats compassion only as the hoarder's judge.

note: Purananuru 192 opens with every town as ours and everyone our kin, as the stance of one who sees through the wise; Nanmanikkadigai says every town belongs to those with something in hand.
teaches: The heroic poem makes belonging everywhere a philosophical stance; the ethics verse observes that wealth secures the same welcome, which sets the ideal against how towns in fact receive people.

note: Elathi 12 says it is good neither to desire nor to look at the killing ground, the gaming place and the like; Elathi 62 says those of conduct do not go to dances, festivals, weddings, killing grounds or the battlefront.
teaches: Read together, the two verses show that the book's bar is on spectacle as such: 12 keeps the eye from scenes of violence, and 62 puts weddings and festivals under the same bar and names the cost of going.

note: Kural 57 asks what use guarding by confinement is and puts a woman's own steadfastness first; verse 53 names five men of her family as the ones who guard her.
teaches: Read as a claim about what keeps a woman, the couplet moves the guard inside her while the verse places it in her husband, brother, uncle, son and father, so the two disagree on where chastity is kept.
list_adds: It names the guard as five kinsmen, a list of external keepers that the couplet's single inner guard sets aside.

note: 97 says the seeker of pleasure does not shun pain; 98 reverses the terms, so the seeker of pain does not hold back from pleasure.
teaches: Taken as a pair the two lines say the same truth from both sides: pleasure and pain are tied so closely that whoever chases either is pursuing the other.

note: 227 tells Death it has cooked and eaten its seed (வித்துஅட்டு உண்டனை) in taking Valavan; 230 likens Death to a failing farmer who eats his seed (வித்து உண்டாஅங்கு) in taking Ezhini.
teaches: Two poets on different kings make the same argument through the seed image, that a slain warrior was the source of Death's future harvest of enemies, which shows that taunting Death with its own loss was a recognised move in kaiyarunilai and not one poet's conceit.

note: Kural 722 says those who make their learning go home before the learned are the learned among the learned; Iniyavai 16 calls setting out one's learning before the learned very sweet.
teaches: The couplet makes the act the test of reputation, the verse makes it a pleasure, so the pair shows the same performance valued as proof to others and as delight to oneself.
list_adds: It joins speaking before the learned to joining one's betters and giving without asking, so the list ranks learned speech first among acts of standing among superiors.

note: Kural 260 says all creatures worship the one who neither kills nor eats flesh; verse 18 says one who does not eat flesh out of craving will hardly take a body again.
teaches: The couplet's reward is honour in this world; the verse's is release from the body, so the same abstention is given a Jain soteriological fruit.
list_adds: It joins refusing meat to truth, honesty and chastity, each tested by its strongest temptation, as joint conditions of release.

note: Kural 221 says giving to those who have nothing is giving and all else is a measured return; saying 48 says what is not given in aram's way is not giving.
teaches: Both redefine giving by denying the name to gifts that look like it; the Kural fixes the test by recipient and expected return, while the saying fixes it by the road of aram and leaves its content open.
list_adds: It pairs the test of giving with a matching test of penance in the next line (அறத்தாற்றின் / திறத்தாற்றின்), so the householder's gift and the ascetic's vow are judged by one rule of right manner, which the couplet does not do.

note: Kural 642 says gain and ruin come from speech and bids one guard against its lapse; the line says a lapse in speech reveals every other lapse.
teaches: The Kural treats a slip of the tongue as a cause of loss, while the line treats it as evidence, so the guarded tongue both protects and conceals.
list_adds: Set beside line 19, it makes speech and understanding the two windows through which all other failings are seen, a pairing the couplet lacks.

note: Kural 43 names five to be tended (ancestors, gods, guests, kin and oneself); Elathi 71 names six to be fed: wayfarers, burden-bearers, the sick, kin, those of the sky and those of the other side.
teaches: Beside the Kural's five, the Elathi list drops the self and widens the circle to the stranger, the labourer, the sick and the adversary, so the household's duty is measured by need more than by bond or rite.
list_adds: It counts the sick, the porter and the adversary as equal claimants on the household's food, which the couplet's ancestral and kin-centred five do not include.

note: Verse 99 likens a house without a good woman to a ruin; verse 103 calls the wife the light of the house.
teaches: The book says the same thing from both sides, ruin without her and light with her, and 103 continues the chain to sons, learning and understanding, so her worth is the first link, not the whole.

note: Kural 92 ranks a glad face and sweet speech above giving with a glad heart; the verse joins soft words and a melting gift in one man.
teaches: The Kural separates sweet speech from giving and ranks speech higher; the verse refuses the choice and makes the soft word the manner in which the gift is given.
list_adds: It places soft speech and the melting gift side by side as the last two of five marks, after inner restraints, so speech and gift become one closing act rather than rivals.

note: Kural 1066 says even asking water for a cow is the most degrading thing for the tongue; Iniyavai calls not going about asking others to relieve one's distress foremost sweet.
teaches: The pair values not asking from both sides, as disgrace avoided and as the first of pleasures, and the verse's ஆற்றாமை widens it from asking for goods to asking for relief.
list_adds: It ranks not asking first and follows it with remembering death and holding to right speech under ruin, so refusing to beg sits among the disciplines of a man facing loss.

note: Elathi 9 says those who give food, shelter and clothing to the destitute live as learned men; Elathi 63 says those who give food, clothing, stylus and book to students live amply in this life.
teaches: The pair shows the book twice making learning or its fruit the reward of a gift, and 63 narrowing the gift to the tools of study, so that the giver shares in the learning he supplies.

note: Kural 61 prizes above all children who come to understanding (அறிவறிந்த மக்கட்பேறு); the Innaa line counts getting children without it (அறிவறியா மக்கட் பெறல்) as painful.
teaches: The Innaa line states the other branch of the Kural's condition, showing that its praise was never of children as such but of children with sense.
list_adds: It sets senseless children beside a snake charmed without knowledge and a secret in a careless ear, as power held without the knowledge to handle it.

note: The Kural explains the image the Innaa line only names: the base are like a beaten drum because they carry every secret they hear to others.
teaches: With the Kural's gloss, the drum-like talker in the Innaa list is seen as a breach of keeping, matching the wall-less gate and the fouled ford beside him.
list_adds: It sets loose talk beside a gate with no wall and a ford fouled by washing, so the talker becomes one more failed guard.

note: Purananuru 330 praises one man who, sword raised, stopped a king's army from passing him as the shore stops the sea; Iniyavai calls checking the army of great kings in the crowded battle sweet.
teaches: The Purananuru makes the stand one hero's glory, and the counted verse files it with civic zeal and tireless effort, showing heroic memory folded into a general ethic of exertion.

note: Kural 13 says that if the sky fails, hunger torments the world though it is ringed by water; Innaa 20 counts the failure of the rain's plenty as painful to a town.
teaches: The couplet speaks of the world and its hunger, and the Innaa of the town and its plenty, flanked by the koel's ill-timed call and a sluggish ox, so the failure is set in the farmer's season rather than the cosmos.
list_adds: It sets failed rain between the out-of-season koel and the weak ox, so drought is counted as one of the farming year's mistimings and lacks.

note: Purananuru 187 says a land is good only where its men are good; Nanmanikkadigai says kings gain glory by the land they rule.
teaches: The pair runs the credit in opposite directions: the Purananuru makes the land's worth depend on its people, the ethics verse makes the king's glory depend on the land, so his glory rests on men he does not make good himself.

note: Kural 227 says hunger does not touch one used to sharing his food; the verse says one who shares his food in a famine lives beyond eighty.
teaches: The couplet promises the sharer freedom from hunger; the verse puts the sharing in a famine, when it costs most, and promises long life instead.
list_adds: It ranks famine-sharing with fearless fighting and giving before eating as one road to long life, joining the householder's and the soldier's merits.

note: Kural 504 bids one weigh virtues and faults and take what predominates; Nanmanikkadigai says no one has faults that hide all virtue.
teaches: The quatrain supplies the ground for the Kural's method: since no one is pure fault, there are always virtues to weigh against the faults.
list_adds: It makes the mixed nature of people a general law beside the limits of knowledge, which is what the Kural's weighing needs.

note: Kural 211 says duty seeks no return, as the world gives nothing back to the rain; verse 51 calls it good to host guests without reckoning a return.
teaches: The couplet's principle of giving without return is carried to the guest at the door, and the verse sets it next to fasting and not eating from others' hands, so giving freely and taking nothing are one ideal.
list_adds: It pairs the host who expects no return with the man who will not eat from another's hand, so the list joins the giver's and the receiver's sides of the same refusal.

note: Kural 1151: if you are not leaving, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will still be alive. Kalittokai 5 ends: whatever day you go, on that day her life will go.
teaches: Both refuse the comfort of a promised return by tying her death to the moment of departure, and the Kalittokai shows the couplet's sharp line as the close of a full argument, after images of the emptied festival ground and the lotus out of water have prepared it.

note: Thirikadugam 12 defines the vellalan as one who does not eat while a guest waits; the verse defines him as one who owns oxen.
teaches: Both define the same birth-group name by a mark, but one by hospitality and the other by owning the plough-ox, so the period's ethics offered rival tests, conduct or possession, for who deserved the name.

note: Naladiyar 386 uses the learning of a man with understanding and bright wealth in a generous man's hands as similes for a modest woman's beauty; Thirikadugam 75 counts the same two as solid heartwood.
teaches: The same paired figures served two works with different ends: the Naladiyar borrows them to praise a woman's beauty, Thirikadugam keeps them as goods in their own right with a heartwood image.
list_adds: It treats the two figures as things in themselves, joined by a leader who knows fit unions, under one tree image.

note: Kural 260 says all creatures fold their hands to the one who neither kills nor eats flesh; Nanmanikkadigai says others' not eating flesh is the refuge of living beings.
teaches: Both speak from the side of the creatures, the couplet as their worship and the verse as their shelter, so abstaining from flesh is a protection given, not only a purity kept.
list_adds: It puts abstention beside givers as the beggar's refuge and valour as an army's, so refusing flesh is counted among the supports others depend on.

note: Kural 221 says giving to those who have nothing is the only true gift; Iniyavai 19 calls giving great wealth 'where it is fit' sweet.
teaches: The couplet makes need the test of a gift and the verse makes fitness of the recipient the test, so the pair shows two criteria in the tradition for where wealth should go.
list_adds: It places giving after making wealth without lack, and after truthfulness and humility, so giving is set as the last stage of a well-conducted life, not as an act prompted by another's need.

note: Innaa Narpathu counts living under fierce kings of bent sceptre as painful; the line says one living in such a land does not blame the king.
teaches: Read together, the pain of misrule and the silence of its subject belong to one situation: the subject suffers it and still holds his tongue, which is prudence, not approval.

note: 218 says the worthy fall to the side of the worthy; 219 tells the fasting king that many have already sat with him in his resolve.
teaches: The maxim of 218 becomes in 219 a crowd on the river island, which shows that the lament poems treat the number of those who joined the king's death as the measure of his worth.

note: Purananuru 92 is Avvai's song to Anji calling her words a child's babble he graciously hears; 352 measures the friend's sweetness against a famous bard's new tune for Anji's praise.
teaches: The praise songs for Anji, which Avvai offers modestly as babble, had become in akam a byword for sweetness, showing that puram performances were known to the love poets' audience as celebrated pieces of music.

note: Kural 55 praises the wife who does not worship a god but rises worshipping her husband; verse 42 counts worship of the deity, beside the one who brings her fortune, as part of a wife's excellence.
teaches: Read flatly, the Kural sets the husband in place of the god while this verse asks the wife to worship both, so the two works divide on whether her devotion may go beyond the house.
list_adds: It sets the deity's worship as a fifth duty beside income, kin and guests, making religion one household task among others rather than the one the husband displaces.

note: Kural 127 says whatever else one fails to guard one should guard the tongue; the verse says the tongue cuts friendship.
teaches: The couplet warns of the suffering an unguarded tongue brings to its owner; the verse names a particular loss, friendship, so the pair shows what is at stake in the couplet's general warning.
list_adds: It sets the tongue beside the fool who lets go and the resolve that fails, so speech is listed among the things that break bonds.

note: Naladiyar 371 says a harlot's love ends when the hand is empty, like a lamp without oil; Thirikadugam says the courtesan herself sinks in the sea of craving.
teaches: The quatrain explains why her love fails (it follows money); the verse names the cost to her, so the same greed that makes her love brief also drowns her.
list_adds: It sets the courtesan beside the gambler and the usurer, making her one of three money-trades rather than a figure of false love.

note: 24 reverses the terms of 23: the rarity of the great is not blamed, then the greatness of the rare.
teaches: The chiasm makes greatness and rarity two faces of one value, so a reader learns that complaining of a thing's cost and grudging its esteem are the same error.

note: Kural 134 says a பார்ப்பான் can relearn the Veda but his birth is ruined when conduct fails; verse 7 defines the பார்ப்பான் by sharing food alone.
teaches: The couplet keeps birth and makes conduct its condition; the verse drops birth from the definition, so the verse goes further than the Kural in detaching the title from birth.
list_adds: By listing the brahmin with titles anyone can earn, the list removes the birth the couplet still assumes.

note: Kural 429 says those whose understanding guards against what is coming meet no affliction that shakes them; the verse says deeds that recoil (அதிர்க்கும்) show themselves only later, except to those who knew beforehand.
teaches: Both use the verb அதிர் for the shock of what comes, and the verse adds that the shock is the delayed result of one's own deed, so the couplet's foresight becomes foresight of one's own acts rather than of outside events.
list_adds: It joins foresight to freedom from craving in one list, so knowing beforehand and wanting nothing are set as the two guards of a deed.

items: வாய்ப்புடைய ராகி வலவைகள் அல்லாரைக் காப்படையக் கோடல்

note: Kural 542 says the people live looking to the ruler's sceptre as the world looks to the sky; verse 14 calls living by the sceptre the virtue of the king's land.
teaches: The couplet speaks of the king's duty to the people's need; the verse turns it into the people's virtue, obedience to the sceptre.
list_adds: It counts living by the sceptre among household and military duties, moving it from the king's chapter into the subject's code.

note: Kural 360 names three, desire, anger and confusion, whose very names must perish; Elathi 61 names six defects of the soul.
teaches: Together they show the Jain list keeping desire and anger but trading the Kural's confusion for pride, avarice, hatred and partiality, so the root faults shift from error of mind to faults of self-regard.
list_adds: It doubles the Kural's three into six and adds pride and avarice, which 360 does not name, so the passions are counted as the Jain stains of the soul rather than as a triad of the mind.

note: Akananuru 9 ends with the returning man asking whether his heart, which went ahead longing for her soft shoulders, has reached her; Kar Narpathu 19 has the man say his heart has gone the long road wanting her as companion.
teaches: Both returning heroes speak of a heart that outruns the chariot, so the figure belongs to the set speech of return; the long poem follows the heart into the house and to her touch, while the venba stops at its setting out.

note: Kural 527 says crows do not hide but call out and eat, and gain belongs to those of that nature; verse 48 counts announcing the meal in one's house before eating as a mark of the future king.
teaches: The verse gives the crow's call a human form, a spoken rice-call (சோற்றரவம்) in the house, and shows the couplet's image was a practice before it was a figure.
list_adds: It plays the rice-call against two other noises the householder avoids (strangers' clamour, hostile talk), so the sound he makes is defined by the sounds he refuses.

note: Naladiyar 363 names three bad wives (the defiant, the one who skips the kitchen, the one who withholds food) as weapons that kill the husband; Sirupanchamoolam 24 names five doings of a bad wife.
teaches: The quatrain's faults all lie inside the house and against the husband, the verse's all lie outside it (drink, absence, other houses, prying, bad company), so together they show the period's norm for a wife policing both her service and her movements.
list_adds: Its five faults face outward from the house, where the quatrain's three are failures of service within it.

note: Verse 1 names the speech of women with pearl-like smiles as sweet; verse 37 names knowing such women as poison as sweet.
teaches: Within one book the same object is sweet to hear and sweet to know as poison, which shows the book addressing the householder in one verse and the would-be renouncer in another rather than holding one view of women.

note: Kural 586 counsels the king to use spies who go in the guise of renunciants and wanderers; 47 insists that the bard's wandering life, crossing many wastes from patron to patron, harms no one. On the reading that 47 answers a suspicion of the wandering bard, the two disagree about whether such travellers should be trusted.
teaches: The Kural's advice to disguise spies as wanderers is the very reason a real wanderer could fall under suspicion, and 47 gives the wanderer's side, a life of gifts and honour that 'knows no harm to others', so the pair shows the cost the state's craft laid on the travelling poet.

note: Kural 247 says that world is not for those without grace as this world is not for those without wealth; Sirupanchamoolam 34 says enjoyment comes of wealth and dharma of melted grace.
teaches: The couplet weighs grace against wealth by the worlds they open; the verse gives each its fruit (enjoyment, dharma) and calls the grace melted, so grace is a softening of the heart, not a possession.
list_adds: It sets the wealth and grace pair at the end of a chain of five causes and effects, so enjoyment and dharma are results like blame and homage.

note: Kural 360's triad whose end ends pain is desire, anger and confusion; Thirikadugam's triad whose end ends birth is attachment, craving and false speech.
teaches: Comparing the two triads shows the Kural placing the root of suffering wholly in the mind, while Thirikadugam counts a fault of speech among the roots of rebirth.
list_adds: It replaces anger and confusion with false speech, so the counted causes of bondage include an act of the tongue and not only states of mind.

note: Kural 443 calls winning the great as one's own the rarest of rare things; Nanmanikkadigai says great things are reached through great men, as iron splits iron.
teaches: The couplet prizes the great as companions, and the verse explains the worth by a law of like working on like, so the great are needed because only they can reach great ends.
list_adds: It proves the claim with two physical cases (iron on iron, water rinsing after water), so the moral rule is given the force of a natural one.

note: Kural 188 asks what those who spread the faults of their intimates will do to strangers; Thirikadugam says the measure of friendship shows in backbiting.
teaches: The couplet reasons from near to far; the verse makes backbiting the gauge by which one learns how far a friendship really reaches.
list_adds: It sets backbiting as a test of friendship beside tests of lineage and of authority, three signs by which hidden worth is known.

note: Kural 386 says the land of an accessible king who is not harsh of speech is spoken of above others; Nanmanikkadigai says the land's prosperity is people saying 'this king is good'.
teaches: The couplet gives the king's conduct that earns praise; the verse makes that praise itself the land's wealth.
list_adds: It sets the king's good name among the prosperity of house and work, so the realm's gain is one of a household series, measured by speech.

note: Kural 263 asks whether the others have forgotten penance in wanting to provide for those who renounced; Elathi 70 says the one who gives alms, food and clothing to ascetics will rule earth and sky.
teaches: Where the couplet treats provisioning ascetics as the reason householders left penance aside, the verse makes that provisioning its own road to heaven, so the giver gains what the ascetic seeks.
list_adds: It lists the gifts in kind (alms, begged food, food, clothing) and adds a reward over two worlds, which the couplet's question leaves unstated.

note: 29 names three faults of the body and closes the scheme begun in 27 and continued in 28.
teaches: With 29 the ten faults are complete, and the pairing shows that the counting form can carry one doctrine across several verses rather than finishing in each.

note: Purananuru 27 reports as hearsay (என்ப ... எனக் கேட்பல்) that those whom poets praise reach a sky-car no charioteer drives; the line states flatly that heaven is easy for those who desire fame.
teaches: The heroic poem hedges its heaven as something heard and grants it to the man others praise, while the maxim drops the hedge and grants it to the man who wants fame, so the pair shows a court belief hardening into a saying and its condition moving from the poet's praise to the seeker's own desire.

note: Both are the friend's assurance that he will return; 231 grants that glory took him away, 237 says no rich town, not even Uranthai, will keep him from her.
teaches: Taken together the two comforts answer the two fears of the waiting woman, that his honour will keep him away and that pleasure will, and show the friend's arguments as a set repertoire.

note: The Kural uses the strider of the earth as the measure of what a king free from sloth gains; the invocation worships the stride itself.
teaches: The same three steps serve the Kural as a measure of a diligent king's reach and the invocation as an act of the god, so the myth is shared ground between worship and statecraft.
list_adds: It puts the stride among three other cosmic deeds (swallowing the earth, lifting the hill, breaking Sho), so the step is one of the god's acts rather than a yardstick of gain.

note: Verse 22 says learning gives eyes cleared of darkness; verse 28 traces learning step by step through lessened ignorance to the path of truth and the higher world.
teaches: Read together, the single sight learning gives in 22 becomes in 28 the first link of a chain that ends beyond this world.

note: Kural 55 says that if the wife who rises worshipping her husband says 'rain', it rains; Thirikadugam gives the same rain-command to the wife who knows her husband's mind, the ascetic true to his undertaking and the king who shuns cruelty.
teaches: The Kural gives the power over rain to the wife alone; the verse shares it with the ascetic and the king, so it becomes the reward of anyone who keeps the line of his station.
list_adds: It names three holders of the rain-power from household, renunciation and rule, turning the couplet's single wonder into a rule about keeping one's station.

note: Kural 548 says a ruler who does not examine and do justice perishes of himself; Innaa 5 counts a kingship that rules without முறை as painful.
teaches: The couplet looks at the unjust ruler's own fall, while the Innaa, by placing him beside a cane field with no fence, looks at what his subjects suffer while he still rules.
list_adds: It makes injustice one of four unprotected things, so the verse judges rule by the protection it fails to give rather than by the king's fate.

note: Sirupanchamoolam calls brooding on harm done to one smallness; Thirikadugam calls not searching out what was done in a quarrel a distinction.
teaches: The pair gives one act two names from both sides, and it supports reading Thirikadugam's doubtful line as forgiving injuries done to one rather than forgetting one's own deeds.

note: Kural 972 says birth is alike for all living beings and distinction comes from the work they do; Innaa 19 counts union where there is no family standing as painful, on the reading that குலம் is birth rank.
teaches: On that reading the two disagree on whether family rank is a ground of worth: the Kural denies it at birth, and the Innaa makes its absence a reason a union is a pain.
list_adds: It places union outside family rank beside the unlearned noble and the immodest woman, so birth, learning and women's conduct are counted as one order of standing.

note: Kural 134 says a brahmin who forgets the Veda can relearn it but one whose conduct fails loses his birth; Sirupanchamoolam 32 says the brahmin is the one who sacrifices.
teaches: Both tie the birth term பார்ப்பான் to something done rather than to birth alone, but the Kural ties it to conduct and the verse to the rite of sacrifice, two different tests for the same status.
list_adds: It puts the brahmin's defining act in a row with a woman's chastity, a scholar's listening, a poet's mind and the father's gift, so each kind of person is named by one mark.

note: Purananuru 55.1-2 (மலைப் பெருவில் பாம்புஞாண் ... ஒரு கணை ... மூவெயில்) and Paripadal 5.24-25 (நாகம் நாணா, மலை வில்லாக, மூவகை ஆர் எயில் ஓர் அழல்-அம்பின்) give the three-forts deed in the same parts: mountain bow, serpent string, one arrow; both also turn on Siva's forehead eye.
teaches: The same tripura formula serves a puram poet as the vehicle of counsel to a Pandya king and a devotional poet as the prelude to Murugan's birth, showing that Siva's deed was common stock usable for statecraft and worship alike in the Sangam period.

note: Kural 1033 says all who do not live by their own ploughing bow to eat and walk behind; Sirupanchamoolam 37 says the worthy do not eat food got by bowing.
teaches: The couplet names the farmer as the one man free of bowing for food; the verse makes refusing such food a rule of the worthy whatever their trade, so the Kural's economic point becomes a point of self-respect.
list_adds: It sets the refusal beside not sleeping in a friend's house and not taking lost goods, so eating by bowing is ranked with small breaches of dignity and honesty.

note: Kural 229 says eating alone to fill one's own store is more bitter than begging; the line says enjoying pleasure alone is no better than solitude.
teaches: The couplet ranks solitary eating below begging, a loss of goods and honour, while the line counts any unshared pleasure as loneliness, so the pair shows the same fault judged once as social shame and once as the self's own isolation.
list_adds: It widens the couplet's solitary eating to every pleasure kept to oneself and pairs it within the ten with the fool's company, both measured by solitude.

note: Kural 787 says friendship turns one from ruin and sets one on the path; Nanmanikkadigai says to increase friends by leading them to the good.
teaches: The Kural describes what a friend does; the quatrain turns that guidance into the way friendships multiply, so guiding friends is also how one gains more of them.
list_adds: It makes leading friends to the good a means of increase, set against diminishing food and anger, which turns a duty into a gain.

note: Kural 1001 says one who stores great wealth and does not eat it is dead; Thirikadugam says one who buries wealth without enjoying it is born yet unborn.
teaches: The couplet counts the hoarder dead at the end; the verse counts him never born, so between them the hoarder's life is cancelled at both ends.
list_adds: It sets the hoarder beside the graceless heart and the overreaching harsh tongue, so hoarding becomes one of three refusals (of grace, of use, of measure in speech) that unmake a birth.

note: Acharakkovai 16 names the king, teacher, mother, father and elder brother as the peerless elders to be worshipped as gods; Thirikadugam counts refusing the five elders' command as the act of those without goodness.
teaches: Acharakkovai supplies who the ஐங்குரவர் are and the positive rule; Thirikadugam names the breach and ranks it with lying in friendship and casting off a chaste wife, setting obedience to elders in one ethic with loyalty to friend and wife.

note: Kural 310 says those who renounce anger equal those who renounce all; Thirikadugam names the strength that wears anger thin as the work of the anciently wise beside household duties.
teaches: The Kural lifts quelling anger to the level of renunciation; the verse keeps it as a householder's strength (விறல்).
list_adds: It places anger's control with conduct toward women and sharing food, so it is counted among household virtues rather than set equal to renunciation.

note: Innaa Narpathu 30 counts a house where a snake lurks hidden as painful; the verse likens the small-minded who hide what has befallen them to an anthill where a snake dwells hidden.
teaches: The Innaa line names the hidden snake as a danger to live beside, and the verse turns it into a person, so the reader learns that the secretive man is that danger.

note: Kural 784 says friendship is for going ahead to rebuke when one oversteps; Nanmanikkadigai likens friends' rebuking words to the lute.
teaches: The Kural states rebuke as the purpose of friendship; the quatrain says how it should be heard, as music, so the duty of the friend is matched by the response of the one rebuked.
list_adds: It sets the friend's rebuke among likenesses of company good and bad, so rebuke is counted as one of the pleasures of good company.

note: Kural 522 says kin whose love does not lapse bring ever-branching gains; saying 43 says a kin bond without tenderness is not a kin bond.
teaches: The Kural values kin by the gains their unfailing love brings, while the saying moves the test inward and denies the name of kin to those without tenderness, before any gain is counted.
list_adds: It puts the kin bond in a run of definitions by inner condition (spouse, house, friend, learning), so kinship is ranked with friendship as a bond made by feeling, where the couplet treats kin as a source of wealth.

note: The Siddhar verse asks what use ash and bathing are without learning to be born otherwise; the verse ranks worship on the Ganga's bank lowest, below restraint.
teaches: The Siddhar dismisses ritual bathing outright, while the ethics verse keeps Ganga worship as a merit but ranks it beneath restraint of presence and speech.
list_adds: Its ranking into foremost, high and lowest places the rite in an order of merits rather than rejecting it.

note: Kural 218 says those who know what is due do not falter in giving even when they have no means; Innaa 6 counts giving by those in distress as painful, on the reading that இன்னா marks a thing to be avoided.
teaches: On that reading the books disagree about the poor man's gift: the Kural praises it as a mark of discernment, and the Innaa ranks it with a warrior idle in battle and a crooked man's word.
list_adds: It sets the distressed giver's gift beside the virtuous man's harsh word, so the verse names gifts and words that go wrong because the giver is in the wrong state, not because he lacks virtue.

note: Naladiyar 347 says a sandal of gold and gems is still for the foot, so the base are known by their deeds though wealthy; Nanmanikkadigai says the base, though bound and polished, show their dirt.
teaches: The Naladiyar's base are dressed up by wealth, the quatrain's are scrubbed by force, and both fail, so neither fortune nor correction changes their nature.
list_adds: It sets the base against a gem that stays itself though soiled, so the base become the reverse of the gem, keeping their dirt as it keeps its worth.

note: Kural 720 says holding forth before those not of one's group is nectar spilled in a drain; Thirikadugam counts not saying what the unreceptive will not accept, even when provoked, as part of a good person's path.
teaches: The couplet gives the reason for silence before the wrong audience as waste; the verse makes that silence a mark of standing, kept even under provocation.
list_adds: It sets restraint before the unreceptive beside being acknowledged by the worthy and the intimate, so the silence counts as one of three signs of a good person's standing.

note: The Kural says men of unsteady heart touch women who join with them while their hearts are elsewhere; the verse counts the courtesan whose heart is elsewhere yet never fails in business as hard to keep.
teaches: Both note the courtesan's divided heart; Thirikadugam adds that her business never fails, so the danger is a reliable trade without love.
list_adds: It sets the courtesan beside a rain-day guest and a defiant servant, so she is counted among household burdens rather than vices.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 71 calls delivering a child, caring for the pregnant and taking up an infant great virtue; verse 55 counts feeding and curing new mothers, the pregnant and infants as acts that earn great wealth.
teaches: Both Jain works make the birth-room a field of merit; Elathi adds food and cure to the care and names a reward where Sirupanchamoolam cites the old books.

note: Kural 363 calls not wanting the finest wealth here and hereafter; the line calls wanting the greatest poverty.
teaches: The couplet makes desirelessness a wealth and the line makes desire a poverty, so together they move both wealth and poverty out of possessions and into the state of wanting.
list_adds: Placed two lines before begging is named the worst disgrace (59), the line sets desire as the poverty that leads to asking, a causal sequence the couplet does not draw.

note: Thirikadugam 73 names the man who says he will make bright wealth by begging as one who lives daring the hard; Nanmanikkadigai says the one who plans to make bright wealth gets no sleep.
teaches: The two books use the same phrase for the plan to make bright wealth and both make it a hardship: Thirikadugam a daring, Nanmanikkadigai a sleepless night.

note: Kural 99 asks why one who sees the good of sweet speech would use harsh words; the verse says the harsh delight in harsh words.
teaches: The couplet's question assumes harsh speech is a mistake; the verse answers that it is a pleasure to the harsh, so the pair shows that reasoning against harsh words will not reach those whose nature enjoys them.
list_adds: It places harsh speech after units of time and the clear-minded, so a speaker's words are shown as following from his nature as watches follow from naazhigai.

note: Both close by naming three who are called the world: verse 26 a considerate guest, a non-killer and a gentle teacher; verse 34 the brahmin, the just king and orderly people.
teaches: The book defines 'the world' twice, once by three private virtues and once by three estates, so the word means both good persons and an ordered society.

note: Thirikadugam 62 names the one who wrongfully keeps a deposit among three who live on with their line lost; the Innaa line counts seizing a deposit as painful.
teaches: The Thirikadugam names the consequence, loss of descendants, that the Innaa line's bare 'painful' leaves unspoken, so the ethics works together give the act and its price.

note: Kural 501 says a man is trusted after being tested by virtue, wealth, pleasure and fear for life; verse 58 says the trusted man has wealth, enjoyment, fearlessness, grace at death and rare dharma.
teaches: Where the couplet uses wealth, pleasure and fear as temptations to test a man, the verse treats wealth, enjoyment and fearlessness as qualities he must have, and adds grace, so the same terms change from tests to credentials.
list_adds: It turns the couplet's four tests into five possessions and adds grace that survives death, which the couplet does not name.

note: Both marutham poems reproach the husband for bathing in the Kaveri flood with the woman he desires (நீ வெய் யோளொடு), and both place it at Matthi's Kazhar near Thithan's Uranthai.
teaches: The shared phrase and places show that the bathing scandal at Kazhar was a set situation of marutham, which each poet then sharpened with a different puram comparison, a rout in 226 and a lost youth in 6.

note: Kural 664 says speaking is easy and doing as spoken is hard; Elathi 39 lists four easy-hard pairs and ends that winning is easy and the word is hard.
teaches: The same easy-hard form ranks speech oppositely in the two books, because Kural 664 means announcing a plan while Elathi means the right and truthful word, so the pair shows how much 'speech' changes with what kind of speaking is meant.
list_adds: It sets four easy-hard pairs in a row, death against character and victory against the word, so speech is ranked among the hard things the Kural keeps for deeds.

note: Kural 800 says to leave the friendship of the unfit even at the cost of a gift; Iniyavai calls sweet leaving the friendship of the worthless even when they embrace one.
teaches: The couplet counts the cost of leaving in goods and the verse in affection refused, so the pair shows two prices a man may pay to be free of an unworthy friend.
list_adds: It closes a list that begins with keeping off the roads at night and speaking without slips, so ending a bad friendship is grouped with other kinds of self-guarding.

note: Kural 335 says to hurry to good deeds before the death rattle stops the tongue; Elathi 37 lists the pleas Death ignores, worship among them, and names penance as the remedy.
teaches: Together they show the urgency of the Kural's couplet sharpened into a Jain argument in which even worship fails before Death and only penance done in time avails.
list_adds: It counts six failed appeals to Death, including worship, so ritual is set aside before penance is named.

note: Kural 251 asks how one who eats flesh to swell his own flesh can have grace; Iniyavai 4 uses the same phrase and calls abstaining foremost sweet.
teaches: The couplet condemns the act by what it costs the eater's compassion, the verse praises the abstention as a pleasure, so the pair shows non-eating of flesh argued both as a moral loss avoided and as a gain enjoyed.
list_adds: It ranks abstaining from flesh 'foremost' beside the sight of an elephant army and a riverside village, so a renunciant's rule is counted among a ruler's and a villager's delights.

note: Naladiyar 52 calls those who prattle endlessly of grammar and astrology the greatest fools; Elathi 38 says the great penance is not removed by letters, numbers or hymns but reached by conduct.
teaches: Read together, both Jain works set letters and number-lore against the real work, and Elathi names that work as conduct within penance where the quatrain leaves it as one's own task.
list_adds: It puts praise and hymns beside letters and numbers as three substitutes for conduct, adding the devotional to the learned ones the quatrain mocks.

note: Kural 588 says to confirm what one spy reports through another (ஒற்றினால் ஒற்றி); Iniyavai calls sweet for kings learning facts ஒற்றினான் ஒற்றி.
teaches: The verse's compressed phrase echoes the couplet's, and read through it the item can mean checking one spy by another, not merely using one.
list_adds: It sets spying beside full inquiry before judgment and sharing with all beings, so intelligence is ranked with justice and care as one royal pleasure.

note: Kural 986 says the touchstone of worth is accepting defeat even from those not one's equal; the verse says nobility is known by helpfulness toward anyone.
teaches: Both make the test of worth one's conduct toward those who are no match for one (துலையல்லார், யார்கண்ணும்), the couplet by yielding and the verse by helping, so the pair shows nobility tested where nothing is owed.
list_adds: It sets the sign of nobility with the signs of a man, a pool and toddy, so worth is known by its outflow as a pool by its water.

note: Kural 150 says that even one who does wrong does well not to desire another's wife; verse 5 promises fortune to one who does not desire her.
teaches: The couplet values the restraint even without other virtue; the verse makes it the gate to fortune, so the same act is moved from a minimum of decency to a source of gain.
list_adds: It sets not desiring another's wife beside penance, giving and learning as four means to four ends, so this restraint is ranked as one of the means of a whole life.

note: Iniyavai 34 names not going about at night as foremost sweet; Innaa 17 names going about when it has grown dark as very painful.
teaches: The same rule appears from both sides with matching intensifiers (முன் in the Iniyavai, பெரிது in the Innaa), so both books rank night travel above their other items.

note: Kural 761 ranks a complete, wound-fearing army first among a king's wealth; the verse says a king's glory withers without one.
teaches: Read together, the army is both the king's chief possession and the root his fame grows from, so losing it is not a loss of goods but a drying-up of renown.
list_adds: It puts the king's army in a row with war for warriors, roots for trees and the sluice for the neytal, so the army becomes the hidden supply of glory, not a holding.

note: Kural 691 tells those who join warring kings to be like men warming at a fire, neither far nor near; the verse sets the warring king among things the wise do not befriend, beside the elephant and the tiger.
teaches: The couplet teaches the courtier how to stand near the dangerous king; the verse, for one not bound to serve, says not to go near, so one danger yields a rule of distance and a rule of avoidance.
list_adds: It ranks the warring king with a loosed elephant and a prowling tiger, so the king is one more natural danger, not a master to be served.

note: Both are reports of having seen the enemy's ruined land (கண்டனென் in Purananuru 23, கண்டுவந் திசினே in Patitruppattu 15), and both mark the ruin by white velai flowers growing over it (வேளை வெண்பூ; வெண்பூ வேளை).
teaches: The shared white velai shows it was a stock sign of a razed settlement in both Pandya and Chera praise, and Patitruppattu 15 extends the form: where Purananuru 23 ends on the waste, the Chera poet adds a second sight, the king's own guarded land, so the ruin becomes one half of a judgment on rule.

note: Both lines close on தனிமையின் துவ்வாது: a fool's support and pleasure enjoyed alone are each no better than solitude.
teaches: Read together, the two make solitude the measure from both sides: one may be alone though accompanied, by a fool, or alone though joyful, by not sharing, so company is defined by what is shared and not by who is present.

note: Kural 560 says that if the guardian does not guard, the cows' yield fails and the men of six duties forget their books; Thirikadugam sets the fire-priests' dharma and the king's just rule side by side as seeds of rain.
teaches: The couplet makes priestly learning depend on the king's protection; the verse makes priest, king and wife coequal causes of the rains, flattening the Kural's order of dependence into a joint one.
list_adds: It adds the wife who follows her husband as a third cause beside priest and king, joining the household to the ritual and royal orders as one seed of rain.

note: Kural 784 says friendship is not for laughing together but for rebuking when one oversteps; Innaa 8 counts the lack of binding affection (நார்) in friends made in laughter as painful.
teaches: The couplet says what friendship is for, and the Innaa names the pain of the friendship that was only laughter: it has no fibre when it is tested.
list_adds: It sets the laughing friend beside the fair-seeming heart without character and the ungracious friend, so the verse ranks three counterfeits of friendship together.

note: Innaa Narpathu 22 is this verse's mirror: kings without elephants, eating flesh to swell flesh and a town cut off by a forest river are painful where elephant armies, abstaining and a town on the river's bank are sweet.
teaches: Side by side they show the two books built as paired catalogues, and the forest river item shows the method is not a simple negation: the same river is sweet as a bank and painful as a barrier.

note: Iniyavai 22 names giving with knowledge of one's income as sweet; Innaa 10 names liberality attempted by those without wealth as painful.
teaches: The two books say the same thing from two sides, and together they make the measure explicit: giving is judged against income, sweet when it fits and painful when it outruns it.

note: Iniyavai 17 nearly quotes Kural 679 (doing good to friends; winning over those not allied), but reads நாட்டார்க்கு, the land's people, and calls both sweet where the couplet ranks them by urgency.
teaches: The couplet's ranking is one of speed, the verse's one of sweetness, and the verse adds granaries and many allies, so the pair shows a counsel of timing turned into a picture of a secure ruler.
list_adds: It adds a third item, full granaries and true allies, so the couplet's two acts of alliance become part of a ruler's provisioning.

note: Naladiyar 53 lists home, youth, beauty, repute, wealth and strength as not lasting, so the best renounce them; Nanmanikkadigai gives friendship, youth, wealth and life each its own end.
teaches: The quatrain says these things do not last; the verse says what each ends in, and three of the ends (falsehood, old age, excess) come from the thing itself.
list_adds: It assigns each thing its own end, so wealth ends in excess and friendship in falsehood rather than all ending alike, and it adds friendship, which the quatrain does not name.

note: In 1130 she uses 'he lives within me' to refute the town's gossip. In 1249 she uses the same fact against her own heart, to stop it from leaving.
teaches: The argument that once consoled her now traps her.

note: Kural 523 says life without mingling with kin is a tank with no bank; Nanmanikkadigai calls leaving one's kin striving after ruin.
teaches: The Kural shows the loss as waste, wealth spilling away; the quatrain names leaving kin as an effort, so ruin is something one works at rather than suffers.
list_adds: It sets abandoning kin as the one wrong striving after three right ones, so the last item reverses the verse's praise of effort.

note: Naladiyar 306 says poverty can be ended by asking oneself rather than begging from strangers; Nanmanikkadigai says begging springs up quickly in the pit of poverty.
teaches: The verse describes begging as poverty's quick crop; the quatrain answers that the crop need not grow if one begs of oneself, so the pair sets the natural course against the discipline that stops it.
list_adds: It sets begging as the last of four growths from their soils, so it appears as a natural consequence where the Naladiyar treats it as a choice.

note: Kural 226 calls removing the hunger of the destitute the place to store wealth; Elathi 36 names whom to feed (the lame, the blind, the mute, the kinless, the unlearned) and says the gods will desire such givers.
teaches: The pair turns the Kural's general 'destitute' into named kinds of person who cannot earn, and moves the giver's return from stored wealth to the gods' regard.
list_adds: It names five kinds of need, bodily, social and of learning, and puts the unlearned among the disabled as people owed food.

note: 216 says the friend, known by hearing alone and never met for many years, will come; Kural 785 says neither meeting nor long acquaintance is needed, feeling alone gives the claim (கிழமை) of friendship.
teaches: The Kural's rule and the king's wager share the technical word கிழமை, so the couplet's claim that friendship needs no meeting has a famous royal case behind it, one staked on a seat kept for a man never seen.

note: Kural 822 says the friendship of those who seem kin but are not shifts like a changing mind; Thirikadugam says deceivers stay deceivers even when they keep close.
teaches: The couplet stresses that false friendship changes; the verse that the false friend's nature does not, so the pair separates the shifting surface of conduct from the fixed nature beneath it.
list_adds: It sets the deceiver against the true ally who stays an ally even when estranged, so the list gives a test of constancy in both directions.

note: Kural 77 says dharma burns the loveless as the sun burns the boneless; Nanmanikkadigai calls dharma death to those who do wrong.
teaches: Read beside the plantain killed by its own fruit, the quatrain makes dharma a death the wrongdoer grows himself, which the Kural's sun, an outside force, does not show.
list_adds: It sets dharma's punishment among deaths that come from within the victim, so retribution becomes self-made rather than imposed.

note: Kural 232 says all that speakers say amounts to praise resting on those who give to askers; verse 41 says the books of the path will recite the worth of one who gives to the resourceless.
teaches: The couplet locates fame in what people say; the verse places it in the scriptures themselves, so giving earns a place in the texts that teach giving.
list_adds: It makes giving the last of six marks after five refusals (the mean, flesh, falsehood, theft, tight-fistedness), so the praise in the books is earned by a whole discipline and not by the gift alone.

note: The Kural says the upright man's wealth is a strength to his descendants; Thirikadugam says the man who speaks crookedly in the assembly loses his descendants.
teaches: Read together, fairness and its breach are both paid in the next generation: the Kural's promise to the heirs of the just has its dark twin in the heirless partial judge.
list_adds: It sets partial speech beside ingratitude and a seized deposit, so unfairness is classed as a breach of trust with a shared penalty.

note: Kural 303 says to forget anger toward anyone, since evils are born from it; the verse says that if one destroys anything, it should be anger.
teaches: The couplet asks for anger to be let go of; the verse turns destruction itself toward anger, so the pair shows the same urge to destroy being redirected rather than given up.
list_adds: It frames each counsel as the best object of a verb (give food, lift fallen kin, destroy anger), so the destructive impulse is given a proper target like the giving and the lifting.

note: Verse 86 calls letting go of the raft of chastity and the loss of friendship's grace an enmity; verse 97 names forsaking a chaste wife and false dealing in friendship as acts of the graceless.
teaches: Verse 97 names plainly the husband's act of forsaking a chaste wife beside a breach of friendship, which supports reading 86's letting go of chastity as his act rather than hers.

note: Kural 133 says conduct is noble birth and failing in it becomes low birth; Nanmanikkadigai says lineage is evil when its principle is destroyed.
teaches: The quatrain goes past the Kural's demotion to call the lost lineage itself an evil, and its கொள்கை, a held principle, names something narrower than conduct in general.
list_adds: It sets fallen lineage beside killing, unlearned children and shameless beauty, so birth is one more good turned evil by a loss.

note: Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world; Sirupanchamoolam 35 assigns enjoyment to giving, heaven to penance and release to knowledge.
teaches: The couplet frees giving from any reward; the verse keeps a reward but ranks it lowest, so both deny that giving is the way to heaven, one by indifference to reward and one by a ladder of rewards.
list_adds: It ranks giving, penance and knowledge on one ladder of fruits, enjoyment, heaven, release, which the couplet never builds.

note: Naladiyar 60 says fools crave pleasure though suffering mounts, while the higher ones see the pain in each pleasure and do not cling; the line says pain comes easily to those who crave pleasure.
teaches: The Naladiyar finds pain lodged inside pleasure itself and so counsels detachment, while the line lays the pain on the craving and not on the pleasure, which leaves room, as its mirror 75 shows, for pleasure that comes to one who did not chase it.
list_adds: Its pairing with 75 makes pleasure attainable by the non-craving, a turn the renunciant quatrain does not allow, since it treats every pleasure as the seed of pain.

note: Kural 966 asks why one should stand behind those who scorn one; Iniyavai calls very sweet the spirit that will not live where it is held in no regard.
teaches: The couplet argues from the loss of praise and heaven, while the verse calls the refusal a pleasure in itself, so the pair shows honour defended first by reckoning and then by taste.
list_adds: It places the refusal to live without regard between two items on giving, so the self-respect of the giver and of the one who will not cringe are made one temper.

note: Kural 788 defines friendship as clearing a friend's distress at once, like a hand catching a slipping garment; the Innaa line counts the mere sight of a friend's distress as a deep pain.
teaches: The pairing shows the feeling behind the Kural's reflex: the friend's hand moves so fast because seeing the trouble already hurts.
list_adds: It sets the friend's trouble against the enemy's pride in the next line, so friendship's pain is measured against its mirror in enmity.

note: Kural 114 says the worthy and unworthy are seen by what each leaves behind; the verse says the rightness of five kinds of person is known when they die.
teaches: Both defer judgment of worth past the life; the verse applies the rule to five stations and names death as the moment of proof.
list_adds: It runs the test through wife, soldier, ascetic, trader and arbiter, so one rule of posthumous judgment is made to cover every station of life.

note: Pazhamozhi 13 says the fine point an unlearned man has found is hard for him to show, so he should not rate himself among the good; verse 4 says that same subtlety makes the good laugh.
teaches: Read together, the pair gives both the cause and the effect: the unlearned man's insight cannot be shown, and so to the learned it is merely comic.

note: Kural 460 says nothing brings more affliction than bad company; verse 60 names the afflictions, sin, blame, enmity, death, ruin and fear, and says they cling in both worlds like a curse.
teaches: The couplet's 'affliction' is left general; the verse itemises it and extends it beyond this life, so bad company is a karmic cost and not only a social one.
