list_adds: It counts the evils that follow from bad company and joins worldly ones (blame, enmity) to otherworldly ones (sin), which the couplet's single word does not separate.

items: வாய்மயங்கு மண்டமருள் மாறாத மாமன்னர் தானை தடுத்தல்
எளியர் இவரென் றிகழ்ந்துரையா ராகி ஒளிபட வாழ்தல்
பாவமும் அஞ்சாராய்ப் பற்றுந் தொழில்மொழிச் சூதரைச் சோர்தல்
உற்றபே ராசை கருதி அறனொரூஉம் ஒற்கம் இலாமை

note: Kural 1078 says the worthy are of use at a word and the base only when crushed like cane; Nanmanikkadigai binds the base with iron and the worthy by courtesy.
teaches: The couplet speaks of what the two yield; the verse of how they are held, so the pair moves from extracting good to restraining harm with the same contrast.
list_adds: It puts the base and the worthy in a row with the raging elephant and the great serpent, so each kind of creature has its own binding and courtesy becomes a bond.

note: Kural 541 says justice is investigating, showing favour to no one and acting after consideration; Nanmanikkadigai defines justice as having no favour toward anyone.
teaches: The same phrase (யார்மாட்டும் / யார்கண்ணும், no favour) defines justice in both, and the quatrain adds inner inquiry for the discerning ruler where the Kural asks for investigation, so the ruler's scrutiny is turned on himself as well.
list_adds: It sets the definition of justice beside definitions of conduct as learning and of wealth as enjoyment with dharma, making justice one of the ruler's set of defined virtues.

note: Kural 36 says to do virtue now, since it is the companion that does not perish when one does; Nanmanikkadigai says that one who wants what goes along with oneself should do virtue.
teaches: Both make virtue the one companion past death, and the verse puts it as a means to a wish, beside fame for lasting here and giving up anger for winning.
list_adds: Its 'if you want X, do Y' frame sets virtue as the means for one wish among four, with begging as the ironic means to pain, so the virtues become instruments chosen by their ends.

note: Saying 8 ranks serving the learned above learning; saying 46 denies the name of learning to what is learnt without submission.
teaches: Across two tens, the book first puts reverence for teachers above learning and then makes it the condition of learning, so reverence moves from the greater good to the thing without which learning does not exist.

note: Kural 969 says those like the yak give up life when honour is lost; Iniyavai calls not living on when dishonour comes foremost sweet.
teaches: The verse names as a pleasure what the couplet presents as the nature of a rare kind of person, so the pair shows an admired temperament turned into something anyone may prefer.
list_adds: It sets dying rather than living dishonoured between the giver's bearing and right receiving, so honour is framed by how one gives and how one takes.

note: Verse 7 gives the purpose of his journey as giving to seekers and destroying foes; verse 8 gives it as lasting fame in this earthly world.
teaches: Read in sequence, the friend's account of his motive moves from duties toward others to fame for himself while her proof stays the same rain-season sign, so the series varies the cause of absence and holds the cure fixed.

note: Kural 280 says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; the verse lists five ascetic forms and says that in the Kali age renunciation is false and the household alone true.
teaches: The couplet discounts the ascetic's marks but keeps renunciation, while the verse, for its own age, discounts renunciation itself, so one critique of outward form reaches opposite ends.
list_adds: It names five ascetic forms where the couplet names two, and ties its judgement to an age (கலி), which the couplet does not.

note: Kural 215 likens the wise man's wealth to a village tank full of water; the verse makes the gift of water itself the first of five charities.
teaches: The Kural's tank is a figure for wealth all may draw on; the verse makes it literal and the lowest step of a scale that ends in founding temples and halls.
list_adds: It ranks the charities from a drink of water to founded buildings and puts a condition on charity at home, which the couplet's single image lacks.

note: Kural 134 says forgotten Veda can be relearnt but a brahmin's birth is ruined if conduct fails; the verse asks what a man of five vows lacks without the scriptures.
teaches: Both rank conduct above scriptural recitation, but the Kural keeps the brahmin and his birth in view while the verse makes the point for any man who keeps five lay vows.
list_adds: It names what the conduct is (five vows against attachment, theft, adultery, slander and killing) where the couplet speaks only of conduct in general.

note: Both name Pulli's Venkatam: in 61 the friend says the man would not stay even for Venkatam with its festivals; in 83 the man says her virtues followed him past Venkatam regardless of distance.
teaches: Pulli's Venkatam served akam poets as the fixed far edge of the wealth journey, and they turned it both ways: a prize too small to hold the man, and a distance too short to stop the woman's pull.

note: Kural 42 makes the householder the support of those who renounced, those who have nothing and the dead; Elathi 16 names drawing near to renunciants, giving to those who have not renounced, speaking well of the dead and tending their kin.
teaches: The verse reads like a gloss on 42: it keeps the three figures and turns the dead into the living kin they leave, so the householder's duty to the dead becomes care of a household.
list_adds: It turns the three dependants of 42 into four acts and adds the kin of the dead, so the list says how the support is given, not only to whom.

note: For Parimelazhagar, the schools conflict on everything in 242 and yet converge on அருள். On 353, he says that their conflict leaves doubt only experience can settle.
teaches: Together they give his view of religious pluralism: agreement in ethics, and no resolution by argument in metaphysics.

note: Innaa Narpathu 33 counts as painful the matter of business a drunkard speaks of; the line says a drinker free of lapses is false.
teaches: The Innaa line names the pain of dealing with a drinker's affairs and the Muthumozhikkanchi line gives its cause, the lapse that is certain in him, so one reports the effect and the other the reason no business with him is safe.

note: Kural 29 says the anger of those who have climbed the hill of virtue is hard to withstand even for a moment; Nanmanikkadigai says sages give harm through their penance.
teaches: The couplet warns of the ascetic's anger; the verse names its weapon, penance itself, and sets it with the snake's tooth and the elephant's tusk.
list_adds: It ranks the sage's penance with the snake's tooth, the elephant's tusk and the sulking woman's face as four instruments of harm, so holy power is classed as a natural weapon.

note: Innaa 9 counts the absence of patrons as the foremost pain of gift-seekers; in Puram 375 a drummer finds no patron but Ay and wishes that, with Ay gone, there be no patrons at all, lest bards praise kings of worthless wealth.
teaches: The bard in the Puram poem prefers the very lack the Innaa ranks first among his pains to service under the ungenerous, which the Innaa counts as a separate pain in its third item.

note: Elathi 66 describes the high state by six things it lacks; Elathi 67 names the seven low states one by one.
teaches: Read in sequence, the two verses map both ends of the same cosmos: the summit is known only by negation, while the depths are given names and an order, so the book makes ruin more nameable than release.

note: 53 calls a desire that can come to pass the best desire; 54 calls a desire that cannot the worst.
teaches: Together the two lines judge desire by its outcome rather than its object, a scale on which the same wish is best or worst depending only on whether it can be fulfilled.

note: Elathi 64 says release comes to one who takes the Exalted one as lord, studies his book and fully performs his penance; Elathi 77 says such penance brings release in three, five or seven births.
teaches: Read together, the verses give the path and its timetable: 64 says what leads to release, and 77 says release is not immediate but measured in births.

note: Kural 220 says loss through ஒப்புரவு is worth buying even by selling oneself; Iniyavai calls doing what is to be done even by borrowing sweet, if செய்வன covers duties of help.
teaches: The couplet's extreme, selling oneself, appears here in a household form, taking a loan, so the pair shows the ethics group pricing duty to others in debt.
list_adds: It sets duties done on credit beside protecting those who came for refuge, so borrowing to do one's part is grouped with protection rather than prudence.

note: After the town without wall (23) and without protection (24), verse 25 names the old town without கட்டு, bonds of order.
teaches: Across three verses the town's weakness moves from its stone to its order, teaching that a town is unsafe for lacking ties as much as for lacking walls.

note: Purananuru 35 counsels Killivalavan that in a land of just rule, where the humble can reach the king when they seek முறை, rain comes when sought, and that if he protects his people the unsubmitting will bow; 99 states the bare rule that security needs just order.
teaches: The poem shows to a named Chola what just rule looks like and what it brings, the king reached by the humble and the enemy bowing, and the line reduces the same counsel to a maxim any ruler can carry.

note: Both call desire for another man's wife பேதைமை; the Kural says it is absent in those who have seen aram and porul.
teaches: The Innaa list explains the shared word by its company: the folly is that of a venture beyond one's strength, like a valourless king in battle, which those the Kural describes would never attempt.
list_adds: It sets the folly beside a valourless king in battle, a bareback ride on a fierce horse and unskilled work, so it is ranked as reckless overreach.

note: Kural 27 says the world lies with one who discerns the five sense-kinds; the verse names three senses with their objects and then thought.
teaches: The couplet ends its list at the five senses; the verse adds thought as a further faculty with its own object, done in company, so the pair shows the ethics group placing counsel beyond the discernment of sense.
list_adds: It pairs each faculty with its object and makes the last one collective (தொக்கிருந்து), a step from individual sensing to shared deliberation that the couplet lacks.

note: Kural 406 likens the unlearned to barren saline ground; Nanmanikkadigai says a body without learned understanding is waste to oneself.
teaches: Both use waste land for the unlearned, but the couplet says they yield nothing to others while the verse says the body is waste to its owner.
list_adds: It sets the unlearned body after a house without a wife, a region without friends and an assembly without elders, so the ignorant self is one of four places laid waste by an absence.

note: 66 rejects the outward marks of ascetics; 68 rejects four austerities and keeps only restraint of the five senses.
teaches: Together the two verses strip ascetic display in two moves, first the marks on the body and then its austerities, leaving only restraint of the senses.

note: 186 says the world lives by its king; 187 says a land is good wherever its men are good, naming no king.
teaches: Placed side by side in the anthology, the two maxims locate the source of a land's well-being in different hands, the ruler in 186 and the men at large in 187, so the reader sees that Sangam counsel did not rest the realm on the king alone.

note: Kural 33 tells one to do virtue without stopping as far as one is able; the verse says the doing of virtue is according to one's strength.
teaches: The couplet uses capacity as a floor (do all you can) and the verse uses it as a measure (each gives by his strength), so read together capacity both limits what is owed and forbids doing less.
list_adds: It sets virtue with a rider's horse, a tank's sluices and a household's spending, so the measure by capacity becomes a principle of proportion across unlike things.

note: Kural 471 says to weigh the strength of the deed, oneself, the opponent and allies before acting; verse 57 says the minister acts after measuring his own state, the work, the opponents' state and the order of things.
teaches: The couplet's four-fold weighing is given to the minister and its fourth term changes from allies to the matchless order of things, so prudence moves from counting forces to reading circumstance.
list_adds: It moves the reckoning to the minister and replaces allies with the order of things, a different fourth term than the couplet's.

note: Kural 301 says restraint of anger counts only where anger can take effect; the line calls anger poor where it inspires no awe.
teaches: The couplet says restraining powerless anger is no virtue, and the line says indulging it is no gain, so together they show that anger without power is worth nothing whether held back or let loose.
list_adds: It judges anger by its effect, as one of ten things emptied by a missing condition, where the couplet judges the restraint of anger as a virtue.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 75 says those who cured the diseases of five kinds of sufferer live now without disease; verse 57 says those who fed and cured six diseases become kings.
teaches: The two works pay the same act of healing differently: Sirupanchamoolam returns it in kind as health, Elathi converts it, like its other gifts, into rule.

note: Pazhamozhi 14 says fine points of learning spoken before the unlearned turn bad; Nanmanikkadigai says a learned man before the unlearned has no standing.
teaches: Pazhamozhi says the words go bad, Nanmanikkadigai that the man loses standing, so the group counts the damage to both the teaching and the teacher.

note: Iniyavai 30 calls the goodness that does not seize a deposit, thinking 'who knew of it then?', the sweetest; Innaa 40 calls seizing a deposit painful. The same thing from two sides.
teaches: The Iniyavai line names the thief's private reckoning that no one saw; set against it, the Innaa line shows the betrayal of trust as painful whether or not anyone knew.

note: Verse 4 lets the books go where six kindly acts are seen; verse 14 puts the books outside one who keeps six abstentions.
teaches: The repeated close shows the chapter treating conduct over books as a refrain, and the two lists divide that conduct into acts of kindness (4) and acts of refusal (14).

note: Iniyavai Narpathu calls sweet not snatching what one sees and desires; Thirikadugam asks for no desire for a thing even once it is in one's hand.
teaches: The pair grades the restraint: not seizing what is seen is the lower step, not wanting what is already held is the higher.

note: Kural 112 says the wealth of the upright does not decay and supports those after them; Thirikadugam says the upright are like rain.
teaches: The couplet keeps the yield of rectitude within the upright man's line; the rain image sends it outward to all, so rectitude is shown both lasting and shared.
list_adds: It sets the upright against two images of dissolution (salt in water, friendship under a lie), so rectitude stands as the one thing in the list that gives instead of melting.

note: Kural 1076 likens the base to a beaten drum because they carry secrets they hear to others; the line says spreading secrets comes easily to those who love tale-bearing.
teaches: The couplet traces the spilling of secrets to a fixed baseness of nature, while the line traces it to an appetite for slander, so the pair shows that the drum-like betrayer is made by a taste he indulges, not only born base.
list_adds: Set among ten desires and their easy outcomes, it gives the betrayal of secrets a cause in a named desire (குறளை), where the couplet gives only an image and a class of person.

note: The two lines are built as twins: அறத்தாற்றின் ஈயாதது ஈனையன்று, திறத்தாற்றின் நேர்லாதது நோன்பன்று.
teaches: The twin form makes the giver's gift and the ascetic's vow two cases of one rule, that an act is named by the way it is done, so the householder's and renouncer's codes are tested alike.

note: Verse 12 says the vellalan does not eat while a guest waits; verse 44 says a day eaten without a guest is a sickness.
teaches: The book treats the guestless meal twice, once as a loss of the title vellalan and once as a sickness of the strong, so the same fault is a loss of rank and of health.

note: Kural 52 says that if the wife lacks household excellence the life is nothing whatever else it has; saying 42 says the same in the அல்ல form.
teaches: The Kural's claim that a wife's excellence decides the household survives the move into a book of bare definitions, where it becomes one of the tests by which a thing earns its name.
list_adds: It sets household life beside kin-friendship, giving, learning and penance as things that lose their very name when one inner condition fails, so the wife's excellence becomes a defining condition of the same kind as aram in giving.

note: Kural 61 says nothing that can be gained matches children who come to know; the verse says no wealth is brighter or fuller than children.
teaches: The couplet's praise is conditional on the children's understanding while the verse gives it unqualified, and the verse places it among other firsts, so children are the first of wealth as the mother is first above the gods.
list_adds: It ranks children as one of four superlatives (eye among organs, husband among kin, mother above gods), so their worth is placed in a hierarchy of bests.

note: The Kural calls good children the ornament of a house's excellence; the verse makes bearing children of an old family the act by which the wife is mistress of the house.
teaches: Children move from ornament to office: what the Kural treats as the crown of a good home, Thirikadugam treats as a debt the wife owes in order to hold her title.
list_adds: It turns three household goods into three roles of one woman, friend, mother and mistress, and frames them all as debts of chastity.

note: Verse 16 says the learned man crosses the deep of the assembly; verse 19 says that if the learned man shakes, the meaning shakes.
teaches: The book qualifies its praise of the learned: he carries the meaning across the assembly only while he holds firm, and his faltering loses it.

items: பெருவகைத் தாயினும் பெட்டவை செய்யார் திரிபின்றி வாழ்தல்

note: Kural 131 says conduct gives excellence and must be guarded above life; Thirikadugam makes joining the road of inherited conduct the third of three things that keep the path of excellence open, after letters and the service of parents.
teaches: Both books tie ஒழுக்கம் to விழுப்பம், but the Kural makes conduct its single source, while the verse makes it the last step of a sequence that begins with learning letters and serving parents.
list_adds: It orders conduct in time, after literacy and filial service, so excellence is reached by a sequence rather than by one virtue.

note: Kural 1014 calls shame the ornament of the worthy; saying 6 ranks shame above beauty or good qualities.
teaches: The Kural's metaphor of shame as an ornament becomes a literal ranking: shame outranks the beauty that ornaments are meant to serve.
list_adds: It sets shame against beauty in a direct comparison, turning the couplet's figure into a ranking among goods.

note: Kural 380 asks what is stronger than fate, which arrives first whatever one devises; Nanmanikkadigai says deeds overrun one when earlier penance was small.
teaches: The quatrain makes fate's power depend on how much penance was stored before, which limits the Kural's unqualified claim for fate.
list_adds: It sets karma's overrunning beside water spilling from a small tank and enemies overrunning the weak, so fate becomes one more force that breaks a container too small for it.

note: Verse 18 says excellent women are the prosperity of a house; verse 20 says the lack of a bright-browed wife lays a house waste.
teaches: The book states the same claim from both sides, prosperity with a good wife and waste without one, so the house is defined by the wife's presence.

note: Naladiyar 70 says no one bitten by a dog bites it back, so the high do not answer the low in kind; verse 16 uses a barking dog to say goodness to the base is wasted and anger is good.
teaches: Both use the dog for the base man and draw opposite counsels: the Naladiyar asks for restraint, the verse for anger and pride.
list_adds: It sets anger and pride as good beside nobility as bad, so the list reverses the Naladiyar's ranking of forbearance above response.

note: Kural 351 says a joyless birth comes from the confusion that takes the unreal for real; Elathi 72 traces not understanding to fault, karma, birth and suffering, and says it turns in a circle.
teaches: The couplet names ignorance as the cause of birth, and the verse adds the middle steps and closes the chain into a cycle, so birth becomes both the fruit and the renewer of ignorance.
list_adds: It sets ignorance at the head of six linked steps and closes them into a circle, where the couplet names only cause and result.

note: Kural 573 asks what use a melody is that does not fit the song, and an eye without kindly regard; the Innaa verse opens with a lute not set to its mode and ends with the enmity of those without coolness.
teaches: Both pass from music out of tune to a person out of tune, which suggests a shared idea of kindness as attunement, with the Innaa verse adding enmity as its opposite.
list_adds: It spreads the Kural's single analogy over four items, three instruments or reckonings out of true and then a hostile temper.

note: Kural 231 says giving and living with renown are the only profit of life; the line ranks giving to askers as the highest distinction.
teaches: The couplet treats giving as a means to renown, the only profit; the line narrows the gift to one made to those who ask and makes its distinction an end, so the asker's presence is what makes the gift supreme.
list_adds: The ten sets giving to askers directly after begging as the worst disgrace (59), so the giver's distinction is ranked against the asker's shame, a contrast the couplet does not draw.

note: Iniyavai calls giving cows and gold to brahmins foremost sweet; Innaa 21 counts the speech of a brahmin without Vedic recitation as painful, and giving to the never-content as painful.
teaches: Together the twin books make the brahmin a privileged recipient but not an unconditional one: the Innaa line ties his standing to recitation, a condition this verse leaves out.

note: Kural 1076 likens the base to a beaten drum that proclaims secrets; Nanmanikkadigai says the elation of the base blares through the town.
teaches: The couplet shows the base unable to keep others' secrets, and the verse shows them unable to keep their own joy quiet, so loudness marks them in both.
list_adds: It sets the base man's elation against the warrior's before kings and the giver's before the poor, ranking kinds of joy by where they show.

note: Kural 969 says men of honour give up life when honour is at stake, like the yak; verse 56 makes perishing, for the man of honour, the last of five acts of wisdom.
teaches: Death for honour, a matter of nature and pride in the couplet, is counted here as wisdom beside forgiveness and care for living beings, so it is framed as discernment rather than temper.
list_adds: It sets dying for honour beside revealing good, forgetting wrongs and helping living beings, so the list makes it one act of wisdom among gentler ones.

note: Kural 706 says the face shows what is strongest in the heart, as crystal shows what is near it; the verse says a man's face tells the desire within him.
teaches: The couplet says the face shows whatever is strongest and the verse names that thing as desire (வேட்கை), so the pair makes the face chiefly a betrayer of wants.
list_adds: It ranks the face with a son revealing his father and rain revealing a land, so the face becomes one case of reading a hidden source from its outflow.

note: Kural 1038 ranks manuring above ploughing and guarding above watering; verse 59 lists storing straw, cattle, tools and manure as care that comes before the plough is set.
teaches: Both put the plough after other care, and the verse widens the couplet's ladder to the farmer's stores and animals, then turns the whole into an image for the scholar's finer plough.
list_adds: It sets manure among the farmer's other provisions and closes with the reciter of texts, so the farming list becomes a figure for study.

note: Verse 14 names youth, folly and meanness as three the wise do not approach; verse 46, with the same closing line, names an unsound horse, a fierce elephant and the place of an angry man.
teaches: Read together, the book's 'the wise do not go near' covers both inner dispositions and outer dangers, and the angry man of verse 46 stands at the join, a human fault treated like a dangerous beast.

note: The Kural likens the wise man's wealth to a village tank filling; the verse calls the man who dug a charitable tank and grove one of the truly rich.
teaches: The Kural's simile is made literal: the public tank is not only like a good man's wealth, its digging is counted as his wealth.
list_adds: It redefines the rich as three givers, of a tank, of Vedic learning and of shared food, so wealth is measured by what one has made common.

note: Kural 336 says the world's greatness is that one who was here yesterday is gone today; the verse says the born and the dying always exist.
teaches: The Kural looks at the individual who vanishes and the verse at the pattern that stays, so impermanence of persons is shown to sit within a permanence of kinds.
list_adds: It places birth and death beside the sun and moon, disease and labour, and givers and takers, all fixtures of the world, so mortality becomes one more constant.

note: Innaa Narpathu calls the liberality of those without means painful; Nanmanikkadigai calls it a fault.
teaches: The two words differ: painful to see in Innaa, a fault in Nanmanikkadigai, so the same act is judged both by its cost to the giver and by its wrongness, and both books stand against the Kural 218 view.

note: Kural 254 says grace and its absence come down to not killing and killing, and eating that flesh is not right; verse 12 calls killing poison and eating meat a cruel poison.
teaches: The couplet derives the wrong of eating from killing; the verse ranks eating as the worse poison, so the eater is held more guilty than the killer.
list_adds: It grades the two acts with நஞ்சு and கொடுநஞ்சு, a ranking the couplet does not make.

note: Kural 52 says if the wife lacks household excellence the life is nothing whatever else it has; Thirikadugam names a wife who wears the house down by falsehood as one of three who are no security for this life.
teaches: The couplet lays the failure of the household on the wife alone; the verse sets beside her the disobedient junior and the abusive head, so the pair shows the house can be ruined from three places.
list_adds: It distributes the household's ruin across junior kin, the head and the wife, rather than resting it on the wife as the couplet does.

note: Kural 424 defines understanding partly as seeing the subtle meaning in others' words; Thirikadugam makes taking the meaning from subtle words a debt the learned owe.
teaches: The couplet describes a capacity; the verse turns it into an obligation that comes with learning.
list_adds: It joins the duty of subtle hearing to two duties of speech, silence when idle words are asked for and speech only to the not-base.

note: Thirikadugam 10 says a town without teachers yields no good; the verse says a town is good if many live in it.
teaches: The verse makes a town good by its numbers and Thirikadugam makes it worthless without teachers, so the pair shows the group measuring a town both by size and by learning, and a populous town can still fail the second test.

note: Kural 559 says the sky withholds rain when the king bends justice; Thirikadugam names the plundering king as one of three malign planets that stop the rain.
teaches: The couplet ties rain to the king alone; the verse adds deceitful men and a transgressing wife, so the power to cause drought, a royal burden in the Kural, is spread over common people and the household.
list_adds: It sets the king beside commoners and a wife as equal causes of drought, widening the couplet's royal sanction to the whole society.

note: Kural 955 says an old family does not part from its nature even when its means of giving shrink; Thirikadugam makes the worth that keeps family standing from falling, even when shaken, one of three things chief among all that is heard.
teaches: The couplet observes that old families hold firm; the verse turns that observation into a thing to be taught and ranked first, so constancy of lineage becomes the content of instruction, not only its result.
list_adds: It ranks family constancy with renown from giving to the distressed and with daily widening of friendship, so lineage is made one of three practices that head all teaching.

note: Kural 418 says ears not pierced by listening are deaf though they hear; Sirupanchamoolam 32 says the one who listens is the flawless great scholar.
teaches: The couplet condemns the unlistening ear; the verse makes listening the very definition of the great scholar, ranking it above reading or composing.
list_adds: It sets the listener beside the poet, whose excellence is in his mind, so hearing and composing are named as two separate excellences.

note: Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world; the verse sets giving with good company and steady hearing and promises the high state.
teaches: The Kural cuts giving loose from reward by a hypothetical; the verse binds it back to a destination, showing the two works disagree on whether the fruit is part of the reason.
list_adds: It pairs giving and company each with its opposite and caps them with hearing as a penance, so giving becomes one step on a road to the high state.

note: Both describe the hero-stone of a man killed recovering cattle, crowned with peacock feather and inscribed with his name (பீலி சூட்டி, பெயர் பொறித்து); 264 mourns the dead man, 131 lines the road with such stones.
teaches: Purananuru 264 shows one stone as a single loss to the bards who depended on the man, and Akananuru 131 shows rows of them as the reason a lover will not travel, so the same memorial carried grief in puram and deterrence in akam.

note: Kural 409 says the unlearned of high birth lack the worth of the learned of low birth; the verse says that in one family the learned youth is praised over the unlearned elder.
teaches: The couplet reverses the rank of birth for learning; the verse reverses the rank of age within a single family, so together learning overturns both of the inherited orders a household runs on.
list_adds: It prefaces the reversal with one fire worshipped in a lamp and scorned in firewood, so the elder and the youth are shown to be one substance valued by what it does.

note: Kural 524 says the fruit of wealth is to live surrounded by one's kin; Iniyavai says the feast for guests of one whose kin stand by him is sweet beyond measure.
teaches: The couplet makes kin the use of wealth and the verse names the guest-feast as the moment that use shows, so the pair links kinship to hospitality.
list_adds: It ranks the kin-supported feast above the fighter's weapons and allies with எத்துணையும் ஆற்ற, so the house's hospitality outranks martial strength.

note: Kural 861 says to avoid opposing the strong and to favour enmity with the weak; Innaa 4 counts doing harm to the very strong as painful, and provoking the fortunate as well.
teaches: The Innaa keeps the couplet's first half and drops its second: the danger of opposing the strong stands without the counsel to turn on the weak, and it is widened to those who merely have fortune.
list_adds: It sets the harm done to the strong beside the ox-less farmer and the fleeing soldier, so the act is counted as self-inflicted loss rather than weighed as strategy.

note: 27 names three faults of the mind, 28 four faults of the mouth.
teaches: Read in sequence, the two verses (with 29) show the work laying out a full ten-part scheme of faults by faculty, mind three, speech four, body three, spread over consecutive verses.

note: Both have the wife's side refuse the husband who has been with other women: the Kural's woman will not touch the chest other women's eyes have fed on, the friend of 46 refuses him the door and says 'go, who stops you'.
teaches: The Kural compresses into one refusal what the Sangam poem makes a situation with a hidden buffalo image, a report of a new marriage and a mocking release, so the couplet is the end point of a whole marutham scene.

note: Akananuru 242 calls the velan who holds the veri rite ignorant (அறியா வேலன்): he blames the god for what is love; Paripadal 5.15-17 says the velan's praise and veri are neither true nor false, since the world lies within the god's bound.
teaches: Read together, the pair shows that the akam mockery of the velan was not a rejection of Murugan: the devotional poet keeps the rite valid at the level of the god while conceding that its particular verdicts may miss, which is exactly the room the akam friend exploits.

note: Kural 262 says penance comes to those who have it and is futile for those without; the Innaa line names what such a man lacks, நிறை, self-restraint.
teaches: The Innaa line fills the Kural's circular condition with content: the 'தவம் one must already have' is the inner restraint without which penance is a pain.
list_adds: It names the missing quality (நிறை) and files the empty penance with other things whose holding power is gone.

note: Kural 968 asks whether feeding the body is a medicine once dignity is lost; Nanmanikkadigai says hunger is better than eating with dignity undone.
teaches: The couplet questions the worth of a life fed without honour; the verse states the choice as a meal: go hungry rather than eat so.
list_adds: It places the choice among three other preferences of the plain over the spoiled (drum over untuned lute, a firm woman over worthless men, fire over parting), so hunger is one of four lesser goods.

note: Kural 214 says one who knows what is fitting lives and anyone else is counted among the dead; the line calls being without understanding the worst death.
teaches: The couplet makes the living death a matter of not knowing ஒப்புரவு; the line widens it to any lack of understanding and ranks it below bodily death, while 52 in the same ten keeps the couplet's other half, knowing ஒப்புரவு as the best gain.
list_adds: The ten splits the couplet's antithesis across two separate lines (52 and 56), so knowing one's duty and lacking understanding become a highest gain and a worst death in a series of superlatives.

note: Naladiyar 268 sees the shameless feasting at home while those with shame walk far and eat scraps; the line counts a shameless life as no better than hunger.
teaches: The quatrain records the outward fact that shamelessness feeds well, and the line answers it by counting that full stomach as hunger, so together they give the complaint and its reply.
list_adds: The line states as a measure what the quatrain shows as a scene, setting the shameless life among ten counterfeit goods that equal their lacks.

note: Kural 360 says pain perishes when the very names of desire, anger and confusion perish; Thirikadugam names a world passing in darkness, anger that speaks without knowledge and desire for worthless things as what belongs to a creature in folly.
teaches: The verse gives each of the Kural's three its mark (confusion as a darkened world, anger as speech without knowledge, desire as love of the worthless), so the couplet's bare names gain definitions.
list_adds: It describes each member of the triad by its effect and assigns all three to the fool, where the couplet only names them as what must be destroyed.

note: Two responses to the same crisis mark the moral range of the Book of Wealth. When honour or distress comes, those like the yak give up life (969), and the base sell theirs for a price, in haste (1080).
teaches: The book ends on the second.

note: Both use the fishhook: Kural 931 likens gambling winnings to the hook a fish swallows; Thirikadugam names the frog wrapped round a hook as bait.
teaches: The ethics group uses the hook for any pleasure that is the means of capture: the Kural shows it from inside the fish after the gain, Thirikadugam at the bait before it.
list_adds: It turns the hook from an image of gambling gains into one of three snares beside flattery by a courtesan and by a foe.

note: Kural 343 says the field of the five must be crushed and all desire let go; the verse sets restraint of the five and wanting nothing against four rejected practices.
teaches: The verse supplies what the couplet leaves out, the practices that do not count, so restraint of the senses is defined against bathing and bodily austerity rather than only stated.
list_adds: It sets the couplet's restraint of the five against four rejected practices, a contrast the couplet lacks.

note: Naladiyar 139 says the unlearned who keep company with the learned gain sense daily; verse 55 says the unlearned who stay outside the learned's company gain only laughter.
teaches: The quatrain gives the remedy and the verse gives the cost of refusing it, so together they make company, not learning alone, the line between gaining sense and being mocked.
list_adds: It grades rewards (gold, wealth, fame, laughter) by kind of learning and company, setting the unlearned at the bottom of a ladder the quatrain does not draw.

note: Naladiyar 11 says the wise renounced in childhood knowing grey hair would come; the verse says no one has gained unaging youth.
teaches: The quatrain turns the loss of youth into a reason to renounce early; the verse states only that the loss is universal, so the pair shows the Naladiyar's renunciation resting on a premise the other book states without that conclusion.
list_adds: It sets youth among strength, life and wealth, all lost alike, so the loss of youth is not singled out as the Naladiyar's chapter makes it.

items: பங்கமில் செய்கைய ராகிப் பரிந்துயார்க்கும் அன்புடைய ராதல்
தந்தையே ஆயினுந் தானடங்கான் ஆகுமேல் கொண்டடையா னாகல்

note: Naladiyar 271 says sharing what is cooked before eating is true cooking, and the door of the next world shuts on those who shut the door and eat; verse 48 has the householder call out the meal and rewards him with kingship.
teaches: The two give the same act opposite outcomes: the closed door and closed heaven in the Naladiyar, the public rice-call and a sword-held kingdom in Elathi, so the meal's openness decides the next life in both.
list_adds: It makes the open meal one of five household marks, with keeping guests and cherishing kin, where the quatrain argues the single act with a punishment.

note: Verse 44 names five qualities without which a woman cannot be held by her husband; verse 52 names six by which a wife holds him.
teaches: The two verses look at the same marriage from opposite ends: what lets a husband keep a wife within bounds and what lets a wife bring a husband to yield, so the book treats control as running both ways.

note: Kural 403 says the unlearned are good if they can keep silent before the learned; verse 9 says the unlearned man's tongue dies before those who know the good.
teaches: The couplet makes silence a choice that redeems; the verse makes it a shame that strikes, so the same silence is a virtue in one and a punishment in the other.
list_adds: It sets the unlearned man's mute tongue beside the killer's, the false witness's and the debtor's, so ignorance is ranked with guilt as a cause of shame.

note: Kural 44 says a household that fears blame and shares its food never loses its line; verse 46 counts not blaming and sharing with all among the marks of a good house.
teaches: The couplet's two conditions of a lasting house reappear inside a longer list that adds care for dependants and for the calf, so the house's sharing is carried to its animals.
list_adds: It places sharing beside not milking a calf to death, so household generosity is extended to the livestock, which the couplet does not reach.

note: Kural 619 says effort yields its wage of bodily strain even where fate will not grant the end; 96 says one who wants plenty does not shun வருத்தம்.
teaches: The line makes toil necessary for plenty and the couplet makes it rewarding even against fate, so the pair gives both halves: there is no abundance without strain, and strain is never wholly unpaid.
list_adds: Among goals and their unbroken practices, the list makes toil the specific price of surplus, beside pain as the price of pleasure, a pairing of goal and cost the couplet's defence of effort against fate does not make.

note: Thirikadugam 4, item 3, counts taking into one's hand a man who once raged against one among the acts of one bound for death; the line calls joining with a hostile intimate poor.
teaches: Thirikadugam calls the embrace of a former foe deadly and Muthumozhikkanchi calls it worthless, so the same act is judged by its danger in one list and by its yield in the other.

note: Line 11 says a great house shows in kindness; line 16 says a small house shows in pride.
teaches: The pair shows the ten treating rank of birth as real yet legible only in conduct, with kindness and pride as its two marks.

note: Kural 395 says the learned learnt by standing before those who know as the poor stand yearning before the rich; 93 says the would-be learner never drops வழிபாடு.
teaches: The couplet gives the learner's posture as a beggar's longing, and the line gives it as worship that never lapses, so the pair shows humility in learning as both a hunger and a sustained service.
list_adds: In a ten that pairs each goal with the practice its seeker never drops, reverence is set beside toil for plenty and penance for steadfastness, so it reads as the price of learning, where the couplet uses it to rank the learned above the unlearned.

note: Kural 773 calls தறுகண் great manliness and gives it kindness to the fallen foe as its edge; the line says that தறுகண்மை in excess (கழி) is no better than the பேடி's lack of it.
teaches: The Kural refines valour by adding mercy as its edge, and the line limits it by measure, so the pair shows two separate checks on courage: mercy to the fallen and restraint in excess.
list_adds: Set in a ten where each thing is equated with its seeming opposite, it makes the over-bold and the coward one kind, a turn the couplet's praise of valour does not make.

note: Verse 53 names five kinsmen who guard a woman; verse 54 says she falls if she herself does not guard her restraint.
teaches: Placed side by side in the book, the two verses split the guard between the men of her family and her own நிறை, so the book holds both views the Kural sets against each other.

note: Naladiyar 135 says learning has no shore and life is short; Thirikadugam praises one who has seen the shore of the texts.
teaches: Read together, mastering a body of texts (நூல்) is possible while learning (கல்வி) itself has no end, so the two claims are about different things.
list_adds: It ranks the one who reached the texts' shore with a steady mind and freedom from delusion as three who stand on truth.

note: Iniyavai calls giving with knowledge of one's income sweet; Innaa 39 counts the liberality of one with nothing to give as painful. They say the same thing from two sides.
teaches: Read as a pair, the twin books fix one measure for giving from opposite ends: the pleasure lies inside one's income and the pain begins outside it.

note: Kural 1065 says nothing is sweeter than thin gruel won by one's own effort; Iniyavai 11 says nothing is nobler than refusing to eat from unworthy hands even unto death.
teaches: Both close on the same 'nothing above it' form, but the couplet praises the food one earns and the verse the food one refuses, so the pair shows the two halves of a single code of eating with dignity.
list_adds: It caps a list about not living off the road and not taking crookedly with a refusal unto death, so the list climbs from avoiding gain to giving up life.

note: Kural 523 likens the life of one who does not mingle with kin to a tank filling with water but with no bank; Thirikadugam says the wealth of one who does not help his kin perishes while seeming to exist.
teaches: The Kural's tank shows the water running off; the verse adds that the loss is hidden, the wealth still seems to be there, so the tank looks full while it drains.
list_adds: It groups kinless wealth with untended farming and a drinker's family name as three goods lost while still in sight.

note: Verse 96 gives the rain-command to the wife, the ascetic and the king; verse 98 makes the fire-priests, the just king and the obedient wife the seed of the month's three rains.
teaches: The pair shows the book's rain list is fixed on king and wife but varies its third member between ascetic and fire-priest, and moves from command to seed, from a single word to a monthly cause.

note: Both are night-tryst poems the lover overhears, and both close on the same formula, a tusker and his mate asleep on the plantain slope (வாழையஞ் சிலம்பிற் றுஞ்சும் / வாழையம் சிலம்பில் துஞ்சும்): in 328 he strokes a mate who has just calved, in 332 he lies down with her after killing a tiger.
teaches: A shared formula takes a different act each time to suit the speech: the calving mate presses toward married life in a poem of fear, the tiger-killing protector confirms the lover in a poem of praise.

note: Kural 80 says a body without love is bone wrapped in skin, implying love makes it more.
teaches: The Naladiyar treats every body as filth wrapped in skin and allows no such exception.

note: 38 reckons the support of a fool no better than being alone; 80 says that for those with no support, violent killing comes easily.
teaches: Joined, the two lines make an argument the book never states: a fool's support leaves one as good as alone, and to be without support is to be easily killed, so a foolish protector exposes a person to the same danger as none.

note: Thirikadugam 16 counts one who digs a well of drinking water without stint among three who gain a body that does not die; the verse counts a shared well among five works leading to heaven.
teaches: The two counted works reward the same well differently, one with a deathless name in this world and the other with heaven, so the group divides on where the fruit of public works falls.

note: Kural 57 asks what use confinement is and says a woman's own steadfastness is the best guard; Nanmanikkadigai says a woman without a bond goes as she pleases though guarded.
teaches: The Kural moves the guard inside the woman; the quatrain adds desire that flows on though blocked and murder that clings though hidden, so the failure of guarding becomes a general law about inner nature.
list_adds: It sets the guarded woman beside desire and a hidden killing, so the claim widens from women to everything that outward control cannot hold.

note: Kural 1147 has the woman say her love-sickness grows with the town's gossip as manure and her mother's words as water; in Akananuru 273 she says the sickness sprouted between her breasts, grew a trunk, spread branches of gossip and budded with scandal into a tree shading the world.
teaches: The Kural's two-line plant metaphor, gossip feeding the disease, is the seed of Avvaiyar's full tree, which adds the stages of growth and makes the scandal not only food for the love but its flowering.

note: Kural 871 says enmity should not be wanted even in jest; Nanmanikkadigai says enmity sprouts from a man's own prior intent and then becomes a seed of suffering.
teaches: The couplet warns against wanting enmity, and the verse explains why: it grows from one's own intention and multiplies into more pain.
list_adds: It sets enmity beside fire from smoke and joy from laughter, so laughter seeds joy while intent seeds enmity, a contrast to the couplet's 'not even in jest'.

note: Kural 325 makes the one who refrains from killing the chief of all renouncers; Thirikadugam counts him among those who are the world.
teaches: The Kural honours non-killing at the head of renunciation; the verse honours it in ordinary social life, so it is a summit in both ways of living.
list_adds: It sets the non-killer beside a considerate guest and a teacher of good conduct, taking non-killing out of the renouncers' ranking into everyday company.

note: Kural 342 says to renounce while there is time; verse 45, on the reading that விடுப்பான் is letting the kingdom go, says the giver will rule, conquer and quickly give it up.
teaches: On that reading the verse makes kingship a stage on the way to renunciation, a reward meant to be left, where the couplet speaks of renouncing what one already has.
list_adds: It sets renunciation at the end of a reward sequence (rule, conquest, release) earned by six marks of conduct, so the couplet's counsel becomes the last step of a karmic career.

note: Kural 972 says birth is alike for all and distinction differs by what one does; Thirikadugam counts the man not born in an excellent line as born yet unborn, on the reading that விழுத்திணை is a high birth-group, not conduct.
teaches: The ethics group splits on whether lineage can void a life: the couplet places worth in work, the verse places a birth condition beside illiteracy and boasting as equal disqualifiers.
list_adds: It puts low birth in one row with two faults one can mend, so birth is treated as a fault of the same kind as conduct, which the couplet denies.

note: The Kural says the great accomplish deeds that are hard; the line says the hardness of great things is not to be complained of.
teaches: Together they show the link between பெருமை and அருமை from both ends: the great man takes on difficulty, and the onlooker should not resent that great things are difficult.
list_adds: Paired with its mirror line 24 in a ten on what is not blamed, it turns the couplet's praise of the great into a rule for those who judge them and their works.

note: Naladiyar 255 has the worthy keep their learning unspoken, even when asked, where it will not be taken in; Pazhamozhi 14 gives the cost of speaking there.
teaches: The Naladiyar gives the practice, silence even when asked, and Pazhamozhi gives the reason, that good words among the unlearned turn bad.

note: Kural 341 says each thing one leaves removes the pain it would bring; Thirikadugam says a mind that has left many things is a rope to merit.
teaches: The couplet gives detachment a negative yield (pain removed); the verse gives it a positive one (merit bound), so letting go both frees and gains.
list_adds: It sets the detached mind beside the gift and honourable conduct, so the renouncer's letting go and the householder's giving are one kind of rope.

note: Naladiyar 158 says one deaf to others' secrets, blind to a neighbour's wife and dumb in evil backbiting needs no teaching of virtue; Elathi 19 names the same deafness to secrets and dumbness to evil speech, with not killing and not lying, as the marks of one greater than a king.
teaches: The shared images of deafness and dumbness show the two Jain works using one figure for restraint, and Elathi's addition of non-killing turns the Naladiyar's man who needs no teaching into a rank above kings.
list_adds: It sets the Naladiyar's restraints of the senses after non-killing, not causing killing and not lying, so sense restraint is ranked behind non-violence and truth in a seven-part list.

note: Kural 113 says to let go at once of gain that leaves fairness, even if it brings good; Thirikadugam counts not speaking partially, whatever one gains, as the work of the pure.
teaches: The Kural sets fairness against gain; the verse calls the same refusal a purity, so impartial speech is a cleanliness and not only a justice.
list_adds: It makes impartiality one of three purities with bathing before meals and nobility unto death, joining a bodily rite to two inner virtues.

note: Kural 1014 calls modesty the ornament of the worthy; Thirikadugam calls it the ornament of a woman in love.
teaches: The Kural gives naanam to the saandror without regard to sex; the verse gives it to the woman, so the same virtue is, in the two books, a mark of nobility and a gendered duty.
list_adds: It sets the woman's modesty between the eye's kindness and learning for the next life, giving each ornament its own wearer.

note: Kural 255 says the standing of life lies in not eating flesh and hell will not release the one who eats; Sirupanchamoolam 33 says the one led upward who never begins on flesh is sure to go there.
teaches: The couplet threatens the meat-eater with a hell that does not open; the verse promises the abstainer a sure passage, and ties the abstention to the teacher who leads him, so diet becomes the proof of being led.
list_adds: It ends a list of true titles (liberal man, merchant, teacher) with abstaining from flesh as the condition of the pupil's passage.

note: The Kural gives guarding against what is coming as a mark of understanding; the verse makes it one of a great minister's three daily practices.
teaches: Foresight that the Kural praises as a private wisdom becomes, in a minister, an office: one prevents the blow by knowing the enemy king's state every day.
list_adds: It binds foresight to self-discipline and daily watch on hostile kings, so prevention is shown as the minister's working method rather than a trait.

note: Verses 18 and 20 both close a list of abstentions, meat last, with the promise that one will not take a body again.
teaches: The book states the same Jain promise twice in three verses, with meat as the final condition each time, which shows how central diet is to its idea of release.

note: Thirikadugam 19 counts one who grips the tusk of a killing elephant among three who hang by a thread; the verse shuns the place where a fierce elephant is let loose.
teaches: Both counted works use the killing elephant as the type of avoidable danger and set human follies beside it, so folly with people is measured against folly with beasts.

note: Kural 303 says forget anger at anyone at all, since evils are born of it; verse 16 says anger is good and nobility bad before people without worth.
teaches: On the plain reading of verse 16 the two disagree about the same act: the Kural allows no exception to forgoing anger, while the verse makes the base an exception.
list_adds: It inverts three house virtues at once (anger, nobility, pride) for one audience, so the exception is a rule, not a lapse.

note: Kural 1046 says the words of the poor go slack even when well understood; the Innaa line counts the very grace of speech in a poor man's mouth as painful.
teaches: The pair moves the loss from the listeners to the speaker: the Kural notes that no one heeds, the Innaa line that fine speech which cannot land is itself a pain.
list_adds: It sets poverty beside want of learning and skill, so wealth and learning appear as the two things that give speech its weight.

note: Kural 218 says those who know what is due do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even when without means; Nanmanikkadigai calls liberality at a time without means a fault.
teaches: On the plain reading the two disagree about giving when poor: the Kural praises it as knowledge of duty, the quatrain counts it a fault of timing, so the ethics books split over whether means limit generosity.
list_adds: It sets giving beyond one's means among faults of wrong timing, learning missed in youth and anger without kin, so liberality is judged by its season.

note: Kural 1039 says land the owner does not visit sulks like a wife; Thirikadugam says the farming of one who does not tend the green crop at ripening perishes.
teaches: The couplet asks for the owner's steady presence; the verse names the moment when absence is fatal, the time of ripening, so neglect is located in time.
list_adds: It sets the untended harvest beside kinless wealth and a drinker's lineage, making all three cases of loss that looks like having.

note: Kural 539 says to think of those ruined by negligence when one is swollen with joy; Thirikadugam counts speaking heedlessly at a time of gain as a sign of the body that does not last.
teaches: The couplet treats elated negligence as a danger to be remedied by memory, while the verse reads the same heedless word as a mark of mortality, so forgetting at a gain is shown to be forgetting that one will die.
list_adds: It sets heedless speech at a gain beside the cry at the end and shame at a withering body, so negligence is ranked with dying itself as a sign of a perishable life rather than as a tactical fault.

note: Thirikadugam 77 opens with கயவரைக் கையிகந்து வாழ்தல் and makes it a mark of those whose family has no stain; Iniyavai 29 opens with கயவரைக் கைகழிந்து வாழ்தல் and calls it sweet.
teaches: The near-identical line shows a saying circulating between the counted works, and the different predicates show each bending it: a sign of good birth in one, a pleasure open to anyone in the other.

note: Iniyavai Narpathu 4 names not swelling one's flesh by eating flesh as foremost sweet; the verse says the one who eats sweetly is the one who eats without killing.
teaches: The two state one claim from two sides: Iniyavai calls the abstention sweet, and the verse calls the meal sweet only if it involves no killing, so sweetness belongs to the eating, not the food.

items: ஊனங்கொண் டாடார் உறுதி உடையவை கோள்முறையாற் கோடல்

note: Kural 323 ranks not killing first and not lying after it; Sirupanchamoolam 38 calls not lying, wealth and not killing each good without ranking them.
teaches: Set beside the couplet, the verse declines the Kural's ranking of the two vows and admits wealth among the goods between them, a Jain list that values non-killing without making it the single highest good here.
list_adds: It lists not lying, wealth and not killing side by side with wealth in the middle, where the couplet orders the two vows and leaves wealth out.

note: Kural 391 says learn flawlessly and then stand by what is learned; Elathi 4 says that where six kinds of kindly conduct are seen, the books of learning may be let go.
teaches: The Kural makes conduct the completion of learning, while Elathi makes it a substitute: together they show two orders, learning that leads to conduct and conduct that makes the books unnecessary.
list_adds: It names the six acts that do the books' work (relieving distress, not scorning, shunning the base, relieving grief, avoiding blame, desired speech), so the conduct that replaces learning is specified, which 391 leaves general.

note: In Purananuru 343 a father refuses suitors even if they bow and offer wealth (விழுப்பொருள்) like Muziri's, where ships bring gold for pepper; in Akananuru 149 the man refuses precious wealth (விழுப்பொருள்) even if easily won, beside Muziri where Yavana ships bring gold and take pepper.
teaches: Muziri's sea trade was the stock measure of the wealth a woman outweighs, used by the war poem for a father keeping his daughter and by the love poem for a husband keeping his wife.

note: Kural 395 says the foremost are those who learnt while yearning before teachers like the poor before the rich; saying 8 ranks serving the learned above learning.
teaches: The Kural makes humility before the learned the posture of learning, while the saying ranks that reverence above the learning it leads to, so the means is put above the end.
list_adds: It ranks the service of the learned against learning itself, where the couplet only makes the one the manner of the other.

note: Kural 46 asks what one gains by leaving a virtuous household for the outside way; the verse says household life is better than a mean dharma.
teaches: The Kural's question reaches toward renunciation itself; the verse limits the claim to a poor or false dharma, a narrower comparison from a Jain text that honours the ascetic.
list_adds: It adds the fruit of the household, that feeding the virtuous returns as the means to feed again, which the couplet's rhetorical question does not name.

note: Kural 369 says that when craving, the sorrow of sorrows, perishes, joy is unbroken; Elathi 66 describes the high state only by six absences, sweet sleep among them.
teaches: The Kural names the goal as unbroken joy, while Elathi refuses even sleep's sweetness to it, so the pair shows two ways of naming release: as fullness of joy or as the cessation of every state, pleasant or painful.
list_adds: It defines the goal by a list of negations that strikes out goods (light, speech, sleep) along with ills, which the couplet's single positive term does not do.

note: Kural 575 calls kindly regard the eye's only jewel; verse 8 calls it the eye's beauty and gives four other members their beauties.
teaches: The couplet stops at the eye; the verse runs the same 'X's beauty is Y' through feet, reckoning, song and king, so the last two beauties are other people's praise.
list_adds: It sets the eye's beauty in a series that ends with a king judged by his people, so kindly regard becomes the first of a scale from the body to rule.

note: Kural 69 has the mother rejoice when her son is called worthy; 183 has the mother's heart turn toward the accomplished child among children of one womb.
teaches: Where the Kural shows a mother's joy at one son's public praise, the Purananuru admits the harder consequence, that learning makes her favour one child over his brothers, so the pair shows that the honour of learning reorders even family love.

note: Kural 1041 says nothing is more painful than poverty except poverty; Thirikadugam names want as the sorrow proper to human birth, beside the ghost's hunger and the beast's fear.
teaches: The Kural makes poverty incomparable among human pains; the verse explains its place: each kind of birth has its own sorrow and want is the human one.
list_adds: It sets human want beside the hunger of ghosts and the fear of beasts, so poverty becomes the human share of a sorrow common to all births.

note: Iniyavai 32 names as sweet the purpose of an undertaking (கருமப் பொருள்) as those who know its surroundings explain it; Innaa 15 names the same thing explained by the unlearned as painful.
teaches: The same phrase is sweet or painful in the two books depending only on who speaks it, which shows that both make the counsellor's knowledge, not the undertaking, decide its worth.

note: Kural 1065 says even thin gruel is sweetest when earned by one's own effort; Thirikadugam says the one who values gruel as ghee-rice has seen the truth.
teaches: The Kural makes gruel sweet because it is one's own; the verse makes it sweet because the seer no longer ranks foods, so one ground is self-respect and the other indifference.
list_adds: It puts the gruel among three reversals of speech and taste, so its sweetness comes from a way of seeing, not from how it was earned.

note: Naladiyar 180 says people spotless in mind are scorned for their company, as sandal burns with the scrub; the verse says blame and fame come from company.
teaches: The quatrain shows the cost the verse only states: a spotless mind does not save one from the blame of one's company.
list_adds: It states the rule in two halves, company for name and mind for understanding, where the quatrain gives only the half on reputation.

note: Kural 408 says wealth in the hands of the unlearned is more painful than poverty among the good; Thirikadugam counts the unlearned among those already joined to poverty.
teaches: Read together, the unlearned rich man is poor twice: the couplet makes his coin a grief and the verse makes him poor in what he never took in, so poverty is a lack of intake as well as of money.
list_adds: It sets the unlearned with a tank whose inlet fails and an infant not fed full, so lack of learning becomes a vessel that cannot fill, a kind of poverty the couplet does not name.

note: The Kural says the asker's heart rejoices at givers who give without scorn; the verse counts the man who laughs at one asking for a gift among those who hold to nothing.
teaches: The Kural shows the asker's side and Thirikadugam the scorner's: mocking an asker is not just meanness but a sign of a man without any principle.
list_adds: It sets mocking a beggar beside killing to eat and presuming on the great, so contempt for the asker is ranked with flesh-eating as a lack of rule.

note: Naladiyar 386 says beauty in a modest woman is like learning in the wise or a sword in a hero's hand; verse 44 says that without modesty and four other qualities even Lakshmi's beauty cannot be held.
teaches: The pair state one claim from both sides: modesty makes beauty serviceable, and beauty without it is ungovernable, so beauty in both works has worth only as the instrument of a virtue.
list_adds: It names four qualities beside modesty and sets them against beauty at its divine limit, a ranking the quatrain's three similes leave implicit.

note: Kural 888: a house with inner enmity wears itself away like gold rubbed by a file; 45: two Cholas wearing the same aar garland fight, so whichever loses, their own house loses.
teaches: The Kural's file image says the house wears itself down, and 45 supplies the political arithmetic behind it, that between two branches of one house no outcome is a win and the only gain goes to rival dynasties, so the couplet's metaphor gets a concrete case and an outside beneficiary.

note: Kural 562 tells the ruler to raise the rod sharply but bring it down lightly; saying 2 ranks being held in awe above being loved, on the plainer reading of கண்ணஞ்சப் படுதல்.
teaches: The Kural allows awe only as a measured show that must not become harm, while the saying ranks awe over love outright and for anyone, so the pair shows how far the measure matters.
list_adds: It ranks awe directly against affection, a contrast the couplet lacks, and carries it beyond the king to every person the frame addresses.

note: Kural 57 says the guarding of women by confinement achieves nothing and their own steadfastness is the best guard; Thirikadugam counts women among three things whose guarding must not be slighted. The tension holds on reading காப்பு in 47 as the householder's watch over women.
teaches: The two books disagree on who keeps a woman's virtue: the Kural moves the guard inside her and calls custody useless, the Thirikadugam keeps it with the man as with his wealth and food.
list_adds: It ranks women with earned treasure and good food as goods to be watched, which is the custodial view the couplet sets aside.

note: Kural 942 says the body needs no medicine if one eats after the last meal is digested; the verse says food burns a body that takes no pleasure in it.
teaches: The couplet gives the rule for eating, the verse the damage when the body cannot take food, so the pair shows food as medicine or fire depending on the body's state.
list_adds: It sets food beside words, past deeds and an army, all things meant to serve that turn and burn their holder.

note: Kural 263 chides householders who have forgotten penance in providing for renunciants; Elathi 3 says outright that penance is easy and giving is hard.
teaches: Read with 263, the verse reverses the ranking the Kural's chiding implies: if giving is the harder task, the householder who gives instead of doing penance has chosen the steeper road.
list_adds: It sets penance and giving as the first of several easy-hard pairs, so the ranking of the two is stated as a rule of difficulty rather than left to a rhetorical question.

note: Purananuru 43 recalls the Chola ancestor who entered the scales for a dove; Elathi 20 praises one who delights in giving even when it is like cutting off a limb.
teaches: Read with Puram 43, Elathi's simile carries the memory of the king who gave his own flesh: the heroic deed of an ancestor becomes the measure of ordinary giving for anyone.

note: Both sayings turn on நேர்தல்: the friend whose heart does not agree, the learning gained without consent or submission.
teaches: Placed side by side, the two make friendship and learning both depend on an act of assent, so the pupil's submission to learning is the same act as the friend's agreement of heart.

note: On the reading that the world abandons those who leave a task short, the Kural blames the shortfall that this line excuses.
teaches: The pair divides the unfinished task in two: abandoning it in the middle draws the world's blame, while a work that simply could not be done in full does not.
list_adds: The ten's predicate puts the onlooker's verdict first, where the couplet speaks to the worker, so the line adds the case the couplet leaves open, a deficiency not chosen.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 35 says giving brings enjoyment, penance heaven and knowledge release; Elathi 76 says giving brings enjoyment, penance heaven and penance that does not cling brings release.
teaches: The two Jain works share the first two rungs word for word but differ on the third, knowledge in one and a deeper penance in the other, so the pair shows a live question within the group about what finally frees.

note: 36 counts a man without wealth longing to be liberal; 39 counts liberality practised by one who has nothing to give.
teaches: The poet counts the moneyless giver twice, once in the wish and once in the act, so the pain is not only frustrated desire but the giving itself carried on without means.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 33 says only he who leads one to the higher state is a teacher; Elathi 75 says a teacher's fitness lies in knowing the six schools and refuting a false teacher's word.
teaches: One verse defines the teacher by where he leads, the other by what he can defend, so together they give the Jain teacher's two tests: the goal he serves and his mastery of rival doctrine.

note: Kural 113 says to let go at once of gain that comes from leaving fairness; Iniyavai calls sweetest the discernment that speaks no wrong even when one's fortune is being destroyed.
teaches: The couplet refuses unfair gain and the verse refuses unfair speech even to escape ruin, so the pair carries fairness from getting to speaking under loss.
list_adds: It puts this item last as the sweetest of three, after not begging and remembering death, so integrity under ruin outranks the other two.

note: The Naladiyar says if poverty makes giving impossible, not begging is worth twice giving; the line says the poor man's lack of generosity is not blamed.
teaches: Together they show the poor man's position from both sides: others owe him no reproach for not giving, and he keeps a virtue of his own in not asking.
list_adds: The quatrain gives the poor man a substitute duty; the line instead binds the onlooker, placing the poor man beside the untrained and the small as people whose shortfall is excused.

note: Verse 12 calls killing and eating flesh poison among five poisons; verse 50 calls not killing good and killing bad, then weighs illiteracy and anger on the same scale.
teaches: Within the book, killing is the fixed first term of two lists, and in each the author sets lesser faults (overpowering the weak, slander, illiteracy, anger) beside it, so its scale of harms keeps killing as the measure.

note: Kural 392 calls numbers and letters the two eyes of living beings; Elathi 74 calls the beauty of numbers and letters the only beauty.
teaches: The verse takes the Kural's very pair, எண் and எழுத்து, and moves it from the sense of sight to the standard of beauty, so learning is both how one sees and how one is seen.
list_adds: It sets the pair of 392 against six bodily beauties, so learning wins a contest the couplet never stages.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 72 says a mouthful given unasked to the weak, the old, those fasting to death, the sick and those who lost their land makes the giver a king; verse 52 makes kings of those who feed people who lost house, eyes, wealth, paddy or herds.
teaches: The two works state one rule, food to the ruined earns kingship, but Elathi defines need wholly by loss while Sirupanchamoolam includes the dying ascetic, so they draw the circle of the needy differently.

note: Kural 62 says blameless children of good character keep evils from a parent for seven births; the verse says a man's blamelessness is seen in his children.
teaches: The couplet makes good children a protection for the parent and the verse makes them the evidence of the parent's worth, so read together the child both shows and secures the father's blamelessness.
list_adds: It puts children among four kinds of evidence (ruin for friendship, wealth's movement for prosperity), so the child becomes a sign to be read rather than a blessing to be had.

note: Kural 421 calls understanding the tool and inner fortress that guards against faults; the line says a lapse of understanding exposes the other lapses.
teaches: Read together, the fortress image explains the line: once understanding gives way, the faults it guarded behind it come into view.
list_adds: It moves understanding from a guard to a sign, placing its failure among the ten's ways of reading a person.

note: Sirupanchamoolam counts the spider's eggs, the crab's young and abuse to the tongue as each one's own death; Nanmanikkadigai has the plantain's fruit and the unlearned man's own words.
teaches: Both books use a creature killed by its own offspring to say that speech kills the speaker, so the image of self-born death is a shared stock of the ethics group, applied each time to the tongue.

note: Kural 1066 says nothing degrades the tongue more than asking, even for water for a cow; the line says no disgrace goes beyond begging.
teaches: The couplet tests the claim at its hardest case, a worthy cause and a tiny request, while the line states it bare, so the pair shows the superlative holds without exception for need or motive.
list_adds: Coupled with 60, the line's list sets the asker's disgrace beside the giver's distinction, so begging is judged inside an exchange rather than alone as the couplet judges it.

note: Kural 1066 says nothing degrades the tongue like begging, even water for a cow; verse 9 says the well-born man's tongue dies when he has eaten and knows it.
teaches: Both place the shame of dependence in the tongue; on our reading of the verse, eating from the wrong hand silences the well-born as begging degrades the asker.
list_adds: It sets the well-born man's shame beside the debtor's, so the list treats owing and being fed as one kind of silencing.

note: Naladiyar 245 says people are not as their kind but as their minds; the verse keeps understanding in the mind while granting company power over blame and fame.
teaches: With the Naladiyar the verse forms a Jain answer to the Kural's chapter on company: mind, not kind, decides what a person is, though the verse concedes that company decides their name.
list_adds: It concedes to company what the quatrain does not, blame and fame, while agreeing that the mind decides understanding.

note: Innaa 4 counts the soil's moisture passing unused for ploughmen without oxen; Innaa 20 counts ploughing with a sluggish ox as painful.
teaches: The book grades the ploughman's lack across two verses: with no ox the wet season is lost, and with a sluggish ox it is wasted, so the ox decides whether the rain is of use.

note: Iniyavai 34 calls leaving the friendship of worthless people, even when they cling, sweet; the Innaa line calls association with those without goodness painful. The same thing from two sides.
teaches: Together they give both the cost and the remedy: the Innaa names the pain of the tie, the Iniyavai the sweetness of cutting it even when the other holds on.

note: Kural 782 says the friendship of the good waxes like the moon and that of fools wanes after being full; saying 10 ranks not dwindling above a large beginning.
teaches: The Kural's moon image is about friendship; the saying states its principle bare, for any course of fortune or bond, and keeps only the half that matters: holding, not starting great.
list_adds: It strips the image and the domain of friendship and ranks endurance over a large start as a general rule.

note: Naladiyar 52 has the best reflect on impermanence, disease, old age and death and do their own work; Elathi 24 lists disease, birth, old age, death, sorrow and want and names the work as the way of release.
teaches: Read together, the quatrain's unnamed 'own work' is given a name and its four evils gain birth and want, so the round of births itself becomes the thing to escape.
list_adds: It adds birth and unending want to the Naladiyar's four, making the list the cycle of births rather than the ills of one life.

note: Here நிறை is the guard that outdoes all confinement. In 1251, speaking as a woman in love, desire's axe breaks the door of நிறை barred with shame.
teaches: The book's ethics section treats inner guard as sufficient, and its love section knows it isn't.

note: Kural 24 guards the five with the goad of firmness, implying elephants without naming them; Elathi 11 names the five elephants (ஐங்களிறு) that toss the one who does not cut desire.
teaches: Elathi makes explicit the elephants the couplet only implies, and shows what happens when the goad is missing: the senses carry their rider into the hole of rebirth.
list_adds: It turns the goad image into a narrative of failure, the rider tossed by the five, which the couplet's image of control does not show.

note: Naladiyar 111 says refusing what one cannot give is no fault, but letting an asker's hope (நசை) die after keeping him waiting is worse than ingratitude; Iniyavai calls not killing the hope (நசை) of those who come sweet.
teaches: Both judge a giver by what happens to the asker's hope, the quatrain condemning its slow killing by false promise and the verse praising its keeping, so honesty to the hope matters as much as the gift.
list_adds: It ties keeping askers' hope to a spirit that will not live without regard and a bond that hides nothing, so generosity is grouped with self-respect rather than with promise-keeping.

note: Thirikadugam 45 says the man who without love hides what he can (இயைவ கரப்பான்) from those who ask falls into hell; the line uses the same words and calls the act the greatest cruelty.
teaches: The two works share the phrase for withholding what one can give, and between them name its moral kind (cruelty) and its fate (hell), so refusal is treated as a harm done to the asker, not just a lack of virtue.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 69 counts the one who agreed to a killing among five who share its sin; Elathi 8 opens its list with not consenting and not killing as two separate acts.
teaches: Together the two Jain lists show consent treated as its own act of killing: one assigns it a share of the sin, the other makes refusing it a virtue in its own right.

note: The Kural says penance comes to those who have it and is futile for others; the verse counts penance taken up by one without restraint as seed cast in a thicket.
teaches: Thirikadugam names what the Kural leaves circular: the missing quality is restraint of the heart, so the futility is located in the will.
