list_adds: It ranks futile penance with unjust headship and unruly beauty, so the failure is shown as a general rule of gifts without their inner condition.

note: Line 8 ranks revering the learned above one's own learning; 93 makes unbroken reverent service the condition of learning at all.
teaches: The first ten treats reverence as a value above learning and the last treats it as the road to learning, so the book holds both that service is the means and that it outranks the end.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 61 counts kin, wife, servant, son and neighbour as five household diseases; Thirikadugam 67 counts wife, servants and kin as devouring old karma.
teaches: Two counted works single out the same household cast as a chronic affliction; Sirupanchamoolam calls it disease and adds son and neighbour, Thirikadugam calls it karma and adds old age.

note: Verse 69 counts the lost, suffering guest as hard to come by; verse 76 counts the guest who arrives on a rainy day as hard to tend.
teaches: The same book holds both sides of hospitality: the needy guest is a rare prize and also the hardest burden, so the value and the strain of the guest come together.

note: The Kural says greatness hides another's weakness while smallness tells faults; the line says even the excellent do not blame the conduct of the small.
teaches: The pair shows greatness proved on the very people who invite contempt: not publishing a fault is hardest and most telling when the faulty are the small.
list_adds: Closing a ten of withheld blame, it turns the couplet's portrait of greatness into the last case of a rule, with சிறந்தோரும் marking the eminent as those for whom restraint is due.

note: Kural 121 says restraint leads among the immortals; Thirikadugam gives the heavenly state only to restraint of deed and reserves release for restraint of heart.
teaches: The couplet's single reward of restraint, a place among the gods, becomes in the verse the middle of three rewards, so heaven is placed below release.
list_adds: It splits the Kural's one restraint into three with three fruits, purity, the divine state and release, ranking them.

note: Kural 1057 says the asker rejoices deep within on meeting givers who do not scorn; the line says giving without regard is no better than withholding.
teaches: The couplet locates the worth of a gift in the asker's inner joy at being spared scorn, and the line draws the conclusion from the giver's side: without that regard the gift is as good as refused.
list_adds: It puts the careless gift beside the shameless life and the false helper, ten things that keep the outward form of a good while lacking its substance, which the couplet, focused on the asker, does not do.

note: Kural 19 says giving and penance will not last if the sky does not give rain; the verse says rain does not fall where there are no ascetics.
teaches: The Kural makes penance depend on rain and the verse makes rain depend on penance, so together they describe a circle in which ascetic and sky sustain each other.
list_adds: It makes rain one link in a chain that ends with king and householder, so the couplet's dependence becomes a whole social order resting on the house.

note: Both counted works place the chaste wife first among things that heal: Thirikadugam calls her shoulders part of a medicine, Sirupanchamoolam calls her amrita.
teaches: In both works the wife's chastity heads a list whose other items are public goods (worthy company, learned friends; land, king, soldier), so the household virtue is ranked as a good of the realm.

note: Kural 35 defines virtue as avoiding envy, craving, anger and harsh speech, mixing faults of mind and of speech in one four; Elathi 27 names three faults (coveting, anger, wrong view) and assigns them to the mind alone.
teaches: Set side by side, the Kural's single list is seen sorted in Elathi by the faculty that sins, and wrong view, a doctrinal error, enters a list the Kural keeps to passions.
list_adds: It sorts faults by faculty, mind here and speech and body in the next two verses, and adds wrong view to the passions, a sorting the couplet does not make.

note: Kural 159 says those who bear the harsh words of transgressors are as pure as renouncers; Thirikadugam says the one who takes abuse as sweet speech lives having seen the true thing.
teaches: The couplet praises bearing abuse as endurance; the verse goes further and has abuse heard as sweetness, so the pair shows two grades, enduring the bitter and no longer tasting it as bitter.
list_adds: It sets taking abuse as sweet beside taking gruel as ghee-rice and bitterness as sugar, so patience in speech becomes one case of a general reversal of taste.

note: Kalittokai 1 names three of Shiva's dances (kodukotti, pandarangam, kapalam); Tirumanthiram 2733 lists kodukotti and pandarangam among the dances whose king he is and places them in the nadis and at Tillai.
teaches: The dance names the Tirumanthiram files into a yogic doctrine were already in the oldest love anthology as stage dances with a partner keeping time, so the later mystic list inherited a performance repertoire, not a private vision.

note: 143 asks who the weeping woman at the door was (யார்கொல் அளியள்) without answering; 144 tells the same kind of scene and lets the woman answer that she is no kin of Pekan's and that he goes to another woman.
teaches: Read in sequence, the Pekan poems work as a cycle in which each poet adds what the last withheld: Kapilar leaves the woman unnamed, Paranar gives her a voice and names the cause, so the reproach of a patron was built up by several poets in turn.

note: Kural 1308 asks what use suffering is where there is no lover to know it; the verse says a sulk dies in one who does not understand sulking.
teaches: Both put the life of oodal in the partner's understanding, and the verse adds that the same is true of gratitude, guests and song, so the lover's plight is one case of a general rule.
list_adds: It sets the sulk beside a kindness, a guest and a song, so love's quarrel becomes one of four gifts that die in an incompetent receiver.

note: Uthiyan Cheral's great feast (பெருஞ்சோறு) is praised in Purananuru 2 as a king's gift; here the crowd at that feast becomes a simile for hills crowding on the desert track.
teaches: An akam poet could assume his hearers knew a king's famous feast well enough to turn its crowd of eaters into a picture of a landscape, which tells us how far puram fame was common knowledge.

note: Kural 542 says the people live looking to the king's sceptre as the world looks to the sky; verse 45 says the king rises only as the field bank, water, paddy and people rise beneath him.
teaches: The couplet makes the people depend on the king, while the verse runs the dependence upward from a mud ridge, so read together they show the dependence runs both ways.
list_adds: Its chain of five causes puts the king at the end of a ladder of rises beginning with a field bank, a causal order the couplet does not trace.

note: Verse 9 lists what utter fools love, beginning with moving away from the company of the great; verse 87 lists who are utter fools, including the man who enters a company remote from learning.
teaches: The two verses share the predicate முழுமக்கள் and both define the utter fool by the company he leaves or joins, so the book makes the choice of company the first test of folly.

note: Kural 46 asks what a man who lives household life in virtue would gain by going the outside way; Elathi 73 calls household life and great penance two noble ways of acting.
teaches: The couplet ranks the household above renunciation, while the verse sets the two side by side as one kind of noble life defined by their relation to attachment, so the pair shows Elathi declining the Kural's ranking.
list_adds: It pairs the two ways under one name (வினைவாழ்க்கை) and defines each by how it handles attachment, where the couplet sets them against each other.

note: Here giving and austerity cannot last without rain. In 34, virtue is simply a spotless mind and everything else is noise.
teaches: If virtue is only inward, the drought in 19 shouldn't threaten it.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 18 lists not lying, not stealing, not desiring women and not eating flesh as what ends rebirth; Elathi 29 names killing, theft and lust as the body's faults.
teaches: Taken together, Elathi's body-faults are seen in Sirupanchamoolam as conditions of escaping rebirth, and the sister Jain work adds flesh-eating to the bodily code Elathi frames by faculty.

note: Kural 259 ranks not killing one creature above a thousand sacrifices; the verse says there is beneficence equal to sacrifice.
teaches: Both measure an ethical act against sacrifice, but the Kural puts non-killing above it and the verse puts beneficence level with it, so sacrifice stays the standard in one and is outranked in the other.
list_adds: It makes beneficence equal to sacrifice as a tank can hold a river and a song reach the Veda, so the claim is one of a set of lesser things rising to the greater.

note: Kural 505 makes one's own deeds the single touchstone of greatness and smallness; the line makes deeds the test of manly ability only.
teaches: The Kural uses one test for all worth, while this ten assigns a different sign to each quality, kindness for birth and giving for kindness, and keeps deeds for ability.
list_adds: As the last of ten paired signs, it shows deeds as one test among several, each matched to its quality, rather than the one touchstone the couplet names.

note: Kural 2 asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge; Elathi 64 orders taking the Exalted one as lord, reciting his book, restraint and penance into a path to release.
teaches: The couplet makes worship the condition of learning, and the verse turns that condition into the first step of a sequence that ends in release, so worship, study and penance become stages rather than separate duties.
list_adds: It sets worship first in a ranked series of four steps ending in release, where the couplet only binds learning to worship.

note: Kural 367 says that if craving is cut off thoroughly, unfailing deeds (தவாவினை) come as one wishes; the verse says the deeds of those without craving do not fail (தவாவாம்).
teaches: The verse repeats the couplet's promise in its own words but sets beside it that the heart of those who have gained is ever craving, which shows why the couplet's condition is hardest for the one who already has.
list_adds: It sets the desireless deed against the craving of those who have obtained, a contrast between two kinds of person that the couplet, which speaks of one, lacks.

note: Kural 890 likens living with those not in accord to living in a hut with a snake; the verse names five such housemates and calls them a disease.
teaches: Read together, the couplet's unnamed discordant housemates become a roster of the house (kin, wife, servant, son, neighbour), so the inner enemy is located in the very people one cannot leave.
list_adds: It names five separate relations of the house and makes them one kind, a disease within, where the couplet leaves 'those not in accord' unnamed.

note: Kural 243 says those whose hearts are joined with grace do not enter the painful world of darkness; Thirikadugam names gracious speech, earning for giving and study for dharma as three ways not to reach the dark world.
teaches: The couplet locates the escape from the dark world in the heart; the verse carries grace into speech and adds two practical means, so the escape becomes a matter of how one talks, earns and studies.
list_adds: It turns grace from a state of heart into a manner of speaking and sets it beside wealth and learning used for their ends, so three daily practices replace one inner condition.

note: Kural 284 says a love ripened in stealth yields undying sorrow; Nanmanikkadigai says not to steal because harsh things follow.
teaches: Both give the reason against theft as its consequence rather than its wrong, so the ethics books argue the point by outcome, not by rule.
list_adds: It sets theft beside rejecting the worthy, befriending the small and making enemies, so theft becomes one of four ways of making trouble for oneself.

note: Kural 619 says that even where fate denies the end, effort pays the wage of bodily strain; saying 47 says strain that does not bring one to live is not strain, on the reading of வருத்தம் as effort.
teaches: The Kural promises effort a wage even in failure, while the saying refuses to count strain that brings no living, so the pair sets a floor (some wage) against a definition by result (a life gained).
list_adds: It names effort among things judged by an outcome or manner beside giving and penance, a measure by result the couplet explicitly sets aside.

note: Naladiyar 123 says the old deed of breaking crabs' legs returns as a disease that rots the fingers; the verse says those who once cured disease now live free of it.
teaches: Read together, disease and health are both the return of old deeds, cruelty coming back as rotting fingers and healing as a body without illness, so the law runs both ways.
list_adds: It names five kinds of sufferer cured and makes healing a merit whose fruit is health, where the quatrain gives only the punishment.

note: Kural 720 likens holding forth before those not of one's kind to nectar spilled in a gutter; Nanmanikkadigai says even a learned man has no standing before the unlearned and foolish.
teaches: The Kural measures the waste of the speech; the quatrain measures the loss to the speaker, and pairs it with the unlearned man's loss before the fit assembly, so standing is shown to depend on the match of speaker and hearers.
list_adds: It makes the learned man's failure the mirror of the unlearned man's, so the list shows a mismatch failing in both directions.

note: Innaa Narpathu 32 calls painful the talk of those who speak behind one's back; Iniyavai 19 calls sweet living without backbiting one's friends.
teaches: They state one thing from two sides, the victim's pain and the speaker's restraint, and together show backbiting judged both by what it does to the hearer and what refraining does for the speaker.

note: 63 says small gifts not called small bear great fruit; 64 names the melting of the giver's heart as what makes a small gift grow like a hill.
teaches: Read in sequence, the first verse sets the gift's size aside and the second names what replaces it as the measure, the melting of the giver's heart.

note: Kural 871 says enmity should not be wanted even in jest; Nanmanikkadigai says one must not take up enmity with anyone.
teaches: The pairing shows the ban on enmity is absolute in both books: the Kural closes the gap of jest, the quatrain the gap of the opponent, with anyone at all.
list_adds: It sets avoiding enmity next to avoiding friendship with the small, so both who one befriends and who one opposes are guarded.

note: Nanmanikkadigai ranks the brahmin's birth above all others; the Siddhar verse asks whether a number is marked on flesh or bone to tell a Paraiyar woman from a Brahmin woman.
teaches: Set together, a birth-rank stated as plain fact meets a later denial that birth leaves any mark on the body, showing the claim the ethics work takes for granted being contested.

note: The Kural tells one to let go that day of gain that comes from leaving fairness; the verse says ill-gotten wealth itself fears the man who keeps dharma in mind.
teaches: The Kural asks for an act of renunciation, while Thirikadugam makes it a property of the person: for the dharma-minded, wrong gain never comes near enough to refuse.
list_adds: It sets dharma beside steadiness and valour as three strengths that make things fear their holder, a ranking of inner strengths the couplet lacks.

note: Verse 49 names five ruins of the ploughman; verse 59 names the care he gives before he ploughs.
teaches: The book gives the farmer's life as a pair of lists, what ruins him and what he must tend, so negligence in 49 is answered item by item by the provisions of 59.

note: Verse 43 tells one to seek the man who knows five parts of astrology and have him fix the wedding day; Naladiyar 52 calls those who prattle of astrology the greatest of fools.
teaches: Two Jain-era ethics works disagree on the worth of the same learned craft: one treats astrology as the expert's knowledge a marriage needs, the other as a madman's distraction from death.
list_adds: It breaks astrology into five technical parts, treating it as a craft to be mastered, which is exactly what the quatrain mocks as endless prattle.

note: Naladiyar 65 calls the gift of one without wealth the true fruit of giving; Iniyavai calls giving within one's income sweet.
teaches: The pair shows the ethics group divided on where giving is best: the quatrain prizes the gift that strains one's means, while this verse prizes the gift that stays within them.
list_adds: It sets measured giving beside independence from others and refusal of indulgence, so giving is ranked as one form of self-limitation rather than a test of sacrifice.

items: மலர்தலை ஞாலத்து மன்னுயிர்க் கெல்லாம் தகுதியால் வாழ்தல்

note: The Kural says beauty without subtle understanding is a clay doll; the verse says beauty in one who does not perfect his conduct is wasted seed.
teaches: The two place the condition of beauty in different places, learning for the Kural and conduct for Thirikadugam, so beauty needs both mind and conduct to count.
list_adds: It moves the test of beauty from understanding to conduct and sets it with rank and penance.

note: 528 tells a king not to look at all alike but by rank; 541 says to show no favour to anyone.
teaches: Household management and the court of justice have different requirements, though they are only two chapters apart.

note: Kural 231 says giving and living with renown is the only gain of life; saying 44 says the man whose hand never loosens is no mountain of renown.
teaches: The Kural joins giving and fame as the one profit of living; the saying shows the same bond from its failure, that the closed hand loses the standing of one's name, on the reading of சொன்மலை as renown.
list_adds: It states the bond negatively and puts the miser among other false holders of a name (the unfeeling kinsman, the friend whose heart does not consent), a contrast of claim and substance the couplet lacks.

note: Kural 922 says not to drink and, if one does, to be one who does not care for the esteem of the worthy; verse 46 bars not only drinking but looking upon drinkers.
teaches: The couplet treats drink as the drinker's own loss of standing; the verse extends the bar to the sight of drinkers, so the rule reaches the company one keeps.
list_adds: It sets three degrees of avoiding toddy (revelry, drinking, seeing drinkers) beside three duties of the table, so abstention is joined to hospitality as one portrait of the householder.

note: Kural 1069 says the heart melts at the thought of begging and is destroyed at the thought of concealment; the line makes concealment the greatest cruelty.
teaches: The couplet weighs concealment by what it does to the asker's heart, the line by what it makes the concealer, and both rank it below begging itself, which 59 calls the worst disgrace.
list_adds: In a ten that also names begging the worst disgrace (59) and giving to askers the highest distinction (60), the line completes a three-way scoring of one exchange (asking, refusing, giving) that the couplet treats only from the asker's side.

note: The Kural says killing is the absence of grace and eating the flesh is not right; the verse counts the man who lives by killing and eating among three who keep no rule.
teaches: The Kural argues from grace, Thirikadugam from discipline: flesh-eating is condemned on both grounds, in one as cruelty and in the other as want of a firm rule.
list_adds: It sets killing to eat among faults of social conduct, so non-killing is read as part of self-rule rather than of compassion alone.

note: Verse 12 defines the vellalan as one who does not eat while a guest waits; verse 42 names three other marks of the vellala family's beauty.
teaches: Read together, the book defines the vellala by four conducts, hospitality, refusing gambling gain, caution toward brahmins and love of the plough, so the title is built from conduct and occupation together.

note: The Kural says the king who bends the sceptre loses wealth and people together; the verse counts the bent-sceptred king among things not joined with fitness.
teaches: Besides the ruin the Kural predicts, the unjust king is also absurd, like a ring on a man with no servant: injustice is shown as a failure of seemliness as well as of rule.
list_adds: It sets the unjust king beside a husbandless woman's ornament and a servantless man's ring, so royal injustice is judged as an empty sign of rank.

note: 29 counts jumping into water without knowing the stakes; 37 counts going down into water without knowing the ford.
teaches: The poet uses the water twice with two kinds of ignorance, of what lies beneath and of the way in, showing knowledge of place as the condition of entering.

note: Naladiyar 52 says the best reflect on impermanence, disease, old age and death and do their own work; Thirikadugam names disease eating one, Death consuming life and wealth passing without worth as what unsettles the raft.
teaches: The quatrain draws the conclusion, do your own work now, while the verse shows what that work is threatened by, so the pair gives both the danger and the answer to it.
list_adds: It adds the passing of wealth to disease and Death as a third force shaking the raft, so loss of goods is ranked with bodily ruin where the quatrain counts only the body's fates.

note: Naladiyar 174 grants that birth is bitter but says no one would resent it given lasting friendship with the good; Thirikadugam lists the sorrow of each kind of birth with no remedy.
teaches: The verse itemises the bitterness of birth by kind of being; the quatrain names the one thing that makes it bearable, so the pair holds the diagnosis and the consolation apart.
list_adds: It divides the bitterness of birth into hunger, fear and want, by kind of birth, where the quatrain speaks of birth whole.

note: Kural 57 says confinement is useless and a woman's own நிறை is her best guard; Iniyavai 10 calls putting away women who lack நிறை sweet.
teaches: The couplet moves the guard inside the woman, and the verse states the consequence when that inner guard is missing, so together they show நிறை made both the woman's defence and the ground on which she may be sent away.
list_adds: It sets dismissing such a wife beside living free of debt and avoiding the mean-minded, so the rule is filed among the household's protections, not among the virtues of marriage.

note: The Kural measures the fruit of hospitality by the guest's worth; the verse prizes the guest who comes in distress after losing his way.
teaches: Against the Kural's ranking of guests by merit, Thirikadugam values the guest by his need: the lost and suffering stranger is the rare prize.
list_adds: It counts the lost guest among hard-to-get goods with a working ox and a maiden, so the guest is valued as a gain to the house, not a cost.

note: Kural 734 defines a land as one free of crushing hunger, unceasing disease and destructive foes; Patitruppattu 13 ends that the land the king guards has flowered, rid of disease and hunger (நோயொடு பசி இகந்து), after showing the enemy lands he ruined.
teaches: The Kural states the absences that make a land; the Chera poem shows who secures them and at whose cost, since the same king's anger is the destructive foe of his neighbours, so the definition is met at home by being broken next door.

note: Innaa Narpathu 21, item 2, calls going to eat with those who do not share their food painful; the line calls going where there is no friendship poor.
teaches: Innaa Narpathu names the particular case, the stingy table, and the line states the general rule behind it, so together they show the visit's worth lying in the host's bond, not in what is offered.

note: Naladiyar 131 says the beauty of hair, garment border and saffron is not beauty and that learning's beauty is; Elathi 74 says the beauty of waist, shoulders, gait, modesty and neck is not beauty, and that of numbers and letters is.
teaches: The Naladiyar dismisses adornment, while Elathi dismisses the body itself and even modesty, so the pair shows the same verdict for learning reached against two different rivals, what one wears and what one is.
list_adds: It replaces the Naladiyar's adornments with six parts and graces of the body, modesty among them, so the rejection reaches a virtue as well as looks.

note: Innaa 40 counts seizing a deposit (அடைக்கலம் வவ்வுதல்) as painful; Iniyavai calls the goodness that does not seize a deposit the finest. They say the same thing from two sides.
teaches: The Iniyavai line adds the temptation the Innaa line omits, the thought that no one knew of it, so the pair shows the deposit as a test of honesty without witnesses.

note: The patikam's first moral, that dharma becomes death to those who err in kingship, is restated here as a common saying proved true.
teaches: The moral announced at the outset as the poem's thesis is here called a saying of the assemblies now proved, so the book frames its plot as the demonstration of a received maxim.

note: Kural 238 calls it a disgrace not to obtain the legacy called renown (இசையென்னும் எச்சம்); the line, using the same two words, calls renown the greatest legacy.
teaches: The couplet makes renown the minimum below which a life is disgraced; the line makes it the maximum above which there is no legacy, so the pair fixes fame as both the floor and the ceiling of what one leaves.
list_adds: In a ten that opens with children as the greatest gain (51), the line separates the legacy of fame from the gain of offspring, two senses that the couplet's எச்சம் leaves folded together.

note: Kural 503 says even the learned and flawless are rarely without blankness when examined; Nanmanikkadigai says no one knows everything and no one knows nothing.
teaches: The Kural speaks of the best; the quatrain adds the worst, so knowledge is never total and ignorance never total, which leaves everyone open to examination.
list_adds: It pairs no one all-knowing with no one all-ignorant, and the same for virtue and fault, so the list denies both extremes.

note: Kural 946 says joy stays with the one who eats knowing when to stop, as disease stays with the one who eats hugely; the line says grave disease comes easily to those who love food.
teaches: The couplet ties disease to the act of eating beyond measure, the line ties it to the love of food that precedes the act, so the pair moves the cause of illness back from the meal to the appetite.
list_adds: In the ten it stands beside blame for the lecher (78) and pain for the pleasure-seeker (76), so gluttony's disease is one instance of a general rule that a desire brings its own harm, where the couplet speaks in a chapter on medicine.

note: Kural 221 says giving to those who have nothing is true giving; Elathi 78 names six kinds of the destitute: the motherless child, the widow, those without livelihood, the ruined trader, those who lost their wealth, and the blind.
teaches: The couplet defines giving by the recipient's want, and the verse names who the wanting are and how they came to want, so the general rule gets its cases.
list_adds: It names each recipient by what was lost (mother, husband, trade, wealth, sight), so the Kural's வறியார் become a list of the newly helpless rather than the poor as a class.

note: Kural 547 says the king protects the world and just order (முறை) protects the king when he keeps it without fail; 99 says the one who wants safety does not leave off acting by just order.
teaches: The couplet explains why the king's safety lies in justice and the line states it as an unbroken practice, so the pair shows justice as the ruler's own shelter and not only a duty owed to the ruled.
list_adds: It puts the king's justice in a list where each seeker keeps a practice for his own end, so just rule is framed as what the ruler does for his own security, the same way the learner keeps reverence.

note: 37 sets turning one's regard away from those one has taken from as no better than cruelty; 55 sets hiding what one can give as the greatest cruelty.
teaches: The book uses cruelty as the measure twice, once as a floor for ingratitude and once as a summit for refusal, so withholding from an asker ranks as worse than the ingratitude it is compared with.

note: Kural 890 likens living with those not in accord (உடம்பாடு இலாதவர்) to living with a snake in a hut; Innaa 11 counts the embrace of a wife without உடம்பாடு as painful.
teaches: The couplet leaves 'those not in accord' open, and the Innaa narrows the same word to the wife, placing the discord at the closest point of the house, the embrace itself.
list_adds: It sets the discordant wife beside the petty friend, the intemperate companion and the creditor's eye, so marriage is counted among the bonds that can turn to pain.

note: Kural 727 likens the learning of one who fears the assembly to a bright sword in a பேடி's hand among enemies; Innaa 7 counts a weapon held by one without strength as painful.
teaches: The couplet uses the powerless swordsman as a simile for useless learning, and the Innaa counts him plainly but puts beside him the speaker who cannot reply, so the verse holds both halves of the couplet's comparison as separate items.
list_adds: It lists the weak man's weapon and the speaker who cannot answer as two items of one kind, where the couplet joins them only as image and subject.

note: Kural 340 calls the soul a lodger in a borrowed corner (துச்சில்) of the body; Iniyavai calls sweet not grieving while living in a துச்சில்.
teaches: Read through the couplet, the verse's lodger may be the soul in the body as well as a poor man in borrowed rooms, which would make its item an image of calm about mortality.
list_adds: It sets the lodger's calm between the alms-eater's restraint and freedom from greedy want, so the image is read inside a renouncer's poverty.

note: Purananuru 183 says learning is good even at the cost of serving the teacher, giving him wealth and accepting the lower place; Sirupanchamoolam 28 says the true teacher seeks no gain and the fit pupil serves with love.
teaches: The Sangam king accepts payment and service as the price of learning; the Jain verse keeps the pupil's loving service but denies the teacher any gain, and adds that learning without casting off the three faults is a sickness.

note: Kural 409 ranks the learned low-born above the unlearned high-born; Nanmanikkadigai says lineage dies beneath want of learning.
teaches: Where the Kural keeps high birth as a rank that learning outweighs, the quatrain makes the rank itself die without learning, a stronger claim about birth.
list_adds: It puts lineage in a row with beauty, paddy and a draught ox, so birth becomes one more thing that needs a support beneath it to live.

note: Thirikadugam 96 names the ascetic who carries out what he has undertaken in the proper way as one at whose word rain falls; saying 49 says a vow not undertaken in its proper way is no penance.
teaches: One work denies the name of penance to a vow wrongly undertaken; the other promises rain to the ascetic who completes his vow rightly, so between them the proper manner is both the condition of penance and the source of its power.

note: The Kural says those who know their duty do not slacken in helping even without means; the line says the poor man who is not generous is not blamed.
teaches: The pair separates the ideal from the verdict: the Kural praises the poor man who still helps, while the line forbids others to condemn the one who cannot, so excellence is not made a debt.
list_adds: In a ten on withheld blame the line speaks to the onlooker rather than the giver, a standpoint the couplet on ஒப்புரவு never takes.

note: Kural 1253 has a woman say her desire shows like a sneeze though she would hide it; Nanmanikkadigai says desire cannot be hidden however hard one tries.
teaches: The lover's confession in the couplet becomes in the verse a general law, so a moment of love poetry is used as ethical knowledge.
list_adds: It sets desire beside fortune and Death as things no one controls, so its showing is ranked with impersonal forces rather than one woman's weakness.

note: Kural 55 praises the wife who worships her husband, not a god, and commands the rain; verse 14 makes walking her husband's way a woman's virtue.
teaches: The couplet gives the wife's devotion cosmic power; the verse sets the same following among son, kin, soldier and subjects, as one case of keeping one's place.
list_adds: It lists the wife's following with the son's, the soldier's and the people's, so the rule for women is presented as one form of a general duty of following.

note: Thirikadugam 100 names a loyal army, a fearless fortress and great treasure as the limbs of kings; verse 48 breaks the fortress into five and makes it the ground of being crowned.
teaches: One counted work treats the fort as one limb among three, the other spells it out as five, with the people among them, so the two together show the fort as both a royal possession and a living defence.

note: Kural 801 defines old friendship as a bond that never curtails the liberties of intimacy (கிழமை); 223 says the king, even as a hero-stone, gives room to friends of old intimacy (கிழமைத் தொன்னட் புடையார்) who come to him.
teaches: The Kural's definition is carried past death in 223: the claim of intimacy that a friend may exercise unasked includes the right to follow the king into death, and the stone honours it by making room, so pazhaimai is tested at its extreme.

note: Kural 306 says anger burns the raft of one's own kin; Nanmanikkadigai calls anger when one has no kin a fault.
teaches: Together they make kin and anger work both ways: anger destroys kin, and without kin anger has nothing to stand on, so the angry man loses the very support his anger needs.
list_adds: It counts anger without kin as a fault of wrong circumstance, beside youth without learning and giving without means.

note: Verse 18 promises no further birth to one who does not lie, steal, desire women or eat flesh; verse 82 lists nearly the same vows and sets them above scripture.
teaches: Read together, the same vows earn two fruits in this book: release from rebirth in one verse, and freedom from needing the scriptures in the other.

note: Acharakkovai fixes the posture and direction of the meal as ஆசாரம்; the line treats ஆசாரம் as varying by country and not to be faulted where it is unknown.
teaches: Holding them together shows that one ethics work treats ஆசாரம் as binding rule while another grants it is a country's custom, so the rule code is local even in the eyes of its own literature.

note: Kural 30 calls those who wear cool kindness toward every living being the அந்தணர்; Elathi 6 calls one who has six possessions a mother to all living beings.
teaches: Both give a title for care toward every creature, but Elathi grounds it in six restraints, keeping out lies and flesh among them, so universal care is built from abstentions, not only from a cool temper.
list_adds: It breaks the single quality of 30 into six possessions, two of them shutting out falsehood and flesh, and gives the outcome a mother's name instead of a status word.

note: Kural 920 names double-minded women, liquor and dice as the company of those Fortune has left; Thirikadugam names the same three as the work of men without goodness.
teaches: Both name the same three vices, and the verse adds what they share: each is a stupor (மயக்கம்).
list_adds: It calls each item a மயக்கம், so paid sex and dice are made forms of intoxication alongside drink.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 65 says one who digs a tank, sets its bank, clears a road, breaks a field and digs a shared well goes sweetly to heaven; verse 51 rewards tanks, wells, shelters, water-booths and halls with a life of music, dance and love.
teaches: Two Jain works price the same public water works differently: heaven in one, sensual pleasure and the akam play of union and sulking in the other.

note: Naladiyar 68 grants that the worthy of standing (சீர்கொண்ட சான்றோர்) feel anger and says it cools of itself; the line says that a man of great standing (சீர்) being without anger is false.
teaches: Together they move the virtue of the eminent from having no anger to letting anger subside, since one says such a man will feel it and the other says how his anger differs from the low man's.
list_adds: Set beside the drunkard's lapses and the greedy judge, it counts anger as a thing that comes with high standing as surely as lapse comes with drink, a turn the quatrain's contrast of the worthy and the low does not make.

items: இல்லாது காமுற் றிரங்கி இடர்ப்படார் செய்வது செய்தல்

note: Naladiyar 200 says the base fill themselves on rice and fried dishes a great patron gives, while to the self-reliant water won by effort is nectar; the verse says all the low delight in rice from paddy.
teaches: Both books define the base by being satisfied with rice, but the quatrain sets against them those who live by their own effort and the verse those who delight in their due standing, so the opposite of the base is labour in one and honour in the other.
list_adds: It sets the low man's rice in a series with the tiger's flesh and the cattle's grass, so appetite for food is made a creature's nature, and the high are marked off by a delight that is not eaten.

note: Kural 532 says heedlessness kills fame as chronic want kills understanding; Thirikadugam says one who has put away heedlessness in settled wealth keeps lasting fame.
teaches: The couplet states the threat to fame in general; the verse says when it strikes, when wealth seems secure.
list_adds: It places the vigilant rich man beside the courteous giver and the man free of envy, so fame rests on three habits of the wealthy.

note: Kural 218 says the discerning do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even without means; the Innaa line counts a man without wealth desiring to be liberal as painful. Not a tension on our reading: the Innaa line names a cost, not a fault.
teaches: The pair shows the pain hidden inside the Kural's praise: giving steadily in want is admirable, and the wish to give without means is also an ache.
list_adds: It sets the giving wish among the pains of want, a rich city around one and eating at others' doors, so it is seen from inside poverty.

note: The Kural calls not hurting others the settled stand of the stainless; the verse names doing no hurt to any creature as purity itself.
teaches: The Kural's stainless people are defined by harmlessness, and Thirikadugam draws the conclusion that harmlessness simply is purity, setting it against ritual senses of the word.
list_adds: It sets purity as harmlessness beside giving to the poor and a life shaped by impermanence, as the three marks of those who know the good.

note: Verse 5 says one who wants to be rid of the body does penance and one who wants standing gives; verse 35 says penance brings heaven and only knowledge brings release.
teaches: Read together, the two verses disagree on what ends embodiment: verse 5 credits penance, verse 35 reserves release for knowledge and gives penance only heaven.

note: 69 argues against flesh from the shared sin of the chain of killing; 74 argues for not eating and not killing from the pains of bearing and rearing a life.
teaches: The book gives two grounds for one abstention: the guilt that runs from killer to eater, and the cost of bringing any life into being.

note: Line 5 ranks freedom from bodily disease above youth; line 84 calls the pleasure of a sick man poor.
teaches: The first ten ranks health above youth and the ninth shows why, since disease empties even pleasure, so health appears as the ground other goods stand on.

note: Kural 323 ranks not killing first and not lying after it; Iniyavai 5 also puts not killing foremost and closes with not speaking evil of anyone.
teaches: Both books place non-killing at the head of a short ranked list and a restraint of speech behind it, so the pair shows the Kural's ranking reused as the frame of a king's list, where justice of the sceptre is slotted between.
list_adds: It sets non-killing in a king's list beside unjust honours and the straight sceptre, so a universal vow is read as the first duty of rule.

note: Kural 301 says only restraint of anger where it can take effect counts; the Innaa line counts rancour held against the small as painful.
teaches: Read together, anger toward the weak is both the Kural's true test of restraint and the Innaa verse's common failure of it, the same ground seen as trial and as fall.
list_adds: It sets rancour toward the weak beside a scentless flower and a fool under questioning, so cruelty is filed with exposures of one's own lack.

note: Kural 56 says she is a woman who guards herself, cares for her husband and keeps their good name without flagging; the verse says the woman of household life has wisdom with her beauty.
teaches: Both make பெண் a title to be earned, but the Kural earns it by guarding and serving while the verse asks for wisdom joined to beauty, a different test of the same name.
list_adds: It puts the wife among definitions of the farmer, the brahmin, the cock and the commander, so a woman's title is one of a set of role-names each tied to a mark.

note: Innaa Narpathu 31 says singing to an untuned lute is very painful; Thirikadugam says song not measured to the beat is painful to hear.
teaches: One verse faults the pitch and the other the beat, so together they show the period held music to two measures, tuning and time, either of which failing makes song painful.

note: Kural 840 likens a fool's entering the assembly of the worthy to putting an unwashed foot on a bed; Innaa 17 counts a fool's entering among the worthy (சான்றோருட் பேதை புகல்) as painful, in nearly the same words.
teaches: The couplet gives the image of defilement and the Innaa gives the worthy their mark, ஆன்றவித்த (full and self-subdued), which is what the fool's entry offends.
list_adds: It sets the fool's intrusion beside a penance without self-subduing, so both are counted as the unsubdued entering where self-mastery is required.

note: Naladiyar 177 says water mixed with milk becomes milk, so the small are hidden by joining the great; Nanmanikkadigai says the vessel spoils the milk, as bad company ruins a lineage.
teaches: The same mixing image runs both ways in the group, the good absorbing the small in one and the container corrupting the good in the other, so company is shown to work in both directions.
list_adds: It sets the spoiled milk among four kinds of ruin (disunity, falsehood, bad company), so mixing is counted as a cause of loss, not of concealment.

note: Kural 261 defines tapas as bearing the pain that comes and harming no life; Sirupanchamoolam 31 keeps both, adds three more, and says penance so made is sweet, not lowly.
teaches: The couplet defines penance by two ethical acts; the verse keeps them, turns bearing pain into forgetting it, and meets an objection the couplet does not raise, that penance degrades the one who does it.
list_adds: It extends the couplet's two marks to five, adding no wrong to another and the giving up of desire and anger, and closes with a verdict on how the penance feels.

note: Thirikadugam 84 joins people of a long line who lack the excellence of learning to poverty; Innaa 19 counts lack of learning in one born to a good family as painful.
teaches: Both books set the unlearned man of good family beside a failed source of growth (the badly made tank inlet, the unsprouting seed), so the two together show a shared image: lineage is a resource that learning must make flow.

note: Kural 720 likens speaking before those not of one's set to nectar spilled in a drain; the line calls speech poor where words do not carry.
teaches: The couplet locates the waste in the hearers' unfitness, the line in the word's lack of force, so together they show that speech fails either from the audience or from the speaker's standing.
list_adds: It puts futile speech beside futile anger (89) and futile sulking (85) in one ten, making each a case of an act without the power to land.

note: Innaa Narpathu 38 calls painful the folly of following after another man's wife; Iniyavai 15 calls sweet the dignity of not looking after her.
teaches: The two lines use nearly the same words and say the same thing from two sides: what Innaa names as folly in the doer, Iniyavai names as dignity in the one who abstains, so the act is judged by its effect on the man's standing.

note: Kural 259 ranks not killing to eat above a thousand sacrifices; Thirikadugam names one who kills in a desired sacrifice as one who knows only his own view.
teaches: The Kural weighs sacrifice against abstention; the verse drops the weighing and calls ritual killing a self-deception.
list_adds: It groups the sacrificer with two flesh-eaters, so ritual killing is reckoned with ordinary meat-eating rather than above it.

note: Kural 392 calls numbers and letters the two eyes of living beings; Thirikadugam makes learning the letters first the opening step on the path of excellence.
teaches: The couplet values letters as sight; the verse gives them a place in time, first, before the parents and inherited conduct, so literacy becomes the start of a moral sequence.
list_adds: It makes letters the first of three ordered steps (முந்தை ... பிற்பாடு), a sequence the couplet does not have.

note: Verse 64 makes tending guests the duty by which a chaste wife is a friend; verse 63 counts a bangled wife who dreads guests among things that yield no good.
teaches: The two adjacent verses give the same rule from both sides: hospitality is the wife's first duty, and failing it alone makes her a loss to the house.

note: In Purananuru 101 Avvai tells her heart that whether Athiyaman's gift is delayed or not it is sure, since he greets her on the hundredth visit as on the first; the Innaa line counts a poet held back by the giver as painful.
teaches: The poem shows the pain the Innaa line names and how it is borne: a patron's constant welcome makes the delay of the poet's send-off endurable.

note: 628 prevents pain by not desiring pleasure. 669 accepts pain for the sake of the pleasure that results. One asks you to stop wanting joy and the other to work for it.
teaches: They may differ in scope, since 628 speaks of how one meets pain and 669 of which tasks to take up, but neither verse says so.

note: Kural 159 says those who bear the harsh words of transgressors are as pure as renouncers; the verse ranks those who bear above those who rise up and revile.
teaches: The couplet measures the forbearer upward against the renouncer and the verse measures him against the reviler beside him, so forbearance is placed both by its reward and by the act it refuses.
list_adds: It sets forbearance in a series of 'better than' rankings with poverty over hoarding, so restraint of anger and restraint of possession are judged by one standard.

note: Kural 1033 says only those who live by ploughing truly live; Thirikadugam makes love of farming the beauty of one family, the vellala.
teaches: The couplet gives ploughing to anyone who will live independently; the verse ties its honour to one birth-group, so the same praise of farming reads in one book as a way of life open to all and in the other as a family's mark.
list_adds: It joins love of farming to two other rules for the same family, so the plough becomes one of three marks of a caste-occupation rather than a universal claim.

note: Kural 632 names a minister excellent in resolve, guarding the people, learning and labour; Elathi 17 names guarding the people, resolve and strength in learning, then adds secret counsel, keeping off sloth and good company.
teaches: The two share three of their qualities in near-identical words (குடி, வன்கண், கற்றல்/நூல்வன்மை), and Elathi's additions show a minister judged also by the company he keeps and by his secrecy.
list_adds: It adds secret counsel and good company to the Kural's core, so ministerial fitness extends from capacity to discretion and associations.

note: Kural 226 says relieving the destroying hunger of the destitute is where one with wealth should store it; the verse says that if one gives, one should give food.
teaches: The couplet says where wealth is best stored and the verse which gift is best, so together food given to the hungry is both the best gift and the safest store.
list_adds: It ranks food first among gifts by setting giving beside letting go, lifting and destroying, each with its one right object.

note: Naladiyar 92 sets death, age and disease before the reader and urges sharing food while wealth is in hand; Elathi 40 joins choosing the way out of impermanence with removing others' hunger.
teaches: Together they show the ethics group tying the feeding of the hungry to the escape from impermanence, and Elathi places it among inner disciplines like not doubting and not wavering.
list_adds: It sets removing hunger beside non-harm, steadiness and the choice of release, so feeding becomes one of the marks of one bound for heaven.

note: Naladiyar 38 says a small gift grows vast when it reaches worthy hands; the verse says it grows like a hill when the giver's heart melts.
teaches: Both say a small gift grows huge but place the cause differently: the Naladiyar in the worth of the receiver, Sirupanchamoolam in the melted heart of the giver.
list_adds: It gives five images of melting as the measure of the giver's heart, a condition on the giver that the quatrain does not state.

note: Verse 23 makes guarding the gate of a wall-less old town painful; 24 makes living in an old town without protection painful.
teaches: The second verse moves the pain from the guard's futile labour to the townsman's daily exposure, so one weakness is felt by both its defenders and its dwellers.

note: Kural 360 names desire, anger and confusion as the three whose end ends pain; Elathi 27 names coveting, anger and wrong view as the three faults of the mind.
teaches: Both books build a triad of inner faults with anger at its centre, but where the Kural ends in confusion, a lack of seeing, Elathi ends in wrong view, a positive false belief, which shows the Jain stress on right doctrine.
list_adds: It replaces confusion with wrong view and puts the triad inside a scheme of ten faults across mind, speech and body.

note: Kural 67 says a father's good to his son is to place him in front in the assembly; Nanmanikkadigai calls letting children grow unlearned an evil.
teaches: The Kural states the father's duty as a gift; the quatrain states its neglect as an evil placed beside killing, which raises the weight of the duty.
list_adds: It ranks neglecting a child's learning with killing everywhere, so a parent's omission joins the gravest wrong in the list.

note: Both describe flesh-eating as feeding flesh with flesh (ஊனைப் பெருக்குதல், ஊன் பெருக்கற்கு); the Kural asks how such a person can hold அருள், the Innaa line ranks the act as the first of pains.
teaches: The pair shows one image doing two jobs: in the Kural it proves the loss of compassion, in the Innaa verse it is a pain ranked above even soured honey and kingless armies.
list_adds: It ranks flesh-eating first (முன்) among things that have lost their proper working, a king without elephants, honey gone sour, a cut-off town.

note: Kural 656 says not to do what the worthy condemn even to relieve one's mother's hunger; Innaa 17 counts abandoning the mother who bore one as painful.
teaches: The Kural uses the mother's need as the hardest case in which a wrong still may not be done, and the Innaa counts her neglect as a pain in its own right, so together they bound the duty: it is weighty, but it does not license blame.
list_adds: It sets the mother's neglect beside a fool among the worthy and a false penance, so care for her is counted among the duties of a person's standing rather than as a test case.

note: 72 promises kingship for one mouthful given to the weak, the old and the dying; 77 promises a glad life to the end for gifts to the wounded, blind and lame.
teaches: The two lists of the helpless overlap but name different rewards, showing the book attaches a distinct fruit to each list rather than one fixed reward for giving.

note: Kural 127 says whatever else one fails to guard, guard the tongue; Thirikadugam singles out the unguarded talk of a man who is not drunk.
teaches: Adding 'not drunk' removes the one excuse for loose speech, so the verse sharpens the couplet: unguarded speech when sober is chosen, not lapsed into.

note: Kural 584 says a spy examines everyone, the king's servants and kin first; Thirikadugam names a secret-leaking friend, a woman without regard for honour and a rancorous servant as those called spies.
teaches: The couplet turns the king's surveillance inward on his own circle; the verse shows why from the other side, since those closest, friend, woman and servant, are the ones who leak.
list_adds: It names the household's own informers by kind, giving concrete cases of the inward danger the couplet only implies.

note: Kural 51 defines the wife by the home's excellence and living within her husband's means; verse 42 opens with knowing the house's ways in proportion to income.
teaches: Both works put income first in defining a wife, and the verse spells out what the couplet's 'excellence of the home' includes: kin kept content, guests and worship.
list_adds: It ranks budgeting first and then lists the duties it must pay for, so the couplet's measure of means becomes the base of a household order.

note: Naladiyar 306 says a mind racked by desire (காதல் கவற்றும் மனம்) sends a man to beg of strangers when he could end his want by asking of himself; the line calls desire the greatest poverty.
teaches: The quatrain shows the mechanism the line only names: it is desire, not lack, that drives a man to beg, so the poverty that matters is the one inside.
list_adds: The line states the root in four words, as one of ten superlatives, where the quatrain needs a scene and a remedy; set beside 59, the ten's list makes desire and begging the worst poverty and the worst disgrace.

note: 55 asks the king to be like the sun in fierce valour and like the moon in cool gentleness; 59 says the king is like the sun to his enemies and the moon to people like the poet.
teaches: The same sun-and-moon pair is counsel in 55 and description in 59, so the anthology shows a stock image of kingship moving between what a king should be and what a poet says he already is, with the second poem naming whom each face is turned to.

note: Kural 978 says smallness adorns itself with self-admiration; the line says birth in a small house shows in pride.
teaches: The same mark of pride serves the Kural as a sign of small character and the Muthumozhikkanchi as a sign of small birth, which shows the ten tying character to family.
list_adds: Paired in the ten with line 11, it sets the small house against the great one, a contrast of birth the couplet, which speaks only of character, does not draw.

note: The Kural says having is worse than poverty under a ruler who does no justice; the line says the subject there does not voice blame.
teaches: The couplet names what the subject loses under misrule and the line names what he must also give up, the open word against the king, so the cost of a bent sceptre falls on speech as well as property.
list_adds: Among the ten's cases of withheld blame it makes silence under an unjust king a rule of the subject's conduct, a side of tyranny the couplet, which speaks of the king's guilt, does not state.

note: Kar Narpathu 9: the flowers speak many sweet words announcing his return. Akananuru 74: the heroine tells the friend she could hold firm on her many sweet words of reassurance (வன்புறை இன்சொல் நன்பல) were it not for the herders' flute at evening.
teaches: Akananuru 74 gives the heroine's answer that the Kar Narpathu never records: sweet words of comfort hold her only until the evening flute, so the reassurance the venbas repeat is shown elsewhere to fail at its own hour.

items: பற்பல தானியத்தது ஆகிப் பலருடையும் மெய்த்துணையுஞ் சேரல்
மறந்தேயும் மாணா மயரிகள் சேராத் திறந்தெரிந்து வாழ்தல்

note: Line 10 ranks not dwindling later above swelling at first; 92 says the one who wants to swell does not leave off gathering renown.
teaches: Read together, the two lines say that greatness is kept from shrinking only by an unbroken run of creditable deeds, so the unslackening of the last ten is the answer to the dwindling feared in the first.

note: The Kural says the man who fears his wife fears to do good to the good; the verse calls the man who lives in fear of his wife an ox whose eating grieves the heart.
teaches: The Kural names the harm, Thirikadugam the scorn: a wife-fearing husband is useless to others and also a beast, set beside the shameless and the lapsed ascetic.
list_adds: It ranks the wife-fearing husband with the blame-fearless man and the lapsed ascetic, as three who should not even be fed.

note: Kural 261 defines தவம் as bearing pain and harming no living being; saying 49 says a vow not taken up in its proper way is no penance.
teaches: The Kural defines penance by its content, endurance and harmlessness, while the saying defines it by how it is undertaken, so the pair shows two separate tests a vow must pass.
list_adds: It sets penance as the twin of giving in a matched pair of lines, putting the ascetic's vow under the same test of right manner as the householder's gift, which the couplet does not.

note: Iniyavai Narpathu calls sweet the austerity of one who wants to win and does not rage, and not craving what one lacks; Thirikadugam says the one without austerity who rages to win and the one who craves what he lacks pound husk.
teaches: The two works state the same pair from opposite sides in nearly the same words, so restraint in contest and in craving is both a sweetness and the only labour that bears grain.

note: Kural 978 says greatness always bows and smallness adorns itself; Nanmanikkadigai says bowing is always the ornament of the worthy.
teaches: The Kural plays bowing against self-adornment; the quatrain makes bowing itself the ornament, and sets it beside the Veda and victory, so humility is the learning proper to the worthy.
list_adds: It ranks humility among the proper excellences of each station, the andhanar's Veda and the king's just victory, making it the worthy man's own accomplishment.

note: Nanmanikkadigai likens the hard-hearted to stone; Naladiyar 334 ranks stones above base people because stones at least serve whoever uses them.
teaches: The two verses use stone in opposite ways, as hardness to be blamed and as plain usefulness to be praised, so the base man is lower than the very thing the hard-hearted resemble.
list_adds: It makes stone one of four likenesses (disease, ornament, weeds), so the image names a kind of person rather than ranking people against things.

note: The Kural says inner purity is seen through truth; the verse counts purity, truth and evil unspoken in mind and word as the ascetic's practice.
teaches: The Kural ties purity to truth; Thirikadugam gives each its own fruit, boldness and beauty, and adds silence of the mind as a third discipline.
list_adds: It separates purity and truth into two items with different rewards and places them in the ascetic's domain.

note: Verse 1 names killing, lying, meat and theft as the four the book sets aside; verse 20 lists theft, gambling, bad company, harmful speech and meat as what frees one from a flesh body.
teaches: The preface's four abstentions are, by verse 20, the price of release from rebirth, so the book's opening ethic is already a soteriology.

note: Verse 93 gives anger and desire to the creature in folly; verse 95 sets anger and desire beside hunger as an army that drives out good deeds.
teaches: Read together, the book treats anger and desire both as the condition of folly and as the force that removes merit, and swaps the third member, delusion, for hunger.

note: Naladiyar 55 laments youth gone and disease and old age coming; saying 5 ranks freedom from disease above youth.
teaches: The quatrain counts youth's passing and illness's coming as one loss that urges renunciation, while the saying pulls them apart and says health, not youth, is the greater good.
list_adds: It ranks two goods the quatrain mourns together, making health a separate and higher thing than youth.

note: Purananuru 9 praises a Pandya who warns cows, brahmins, women, the sick and the sonless to take shelter before he shoots; Sirupanchamoolam 40 names five who give up in battle and must not be approached.
teaches: The Sangam king protects those who never fight by warning them before battle; the verse protects those who stop fighting during it, so together they give both ends of the period's code of sparing in war.

note: Kural 402 likens the unlearned man's wish to speak to a woman without breasts desiring womanhood; verse 4 sets the unlearned man's subtlety beside the pride of a woman lacking both ears.
teaches: The two share an old figure of the unlearned as a body lacking its marks, but the verse splits the simile into two separate objects of laughter and adds a third, the poor man's boast.
list_adds: It turns the couplet's single simile into a list of three pretensions, so the woman's pride is no longer a figure for the unlearned but a ridiculous thing of its own.

note: Naladiyar 11 says the wise, knowing grey hair will come, renounced in childhood; Iniyavai calls knowing youth to be old age sweet.
teaches: The quatrain draws the conclusion, early renunciation, that the verse leaves implicit, and the verse calls that foresight sweet rather than grim.
list_adds: It joins the foresight of age to seeing desire as poison and to the comfort of safe kin, so two renunciant insights are framed by a household one.

note: Verse 33 ranks brahmin birth highest; verse 40 says fortune does not abide by rank or kind.
teaches: The book ranks births yet denies that birth secures fortune, so within one work high birth is honoured but given no hold on prosperity.

note: Kural 361 calls craving the seed of unceasing birth; Thirikadugam makes craving one of three whose seed, once destroyed, ends birth.
teaches: The seed image is shared, but Thirikadugam widens what the seed is made of from an inner craving to include an outward act, false speech.
list_adds: It sets craving beside attachment and false speech, so a lie becomes one of the seeds of rebirth, which the couplet does not say.

note: Kural 441 counsels choosing the friendship of those mature in virtue and knowledge; verse 59 sets taking the words of the excellent among a learner's acts and makes them the making of a blameless king.
teaches: The couplet speaks to a king choosing counsellors; the verse shows the same habit begun as a learner's discipline of bowing and study, which yields the king.
list_adds: It sets taking counsel between bowing and close study, so heeding the great is one of six habits of learning rather than a separate policy of state.

note: Kural 541 defines justice as investigating (ஓர்ந்து), showing no favour and acting after consideration; Thirikadugam names the king who weighs matters (ஓர்ந்து) and does not bend justice.
teaches: Both put weighing first in justice, but the verse makes the just king only one third of what makes a world.
list_adds: It places the just king between the dutiful brahmin and the orderly people, so justice is one estate's part of a shared order.

note: The Kural likens the brief want of the renowned rich to rain-clouds running dry; the verse counts the poverty of men with the manliness to give as a sight the eye cannot bear.
teaches: Both treat a giver's poverty as a public loss rather than a private one; Thirikadugam adds the witness's pain, so the giver's want hurts those who watch.
list_adds: It sets the giver's poverty beside two shameful sights, so the generous man's want is ranked as a kind of indignity.

note: Kural 478 says there is no ruin if the outflow is not wider than the inflow, using the image of channels; the verse says sluices are as wide as the dug tank and people live according to their means.
teaches: Both picture a household as water and channels, and the verse adds that the outlet should be cut to the size of the tank, so the couplet's rule of balance becomes a rule of construction made when the tank is dug.
list_adds: It sets the sluice beside the measure of virtue by strength, so spending and doing good are governed by the same proportion.

note: Thirikadugam 10 names an assembly with no elders to settle quarrels among three things that yield no good; Nanmanikkadigai calls lack of elders waste to the assembly.
teaches: Both short works make elders the thing an assembly cannot do without, and Thirikadugam gives the reason the verse omits: elders settle disputes.

note: Both set a wife's or beloved's shoulders against heaven. 906 says that fearing those shoulders leaves no worth even in a godlike life, and 1103 asks whether the lotus-eyed god's world is sweeter than sleep on them.
teaches: Fear and love differ, but the books value the same intimacy in opposite ways.

note: Kural 890 makes living with those not in accord like living with a snake in a hut; the Innaa line names the house with a hidden snake plainly, as a bodily danger.
teaches: Placed together, the Innaa line gives the literal fear on which the Kural's figure rests, so the reader sees why discord at home is felt as close, quiet and constant danger.
list_adds: It keeps the snake-house literal beside a high leap, a raging elephant and a tiger's path, four plain dangers with no moral item.

note: Kural 694 says to suppress whispers and shared smiles before the great; the verse lists five things not wanted where elders sit.
teaches: The couplet's two signs are about what a ruler might read into them; the verse widens the rule to elders generally and adds faults of judgment such as favouring friends.
list_adds: It adds counsel, partiality to friends, enmity and song to the couplet's laughter, and cites the old treatises as its authority, turning a courtier's caution into a code of the assembly.

note: Kural 269 says that even leaping past death is possible for those who have the power of austerity; Elathi 65 says that one who would see Death's strength cut down must study the all-knowing one's book and do a penance that harms nothing.
teaches: Set beside the couplet, the verse names the conditions the Kural leaves out: the austerity that defeats death must be guided by scripture and must injure no creature, so non-harm becomes part of the power over death.
list_adds: It turns the Kural's bare power of austerity into a sequence of conditions (scripture, undistracted mind, harmless penance), each needed for the same victory over Death.

note: 51 names the getting of children the greatest gain; 58 names renown the greatest எச்சம், a word that also means offspring.
teaches: Within one ten the two superlatives divide the field: children are the greatest gain in life, but what survives a person is ranked as fame, not progeny.

note: Kural 184 grants that harsh words to the face are better than careless words behind the back; the Innaa line names the backbiter as one who will not speak to the face (முன்னை உரையார்).
teaches: Both rank the face above the back, and the Innaa wording makes the backbiter's fault a refusal of the open speech the Kural concedes, so cowardice is seen inside the malice.
list_adds: It sets backbiting beside failing to guard oneself and bad company, as ways a person is undone without seeing it.

note: Thirikadugam 80 counts penance taken up by one without restraint of heart (நிறை) as seed sown on scrub; the line says penance by one who is not pure (வாலியன்) is false.
teaches: The two name different lacks, restraint of heart and purity, that make penance void, and one calls it barren where the other calls it false, so together they show the penance of the unfit failing both as fruit and as truth.

note: Verse 78 names the practices of those strong in penance; verse 80 counts penance taken up by one without restraint of heart as wasted seed.
teaches: The two verses together give the condition and its failure: penance bears fruit with purity and restraint of mind, and is seed lost in a thicket without them.

note: Kural 30 says those called அந்தணர் are the virtuous who wear kindness to every creature; verse 7 says the பார்ப்பான் is the one who shares his food.
teaches: Both define a priestly title by conduct rather than birth, and the verse makes the conduct a concrete daily act, sharing food, where the couplet names a disposition.
list_adds: It defines the brahmin in a row with the ascetic, the leader and the worthy man, so the birth title is treated as one more role earned by an act.

note: 29 counts a secret heard by one who cannot hold it; 23 counts the talk of those who are like a beaten drum.
teaches: The two lines describe one leak from both ends, the careless hearer and the broadcasting talker, so the book shows a secret failing first in the ear and then on the tongue.

note: Both are a friend comforting a woman whose man has crossed the desert, and both argue that no gain could keep him: 201 says not even the Chola rice country, 213 not even the world of the worthy with its nectar.
teaches: Side by side they show the friend's reassurance as a scale that can be pushed from an earthly kingdom to heaven, always measuring his love by what he would refuse rather than by any promise he made.

note: Kural 557 likens a king's want of kindness to the earth's want of rain; Innaa 3 sets living under a cruel king beside swimming long water without a float.
teaches: The couplet measures a cruel king by what the land loses; the Innaa measures him by the subject's helplessness, a swimmer with nothing to hold, which turns the public loss into a private danger.
list_adds: It puts life under a cruel king beside the floatless swimmer and the harsh speaker's company, so tyranny is counted among the dangers a person meets rather than among the faults of a ruler.

note: Kural 671 says deliberation ends in resolve and that delay after resolving is an evil; 95 says the one who wants a good life never leaves off deliberation.
teaches: For a single task the couplet closes deliberation once resolved, and for a whole life the line keeps it always open, so the pair shows deliberation ending task by task while never ending as a habit of living.
list_adds: It carries சூழ்ச்சி from the minister's work on one undertaking, where the couplet places it, to the making of a whole life, by setting it in a list of lifelong practices.

note: Verse 101 says reviling yields reproach; verse 104 says harsh speech yields a reviling mind.
teaches: Read together, the book places the reproach first in others' mouths and then in the speaker's own mind, so harsh speech damages the speaker twice.

note: Iniyavai 28 calls not going about crying for relief from one's distress foremost sweet; the Innaa line calls telling one's suffering to those who do not care painful. They agree from two sides, but the Innaa line narrows the fault to an uncaring listener.
teaches: The pair separates self-restraint in grief from the choice of listener: the Iniyavai praises not complaining at all, the Innaa only counts complaint to the indifferent as a pain.

note: Innaa Narpathu 35 names the sickness that infants suffer as painful; Iniyavai 12 names a child living without sickness as sweet.
teaches: The two books say the same thing from its two sides, and the pairing shows that the child's health is the first item in the sweet list but the third in the painful one, so each book ranks it by what surrounds it.

note: Kural 167 says the goddess shows the man of twisted envy (அவ்வித்து அழுக்காறு) to her elder sister; Iniyavai calls not speaking out of twisted envy foremost sweet, in the same words.
teaches: The couplet punishes envy held and the verse praises envy unspoken, so the pair shows the ethics group separating the feeling from its voicing and treating restraint of the tongue as a partial cure.
list_adds: It puts restraint of envious speech first, ahead of conquered anger and refusing to snatch, ranking a fault of the tongue above faults of temper and hand.

note: Both are Kapilar's friend speaking to the hill lord about his night visits: in 18 she asks him to come by day instead, to the kanthal grove; in 12, by its colophon after day meetings have been stopped, she refuses the night as well and demands marriage.
teaches: The two poems show the friend's options closing one by one, night refused for day and then day lost to confinement, so the only path left is marriage, the end both poems are built toward.

note: Purananuru 117 says Pari's land kept its rain even when Venus ran to the south and other evil signs appeared; Patitruppattu 13 says that in the king's guarded land Venus does not run into the burning quarter and rain stands where it is wanted.
teaches: Read together, the two show two views of the omen: the lament makes a just ruler's land immune to the bad sign, while the Chera praise has the good ruler prevent the sign itself, so royal virtue was imagined as reaching even the planets' course.

note: Naladiyar 53 says the best renounce home, youth, beauty, repute, wealth and strength on seeing they do not last; Sirupanchamoolam 23 says those who rely on form, youth, beauty, family and lineage and do not renounce young never see the unshaken state.
teaches: The quatrain gives impermanence as the reason to renounce; the verse adds a deadline, youth itself, and a second obstacle, pride of birth, so delay and lineage join transience as what keeps a man from release.
list_adds: It sets family and lineage (குடி, குலம்) in the same list as the body's goods and makes youth both an item and the time limit.

note: Kural 66 implies children's babble is sweeter than flute and lute; Iniyavai 14 calls hearing it sweeter than amrita.
teaches: The couplet measures the child's voice against the best of art, the verse against the food of the gods, so the pair shows the babble outranking both human and divine sweetness.
list_adds: It sets the babble beside the child's first steps and then beside steadiness when one's deeds come home, so the household's joys and the courage to suffer are counted together.

note: Naladiyar 56 says that even a wife without good qualities cannot be put away, and that this is why marriage is called கடி; saying 42 says a house whose wife is not excellent is no household life.
teaches: Put together, the two say that the life which the saying denies the name of household is one the man still cannot leave, so 'not a life' names a bond that persists as a hardship.
list_adds: Its list denies such a house the name of a life outright, where the quatrain keeps the marriage and counts its cost.

items: எஞ்சா விழுச்சீர் இருமுது மக்களைக் கண்டெழுதல் காலை

note: Kural 86 says the host who tends guests will be a welcome guest to the gods; Elathi 34 says the gods seek with love one who gives what fits and keeps from angry and boastful speech.
teaches: Both books put the giver's reward in the gods' welcome, and Elathi adds that restraint of speech and anger, not hospitality alone, is what the gods are drawn to.
list_adds: It sets the giving beside five restraints of speech and temper, so the gift alone does not earn the welcome.

note: The Kural reads a friend's hurtful act as folly or great intimacy; the line extends forbearance to good kin who fail to do what they should.
teaches: The pair carries the Kural's charity of interpretation from friends' acts to kinsmen's omissions, and keeps its limit: in both, the tie must first be a good one.
list_adds: It moves the couplet's rule from friendship to kin and from a wrong done to a duty left undone, and sets it beside excuses for the poor and the small.

note: Naladiyar 197 says a son props a failing father as aerial roots hold up a termite-eaten banyan; Thirikadugam says a good minister holds the people like the banyan's aerial roots.
teaches: The same image of support from below serves the family and the state: the minister is to the kingdom what a son is to an ageing father.
list_adds: It sets the root-like minister between the sceptre-fearing people and the firm guard as one of a king's three supports.

note: Naladiyar 101 pictures an old deed seeking out its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; the verse calls one's former deed one's mother.
teaches: The two images run the bond in opposite directions: in the Naladiyar the deed hunts the doer like a calf its mother, here the deed is the mother who bore the doer.
list_adds: It ends a list that redefines stranger, beloved and father, so karma takes the place of the mother in a whole remade family.

note: 58 warns two allied kings against outsiders who come between them 'seeming good, seeming kind, seeming to follow the old ways'; Kural 826 says the words of the unreconciled, though they speak good things like friends, are soon seen through.
teaches: The Kural's general warning about feigned friendship is applied in 58 to an alliance of kings, where the danger is not the enemy's attack but his pleasant counsel, so the pair shows the couplet's subject was already a matter of statecraft.

note: Verses 89 and 92 share the predicate 'born yet unborn'; 89 lists failures of grace, use of wealth and speech, 92 failures of birth, letters and speech.
teaches: Both lists include a fault of speech, but 92 adds birth and literacy where 89 has grace and wealth, so the book's 'unborn' joins conditions one chooses with a condition one cannot.

note: Innaa Narpathu 28 calls painful the gallop of a spirited horse ridden by one who has not learned; Iniyavai 8 calls sweet the strength of the spirited horse one rides.
teaches: The same spirited horse is a pleasure or a pain according to the rider's training, so the pair locates the sweetness not in the horse but in the skill that can bear its strength.

note: Kural 773 says fierceness is great valour but help to a foe in trouble is its cutting edge; Sirupanchamoolam 40 names five helpless enemies whom true soldiers never approach.
teaches: The couplet makes mercy to the fallen the edge of valour as a principle; the verse turns it into signs a soldier can read on the field, and makes the restraint the definition of a true soldier.
list_adds: It turns the couplet's one principle into five recognisable signs of surrender or helplessness.

note: Iniyavai Narpathu calls giving with knowledge of one's income sweet; Thirikadugam fixes the share at a quarter of what comes in.
teaches: Read together, the two show that 'knowing one's income' had a number attached: the income is known so that a fixed fourth can go out.

note: Kural 754 says rightly gained wealth yields both dharma and pleasure; Nanmanikkadigai gives pleasure to wealth and dharma to softened grace.
teaches: Where the Kural lets good wealth bear dharma, the quatrain assigns dharma to grace alone, which separates the two that the couplet joins.
