list_adds: It lays out a table of causes in which wealth and grace sit side by side with different fruits, so dharma is pointedly not among wealth's results.

note: Kural 410 says others are to the learned as beasts are to people; verse 19 calls the learned gods and the unlearned ghouls.
teaches: The couplet uses one step, beast to human; the verse widens the scale to god and ghoul and saves the beast for the boaster, so learning is placed on a three-step ladder of beings.
list_adds: It sets learning beside early earning and against nostalgic boasting, ranking each as god, ghoul, wretch or ox.

note: Kural 525 says one who gives and speaks sweetly is surrounded by kin layer on layer; Thirikadugam makes giving by old ties, embracing kin and gathering one's people with close words the work of the king's younger.
teaches: The couplet gives anyone the means to gather kin; the verse assigns that work in a royal house to the junior prince, so kin-keeping becomes a delegated office of state.
list_adds: It moves the kin-gathering acts into the royal household and gives them to one office, the king's younger.

note: Both sayings place learning below something else: conduct in 1, serving the learned in 8.
teaches: Within one ten learning is twice ranked second, once to conduct and once to reverence for those who have learnt, so the book never lets learning be the highest good.

note: Naladiyar 363 calls three kinds of wife weapons that kill the husband; Thirikadugam 67 counts the wife who stands against her husband with bad servants and faulty kin as old karma that devours him.
teaches: The Naladiyar blames the wife as an agent, while Thirikadugam spreads the harm across the whole household and calls it past karma with no remedy, shifting from blame to endurance.
list_adds: It widens the Naladiyar's three bad wives to wife, servants and kin, and explains them as karma ripening in old age.

note: Kural 1019 says lasting shamelessness burns every good; the verse says fortune perishes the moment shame is lost.
teaches: The verse makes the couplet's slow burning instant (போழ்தே, the very moment), so the loss of shame is shown as a sudden rather than gradual ruin.
list_adds: It puts the loss of shame first in a list of four ruins of the same form, so shame stands with water for crops as the thing whose absence ends goods at once.

note: Naladiyar 65 says the gift of one without wealth is the true fruit of giving; the Innaa line counts liberality in one who has nothing to give as painful. On the reading that the Naladiyar's giver has little and the Innaa's has nothing, they meet at a limit rather than conflict.
teaches: Together they mark where giving from want stops being the highest giving and becomes pain: the point where nothing is left to give.
list_adds: It files moneyless liberality with a stone in the chewed areca and broken patronage, as an act that breaks in the middle.

note: Kural 691 tells those who serve kings to be like men warming at a fire, neither near nor far; Thirikadugam tells the vellala family to behave toward brahmins as toward fire even when familiar.
teaches: The ethics group uses one fire image for two powers: the Kural for the king, the Thirikadugam for the brahmin, so the cultivator's caution toward a birth-group is modelled on the courtier's caution toward the throne.
list_adds: It sets the fire-caution among a farming family's marks of beauty, between refusing gambling wealth and loving the plough, so a rule of birth-rank becomes part of a household's grace.

note: Naladiyar 65 calls true patience that of a strong man able to punish; Iniyavai calls sweet the austerity of one who wants to win and does not rage.
teaches: Both place the worth of restraint where the urge to strike is live, and the pair shows the group treating anger held back in a contest as a form of penance.
list_adds: It names the restraint நோன்பு, a word of austerity, and sets it beside endurance and freedom from craving, so mastering anger is filed with ascetic practice.

note: Kural 398 says learning gained in one birth protects through seven; Nanmanikkadigai traces how learning reaches the other world step by step.
teaches: The couplet states that learning outlasts a life, and the verse supplies the stages by which it does so, ignorance lessening into insight, insight into the true path, the path into fame and the higher world.
list_adds: It turns the couplet's single benefit into a chain of four causes, so the reward beyond this life is earned through intermediate changes in the learner.

note: Kural 429 says those whose understanding guards against what is coming are not shaken by affliction; the line says one who does not know what is coming cannot guard himself.
teaches: The couplet joins knowing and guarding in one phrase and promises calm; the line pulls them apart and makes knowing the prior condition, so the pair shows that the Kural's guarding is itself a kind of knowledge, not a separate defence.
list_adds: In a ten that sets each act against the lack that makes it false, it isolates foresight as the single lack that undoes self-protection, where the couplet praises understanding in general.

note: Kural 134 says a brahmin can relearn a forgotten Veda but his birth is ruined if conduct fails; saying 1 ranks conduct above recitation for all people.
teaches: The Kural's ranking of conduct over recitation, made for the brahmin whose role is recitation, is here lifted off birth entirely and given to everyone the frame line addresses.
list_adds: It sets the ranking first in a ten of rankings and removes the brahmin, so conduct over study becomes the opening rule for all people rather than a warning to one varna.

note: Kural 160 grants greatness to those who fast but ranks them after those who bear harsh words; the verse says refusing food befits a rich man.
teaches: The Kural ranks fasting as a whole; the verse makes its worth depend on who fasts, fitting most where food is plentiful and the refusal costs something.
list_adds: It pairs each virtue with the person in whom it costs most (penance with youth, fasting with wealth, beauty with chastity), a matching of virtue to station the couplet lacks.

note: Naladiyar 303 says the worthy go before no one except those who embrace them and say 'come in, eat'; the verse says begging from one who does not know one's plight becomes enmity.
teaches: The quatrain says whom the worthy may approach and the verse says what happens if they approach the wrong one: the request turns into enmity.
list_adds: It sets this cost beside the giver's fame, the taker's name and the laughter of going before strangers, so asking is weighed by its consequences on both sides.

note: Kural 890 likens living with those not in accord to living with a snake in a hut; Innaa 13 counts a house where people like a disease live as painful.
teaches: The couplet's image is sudden danger and the Innaa's is slow sickness, so the pair shows two ways a house of the wrong people harms: the bite and the wasting.
list_adds: It sets the diseased house among the king's and courtier's pains, so a household trouble is counted beside a bell-less elephant and submission to proud kings.

note: Kural 796 says ruin is the rod that measures one's people; the line names help as the mark of a friendship that does not fail.
teaches: The Kural gives the occasion of the test and the line gives its measure, so together they say what ruin reveals: who still helps.
list_adds: It places the friendship test among tests of birth, learning and ability, so friendship is judged by the same rule of outward proof as every other claimed virtue.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 89 has nearly the same lines: sweet speech makes kin, harsh speech enmity, gentle speech grace, and grace release.
teaches: The one variant matters: Sirupanchamoolam has harsh speech make enmity (பகைமை), Nanmanikkadigai a reviling mind (வசைமனம்), which moves the damage from one's relations to one's own mind.

note: Kural 575 says kindly regard is the ornament of the eye and without it the eye is a sore; Thirikadugam opens with the same ornament and says it is found only with modesty and learning in those of worth.
teaches: The couplet judges the eye by kindly regard; the verse says that regard is not found alone but in the same people as modesty and learning, so it becomes a sign of a whole character.
list_adds: It assigns three ornaments to three wearers, the eye, a woman and the next life, and says all three gather in one kind of person.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 7 says the பார்ப்பான் is one who shares his food; verse 54 lists பார்ப்பார் first among those to be fed, beside the hungry and ascetics.
teaches: One Jain work defines the brahmin by giving food, the other names brahmins by birth as receivers of it, so the same word marks a giver's virtue in one and a recipient's rank in the other.

note: Kural 152 says bear with excess and better still forget it; verse 15 calls bearing a wrong greatness and brooding on harm smallness.
teaches: The couplet ranks forgetting above bearing; the verse names brooding as the opposite of forgetting and calls it smallness, so it supplies the failure the couplet leaves implied.
list_adds: It sets greatness and smallness as a contrasting pair and adds ending enmity as a third good, a contrast the couplet does not draw.

note: 59 makes begging the deepest disgrace; 60 makes giving to those who beg the highest distinction.
teaches: The ten scores one exchange twice, from both sides, so the asker's lowest point is the giver's highest, the same thing seen as shame and as honour.

note: Kural 913 likens the false embrace of women bought with wealth to embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room; Thirikadugam calls it seeking a base stupor (புலைமயக்கம்).
teaches: The couplet's corpse and the verse's புலை both make the bought embrace a contact with something vile, one by image, one by name.
list_adds: It sets the bought embrace in a series of three stupors with drink and dice.

note: 183 says that it is better to die than to live by backbiting, because it is a false kind of life. In 1141 backbiting is what keeps someone else alive.
teaches: The same act has a very different moral look from the side of its target.

note: Kural 230 says nothing is more bitter than death, yet even death is sweet when giving cannot be done; the line says giving to the asker's wish comes easily to those who love kindness.
teaches: The line explains from the giver's side what the couplet asserts as a ranking: for one whose heart is moist, giving is so natural that being unable to give becomes, as the Kural says, worse than dying.
list_adds: It puts the ease of giving down to a disposition (ஈரம்) and sets it in a ten of desires and their yields, so generosity appears as the fruit of a love of kindness, where the couplet only ranks giving above life.

note: The invocation's demons who lost their god's refuge are, in the story, the demons who complain to Neelakesi that the sage stopped their offerings.
teaches: The phrase 'removing refuge in the god' turns out to mean ending blood offerings, so the demons' grievance is the loss of sacrifice, the poem's first act against killing.

note: Kural 397 says every land and town becomes one's own, and asks why one stays unlearned; Nanmanikkadigai gives the belonging to the good and the renouncer, and ends with the man of wealth.
teaches: The Kural ties belonging everywhere to learning alone; the quatrain shows virtue, renunciation and plain wealth also open every town, and names the base for whom none opens.
list_adds: It splits the Kural's single case into four holders, three by virtue or vice and the last by money, and the last item ironically undoes the first.

note: Kural 148 calls it manhood not to look at another's wife; verse 41 puts another's wife last in a list of five women men avoid.
teaches: The couplet's one rule becomes a whole map of forbidden women, so the Kural's virtue of restraint is turned into a period code drawn by age, menses and vow.
list_adds: It sets another's wife among a girl, a woman past her menses, a female ascetic and an unguarded woman, so adultery becomes one case of a wider bar by bodily state and vow.

note: Kural 127 says guard the tongue whatever else goes unguarded; Thirikadugam makes restraint of the mouth only the first of three restraints, yielding purity, below restraint of deed and of heart.
teaches: The Kural puts the tongue first as the one thing to guard; the verse ranks it lowest of three, so what the Kural sets as the minimum the verse treats as the first rung toward release.
list_adds: It turns restraint into an ascending ladder, mouth, deed, heart, with a rising fruit at each rung, a ranking the couplet does not make.

note: The Kural calls nothing harder than the hardness that would end poverty by begging; the verse counts the man who would build wealth by begging among three who dare the hard.
teaches: Thirikadugam pushes the Kural's case further: begging not to escape poverty but to grow rich, and it ranks this with crossing the sea as a reckless venture.
list_adds: It sets begging-for-wealth beside trusting a roving woman and a sea voyage, so the folly is judged as a physical gamble.

note: Kural 417 says those whose listening is gathered on close study do not speak folly even when they misunderstand; Iniyavai says even those of excellent learning by listening should speak only after examining.
teaches: The couplet trusts deep listening to protect speech even through error, while the verse still asks the learned to examine first, so the pair shows the counted work refusing learning as a guarantee.
list_adds: It ranks examined speech with protecting refugees and doing one's duties even on borrowed money, so careful speech is made a duty owed to others.

note: Thirikadugam 52 calls modesty the ornament of a woman in love and learning the ornament for the next life; Nanmanikkadigai calls modesty the ornament of women's beauty and virtue the ornament for the world one goes to.
teaches: Both short works pair a woman's modesty with an ornament for the next life, so the gendered ornament and the otherworldly one are a shared pairing of the group, not one poet's choice.

note: Kural 415 says the words of the good are like a staff on slippery ground; the verse says the learned man rises if he stumbles while the fool breaks his leg.
teaches: The couplet gives the staff to the hearer as another's words; the verse puts the support inside the learned man himself, so learning is shown as the staff once it has been taken in.
list_adds: It sets the learned and the fool side by side in the same fall and then names the cause, a means made with single-minded care, which the couplet's image does not explain.

note: Patitruppattu 11 likens the Chera, who reached the sea and felled the enemy's guarded kadamba at the root (முழுமுதல் துமிய), to Murugan who cut down Sur at the root (சூருடை முழுமுதல் தடிந்த); Thirumurugatruppadai 45-60 tells the god's deed itself: he entered the cold sea and cut Sur at the root (சூர்முதல் தடிந்த), the mango at its trunk.
teaches: Thirumurugatruppadai shows that cutting the root in the sea was already the god's signature deed, so the Chera poet's repeated phrase is a claim that the king's sea raid re-enacted Murugan's myth, with the enemy's guardian tree standing in for Sur's tree.

items: கவ்வித்தாங் கொண்டுதாங் கண்டது காமுற்று வவ்வார் விடுதல்

note: Line 26 says those living under a king who keeps no justice do not openly censure him; line 81 says his land is poor.
teaches: Read together, the subjects keep silent about an unjust king but the land itself shows the injustice through its poverty, so the blame the people withhold is spoken by the country.

note: In kaathai 26 she is told to hear each school's doctrine, see it lacks truth, and only then follow the Buddha's way, and she takes an ascetic's form to do so.
teaches: The debate chapter carries out a method laid down beforehand: hearing the schools is a prescribed stage of her training, not an open inquiry.

note: Kural 256 argues that buyers cause the killing, since no one would sell flesh if none bought; Nanmanikkadigai counts buying and eating flesh as a fault in its own right.
teaches: The couplet needs an argument to make the buyer guilty, while the verse simply lists buying and killing as two faults, showing the group's code taking the Kural's conclusion as settled.
list_adds: It sets the buyer's fault beside the killer's and beside rearing beings to torment them and improper speech, so flesh-buying becomes one of four plain faults rather than the end of an argument.

note: Kural 605 calls delay, forgetting, sloth and sleep the pleasure-boat of those bound for ruin; Nanmanikkadigai says sloth stays with those who are to perish.
teaches: The two books use the same phrase for the ruined (கெடுநீரார், கெடுவார்); the quatrain sets sloth's dwelling beside a tethered elephant, so sloth is pictured as a thing that stays, not a boat that carries one off.
list_adds: It puts sloth in a row with cruelty, women's shame and a tethered elephant under one verb, staying, so vice and restraint both become things that hold a person.

note: Naladiyar 131 says beauty of hair, garment and saffron is not beauty and the beauty of learning is; Sirupanchamoolam 36 says beauty of hair, chest, nails, ears and teeth is not beauty and speech fitted to learning is.
teaches: Both deny outward beauty to praise learning, but the quatrain rests learning's beauty on fairness of heart, while the verse rests it on speech that fits the books, so one makes it inward and the other audible.
list_adds: Its list is all of the body (hair, chest, nails, ears, teeth), not adornments, and it turns on speech rather than learning itself.

note: Kural 600 says a man's உரம் is the abundance of his உள்ளம் (inner drive); Innaa 18 counts the உள்ளம் of a man who has உரன் lying idle as painful.
teaches: The Kural defines strength as drive, so the two cannot come apart; the Innaa names the case where they do, a strong man whose mind sleeps, and counts it as a pain.
list_adds: It sets the idle strong man beside the man who faces a warrior's chest, so lost strength and rash strength are counted together.

note: Kural 920 makes double-minded women, liquor and dice the company of those Fortune has abandoned; Elathi 18 lists indulgence, waste, hunting, toddy, gambling, harsh words, harsh punishment and unrestraint as what a king must guard against.
teaches: The couplet's three ruinous companions reappear inside Elathi's longer list of the king's vices, which shows the Kural's general warning taken up into a royal code where it secures the kingdom against rivals.
list_adds: It places the Kural's three vices among the seven of kingship (adding hunting, waste, harsh words and harsh punishment) and closes with unrestraint as their sum, carrying the warning into the king's domain.

note: 291 defines truthfulness as speech without harm; 200 demands use.
teaches: Harmless idle talk passes the one test and fails the other, so the two chapters set different standards for speech.

note: Innaa Narpathu calls beauty in those without means painful; Nanmanikkadigai says beauty and youth die beneath poverty.
teaches: The two books say the same thing from two sides: Innaa names the sight of beauty in want painful, Nanmanikkadigai says the beauty itself does not survive it.

note: The Kural says understanding lives as the world lives; the line applies that to the customs of an unknown country.
teaches: The pairing shows the couplet's conformity turning outward: wisdom not only follows the ways of one's own world but withholds blame from a world whose ways it does not know.
list_adds: It names the thing the couplet leaves general, ஆசாரம் of a தேசம், and so makes custom local and the judge's ignorance a reason for restraint.

note: Kural 628 says the one who does not desire pleasure and takes suffering as natural is never distressed; 97 says the one who wants pleasure does not shun pain.
teaches: Both bind pain to the pursuit of pleasure, but the couplet frees the man who stops desiring pleasure while the line binds the man who keeps desiring it, so the pair gives the two exits from the same bond.
list_adds: Placed beside its mirror in 98, the line makes pleasure and pain each the cost of the other, a symmetrical turn the couplet, which speaks of only one direction, lacks.

note: Saying 34 reckons giving without care for the receiver no better than refusing; saying 48 says giving not along aram's way is not giving.
teaches: The book judges giving twice by its manner, once by care for the receiver and once by aram's road, so a gift's worth never rests on its size in either ten.

note: Kar Narpathu 5: he left fearing the words of those who scorn. Akananuru 111: the friend says he will come back, ashamed of the mocking words of hostile men (ஏஎச்சொல் நாணி).
teaches: Taken together, other men's contempt both sends the hero away for wealth and, in the friend's argument, drives him home again, so shame works on him at both ends of the journey.

note: Kural 84 says the fair goddess dwells gladly in the house of one who tends guests with a glad face; the verse says a host of fortune comes when the bright lady looks on one.
teaches: The couplet tells what keeps the goddess in a house and the verse what her look does, so together hospitality is the cause and the goddess's glance the means by which fortune gathers.
list_adds: It ranks her glance with water for seed and wealth for desire, then adds that her grief undoes it, so fortune is shown as conditional where the couplet shows only her staying.

note: Kural 287 calls stealth a dark knowledge absent in those who love measure; the line names trickery as what shows a man to be a thief.
teaches: The Kural places theft in a kind of cunning, and the line turns that cunning into the evidence, so the thief is known by his method before any taking.
list_adds: Among signs of good birth, kindness and learning, it gives the one sign of a crime, so the ten's method of reading people from acts reaches the detection of a thief.

note: Kural 146 says enmity, sin, fear and blame never leave one who crosses into another's home; the line says grievous blame comes easily to men who lust after women, naming no other's wife.
teaches: The Kural fixes blame on a single transgression against another man's house, while the line widens it to the roving desire itself, so the pair shows blame attaching first to the trespass and then, in the maxim, already to the appetite before any trespass.
list_adds: Among the ten's desires and their easy harms, the line gives blame as the natural yield of a craving, like disease for the glutton, where the couplet lists blame as one of four penalties for a specific act.

note: Kural 908 says those who act as a woman wishes fail their friends and do no good; verse 43 sets not trusting women's words beside feeding great ascetics, both as a giver's marks.
teaches: Read together, the period rule against heeding women is tied in both works to giving: the Kural says it stops good deeds, and Elathi sets it beside the meal for ascetics it protects.
list_adds: It puts distrust of women's words among gambling, deceit and disputes, as one more distraction a giver must refuse, where the Kural's chapter treats it alone as a fault of the husband.

note: Kural 1067 begs beggars not to beg of those who conceal; Thirikadugam sends the one who without love hides from askers what he could give into hell.
teaches: The couplet speaks to the beggar and protects him from the concealer; the verse speaks of the concealer and names his punishment, so the two together cover both sides of the refused request.
list_adds: It sets concealment from askers between tormenting the unable and forgetting death, so withholding is ranked with cruelty and heedlessness as a road to hell.

note: Kural 60 calls good children the ornament of a home's excellence; verse 52 counts bearing children first among a wife's medicines that make the husband yield.
teaches: Children, an ornament of the house in the couplet, become in the verse the wife's first hold over her husband, so the same good is read for its effect within the marriage.
list_adds: It sets childbearing beside beauty, accord and restraint in food as means of holding the husband, a use of children the couplet does not name.

note: Thirikadugam 96 names the wife who knows her husband's hint as one at whose word rain falls; saying 41 denies the name of spouse to one who does not act knowing the other's nature.
teaches: The same virtue, knowing the partner's nature, is a power over the rains in one work and the bare minimum of being a spouse in the other, so it is both the ceiling and the floor of marriage.

note: Both have the waiting girl say her pallor is like the peerkku flower (பீர்) and her bewilderment like Aathi Manthi's (பேதுற்று), alongside a siege simile for her state.
teaches: The repetition of three linked images in two poems by different poets shows that pallor, Aathi Manthi and a besieged town formed a ready set for the abandoned girl's lament.

note: Kural 226 says relieving the hunger of the destitute is where the wealthy should store their wealth; Elathi 80 says those who feed outcastes, the wounded, the blind, the immobile, the fallen and the eminent in need will live as kings.
teaches: The couplet calls feeding a store of wealth, and the verse names the stored return (living as kings) and widens the hungry to include the outcaste, so the gift crosses lines of birth the couplet does not mention.
list_adds: It names the hungry one by one and puts the outcaste first, so feeding is extended across rank as well as need.

note: Kural 46 asks what one gains by leaving a household run in dharma; Iniyavai 2 agrees while the household goes well but makes renunciation the highest sweetness when it does not prosper.
teaches: Read together, the couplet's rhetorical question turns out to carry a condition: household life wins only while it succeeds, and the verse names the failure that opens the outer path.
list_adds: It orders household and renunciation as first and highest under a stated condition, a ranking with a hinge the couplet's question does not supply.

note: Kural 343, in the chapter on renunciation, says the field of the five senses must be crushed and all desires let go at once; Iniyavai calls curbing the craving of the five senses foremost sweet, with no renouncer named.
teaches: The pair shows sense-restraint moving from the renouncer's whole programme in the Kural to a first pleasure open to anyone, its demand softened from abandoning to curbing.
list_adds: It ranks sense-restraint first and pairs it with keeping away from the unlearned and the unsteady, so the inner gate and the outer company are guarded together.

note: Kural 559 says that when the king bends justice the sky bends and withholds rain; the line says the land of a king without justice is poor.
teaches: The couplet gives a mechanism, the failed rain, and the line gives only the result, a poor land, so together they show the period's chain from royal injustice through the weather to the country's want.
list_adds: It sets the unjust king's land first in a ten of things that fail for lack of their ground, so misrule becomes the type of all such emptiness rather than a cosmic exception.

note: Kural 423 says understanding is seeing the true substance of whatever is heard from whomever; the verse says the meanings of the many books are things to be examined.
teaches: The couplet gives the test for any utterance, and the verse applies it to the many books themselves, so even the written tradition must be sifted, not merely received.
list_adds: It puts sifting the books last in a sequence of right responses (deride contempt, ponder counsel, join dharma), so examination is the final act of a learner's conduct.

note: Kural 72 says the loving belong to others even to their bones; Elathi 68 names dying for the beloved first among six marks of love.
teaches: The couplet states love's self-surrender as a claim about ownership, and the verse spells out what that surrender does in practice, from giving life and wealth down to grieving at a parting.
list_adds: It ranks love's marks from the gift of life down to feeling at union and parting, so the bones of 72 head a list that also counts speech and grief as love.

note: Kural 213 says nothing here or in the gods' world is as good as ஒப்புரவு; the line says nothing is a more fitting acquisition than knowing it.
teaches: The couplet ranks the duty itself above all goods; the line ranks the knowledge of the duty, so that merely learning what one owes the world already counts as the best thing one can gain.
list_adds: Placed in a ten of gains, losses and disgraces, the line turns ஒப்புரவு from a good done for others into an acquisition of the doer's own, set beside children and fame as things one gets.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 68 says long bathing at a ghat does not remove the blemish; Elathi 13 counts not bathing (ஆடாமை, on our reading) among the six marks of ascetics.
teaches: On this reading the two Jain lists move from denying bathing any cleansing power to making its refusal a mark of the renunciant, the reverse of the bathing rules of the Acharakkovai.

note: Kural 1134 has the lover say the flood of desire carries off the raft of shame and manliness; Thirikadugam names letting go the great raft of chastity out of desire as an enmity that brings fault.
teaches: Both make a virtue the raft that desire tears away, but the love couplet voices it as a lover's helpless loss while the ethics verse judges the same release as a culpable fault.
list_adds: It sets the abandoned raft of chastity beside a loosened bond of love and friendship's lost grace, so the release becomes one of three broken bonds that turn into enmity.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 69 says the one who consented, the buyer, the cook and the eater share the killer's sin; Thirikadugam mocks one who says the deed is done without his consent.
teaches: Both answer the disclaimer by spreading guilt along the chain: Sirupanchamoolam lists the chain, Thirikadugam ridicules the man who denies his link in it.

note: Kural 226 says relieving the hunger of the destitute (அற்றார்) is where one should store wealth; Elathi 9 says giving food, shelter and clothing to the destitute (அற்றார்கட்கு) makes one live as a learned man.
teaches: The couplet makes the gift a bank for wealth and Elathi makes it a source of wisdom, so the same act toward the destitute is repaid in two different coins.
list_adds: It widens the gift from food to food, shelter and clothing and adds giving without regard to the receiver's learning or kinship, which 226 does not mention.

note: Kural 596 says whatever one thinks, think of rising; Iniyavai calls sweet the zeal born of thinking of rising, using the couplet's own word உயர்வுள்ளி.
teaches: The verse borrows the couplet's phrase and names what the thought produces, zeal, so the pair shows aspiration as the root and ஊக்கம் as its fruit.
list_adds: It brackets the thought of rising between leaving the base and not scorning the lowly, so aspiration is hedged on both sides by conduct toward others.

note: Iniyavai 22 calls giving with knowledge of one's income sweet; Innaa 36 calls longing to be liberal without wealth painful. The same rule seen from two sides: giving should match means.
teaches: Together the two books set a measure on liberality, the sweet side naming the rule and the painful side the cost of breaking it.

note: Verse 15 says the man who lives by lies is not to be befriended; verse 83 says a lie dissolves friendship's thriving shoot as water dissolves salt.
teaches: One verse keeps the liar out of friendship at the start and the other shows a lie undoing friendship already grown, so the book makes falsehood fatal to friendship at both ends.

note: Iniyavai Narpathu 30 names as sweet the three virtues whose breach Thirikadugam 62 counts: weighing a kindness, no crooked word in the assembly, not seizing a deposit.
teaches: The two books count the same three acts of trust from both sides, sweetness for keeping them and loss of heirs for breaking them, so the triad was a fixed set in the period's teaching.

note: 30 names six kinds of legal son and 31 names the remaining six.
teaches: Only read together do the two verses give the twelve kinds of son of the law-books, showing the work importing a Sanskrit legal classification whole into Tamil verse.

note: Lines 18 and 19 share one frame: a lapse in one place reveals lapses elsewhere, first in speech and then in understanding.
teaches: The repeated frame shows the ten holding that faults do not stay single: one visible slip is read as the index of hidden ones.

note: Acharakkovai 6 lists the dog among things a person in எச்சில் does not look at; Innaa 2 counts a fowl and a dog entering a brahmin's house as painful.
teaches: Read together, the two show the dog as a standing source of pollution in the period's code, kept from the eye of the impure person in one book and from the threshold of the brahmin house in the other.

note: Kural 391 says to learn faultlessly what should be learned and stand by it; Iniyavai calls the firm core of learning what has worth, faultlessly and over many days, the sweetest thing.
teaches: The verse adds duration and names the result காழ், a hard core, so the pair shows flawless learning as something that hardens over time.
list_adds: It closes the book on learning after staying in one's town at a cost and not eating the seed-grain, so learning is grouped with the household's ways of keeping what feeds the future.

note: Both verses name learning the good after surveying many things and set it beside giving from the household's income.
teaches: The book twice pairs selective learning with measured household giving, so the pairing is a doctrine of the work and not a chance of one list.

note: Kural 892 says neglecting the great brings ills through them; the Innaa verse counts doing evil to the great as painful and opens with letting go of a bond with them.
teaches: Together they show neglect and injury of the great as stages of one fault, the Innaa list naming the first step, loosening the bond, that the Kural leaves implicit.
list_adds: Its first and last items both concern the great, so harming them is shown as the end of a course that begins with letting go of them.
